Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 23, verse 1:

﴿Truly the believers have attained success.﴾

Page 8

This is a marvelous opening, for it is among the comprehensive utterances (jawami' al-kalim), since success (al-falah) is the goal of everyone who strives toward his work. The announcement of the success of the believers without mentioning any object of the verb "attained success" implies, in this rhetorical context, the generalization of that by which the sought success is achieved. It is as if it were said: "The believers have attained success in everything they desired."

Since the aspiration of the believers is directed toward the firm establishment of faith and righteous deeds within their souls, this is an announcement that they have succeeded in what their aspirations were set upon, of the good of the Hereafter and, to the extent of truth, of the good of this world. It also contains good news of God's pleasure with them and a promise that God will complete for them whatever good they seek.

This report is emphasized by the particle (qad), which, when it enters upon the past-tense verb, conveys confirmation (tahqiq), i.e., emphasis. The particle (qad) in a verbal sentence has the same effect as (inna and the lam) in a nominal sentence; that is, it conveys strong emphasis.

The reason for the emphasis here is that the believers had been hoping for such good news in what preceded for them, the hope of their success, as in His saying: ﴿And do good, that you may succeed﴾ [al-Hajj: 77]. They did not know with certainty that they had done what pleased their Lord, and they feared that they might have fallen short in its causes and in what His promise was conditioned upon. Much less did they know that this was near. So when they were told that what they hoped for had already occurred, it was confirmed for them by the particle of confirmation and by the past-tense verb used to mean certainty. Thus the use of the particle of confirmation serves to treat their longing for it, due to their intense desire and anticipation, as if it were a doubt about its occurrence. Perhaps from this is: "The prayer has been established" (qad qamat al-salah), indicating the desire of worshippers for the arrival of the time of prayer. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Give us rest through it, O Bilal." The nature of the believers is to yearn for their worship, as is observed in the great yearning of many for the night prayers of Ramadan.

The omission of the object of the verb is to indicate that they attained success in a complete way.

Al-falah: attaining the sought result of the worker's deed. It has been discussed at the beginning of al-Baqarah. Success is attached to the description of faith to indicate that it is the greatest cause of success, for faith is a description that comprises perfection, since all perfections branch out from it.

[Page 9]

﴿Those who are humble in their prayer﴾. The description of the believers (*al-Mu'minun*) is given in definite form, through the relative pronoun (*al-mawsul*, the relative construction), and is repeated to indicate the reason for their success and its cause. That is, each of these qualities is one of the causes of their success. This implies that each of these qualities is a cause of success, because he did not intend that the cause of their success is the totality of the qualities listed here. Success is not complete except with other qualities that belong to *taqwa* (God-consciousness). But since each of these qualities indicates the firm establishment of faith in its possessor, each is considered a cause of success, just as their opposites were in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿What has brought you into Saqar?﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 42] ﴿They will say, "We were not of those who prayed"﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 43] ﴿"Nor did we feed the poor"﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 44] ﴿"And we used to enter into vain discourse with those who engaged in it"﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 45] ﴿"And we used to deny the Day of Recompense"﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 46]. Moreover, mentioning a number of things does not require limiting the purpose stated to them.

*Khushu'* (humility, reverence) has been discussed in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, it is difficult except for the humble﴾ [al-Baqarah: 45] in Surat al-Baqarah, and in His saying: ﴿And they used to be humble before Us﴾ [al-Anbiya: 90] in Surat al-Anbiya. It is a fear that necessitates glorifying the one feared. There is no doubt that *khushu'*, that is, humility before God, requires *taqwa*, so it is a cause of success.

Restricting it here to being "in their prayer" is intended to combine their description with performing the prayer and with humility, especially when it occurs during the prayer. This is because humility before God occurs both during prayer and outside it, since humility's seat is the heart. It is not one of the actions of the prayer, but the one praying is clothed with it during his prayer. It is mentioned together with the prayer because the prayer is the most fitting of states to arouse humility and strengthen it, and for this reason it was placed first. Also, because it is more closely connected to the prayer: the prayer is humility and submission to God, exalted is He. Also, because humility is for God, exalted is He, the most appropriate state for it is the state of prayer, since the one praying is communing with his Lord, so he makes himself aware that he stands before his Lord, and thus he is humble before Him.

This is among the etiquettes of dealing with the Creator, exalted is He, and it is the head of the legal etiquettes and the source of all goods.

[Page 10]

For this consideration, this description was placed before the rest of the believers' attributes and made to follow faith, so praise of them is attained through two attributes.

The placing of ﴿in their prayer﴾ before ﴿humble﴾ is for emphasis on the prayer, to announce that they have a strong attachment to the prayer, because the function of the construct (*idafa*, the annexation construction) is to indicate the intensity of the connection between the annexed and the annexing term, since it carries the meaning of the lam of specification (*lam al-ikhtisas*). If it were said, "Those who, when they pray, are humble," this meaning would be lost. Also, their description as being humble could not be achieved except through another word such as "they were humble." And if it were not so, what the nominal sentence (*al-jumla al-ismiyya*) indicates of the stability and permanence of humility for them would be lost, that is, that humility is a disposition for them. This differs from "those who were humble," so brevity is achieved, and inimitability is not lost.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 23, verse 3:

﴿And those who turn away from idle talk.﴾ The conjunction here is of attributes (ʿatf al-ṣifāt) applied to one subject, as in the verse of one of the poets, which is among the witnesses cited by the grammarians (al-nahw):

To the king, the lord of mighty men, and the son of the Hamm,
and the lion of the battalion in the crowd.

The repetition of the attributes serves to strengthen the praise of them.

The discussion concerning the construction of the clause ﴿they turn away from idle talk﴾ is like the discussion concerning ﴿they are humbly submissive in their prayer﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 2], and likewise the fronting of (ʿan al-laghw) before its complement.

The repetition of the relative pronoun (ism al-mawṣūl), rather than suffice with conjoining one relative clause to another, serves to indicate that each of the attributes is by itself a cause for success (al-falah), so that it is not supposed that they would not succeed unless they combined all the meanings of prayer together. It also serves, through the use of the apparent noun in place of the pronoun, to increase the confirmation of the report in the mind of the hearer.

Al-laghw: vain, false speech. It has been mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah will not hold you to account for the idle oaths in your oaths﴾ [al-Baqarah: 225] in al-Baqarah, and in His saying: ﴿They will not hear therein any idle talk﴾ [Maryam: 62] in Surat Maryam.

Page 11
Al-iʿrāḍ (turning away): avoidance, i.e., not giving attention to a thing, from al-ʿurḍ (with the ʿayn vowelled with a ḍammah), which is the side, because one who leaves a thing turns his side to it and does not face it. Thus turning away includes turning away of the hearing from idle talk. It has been mentioned at His saying: ﴿So turn away from them and admonish them﴾ [al-Nisa': 63] in Surat al-Nisa', and at His saying: ﴿And when you see those who engage in vain discourse concerning Our verses, turn away from them﴾ [al-An'am: 68] in Surat al-An'am. Most important of it is turning away from the idle talk of the polytheists when the Qur'an is recited: ﴿And those who disbelieve say: "Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it, that you may overcome.﴾ [Fussilat: 26] And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And when they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity﴾ [al-Furqan: 72]. It also includes turning away from idle talk with the tongues, i.e., that they do not engage in vain speech in their conversation.

He followed the mention of humble submission with the mention of turning away from idle talk, because prayer in its origin is supplication, which is among the good sayings, so idle talk came to mind when prayer was mentioned, by way of opposition. Thus turning away from idle talk in both senses is among what prayer and humble submission require, for whoever is accustomed to good speech avoids false speech, and whoever is accustomed to humble submission to Allah avoids speech of falsehood. In the hadith: "Indeed a servant may speak a word of Allah's pleasure, paying no attention to it, and Allah raises him by it in degrees; and indeed a servant may speak a word of Allah's anger, paying no attention to it, and it casts him into Hell."

Turning away from the category of idle talk is among the character of seriousness (al-jidd), and whoever adorns himself with seriousness in his affairs, his soul is perfected and nothing proceeds from him except beneficial deeds. So seriousness in matters is among the character of Islam, as Abu Khirash al-Hudhali made clear in mentioning Islam:

"The youth has become like the elder, saying nothing
except what is just, so the blamers have rested."

Turning away from it necessarily requires avoiding the speech of idle talk, and requires avoiding the gatherings of its people.

Know that this is a great etiquette among the etiquettes of dealing with some people, namely the class that is not esteemed, for the people of idle talk are not of a rank deserving respect; so turning away from their idle talk is a safeguard against lowering oneself by associating with them.

[Page 12]

﴿And those who are active in paying zakah﴾. The original meaning of zakah (obligatory almsgiving, lit. "purification") is the verbal noun of zakka (purify) in its intensive form, meaning that one purifies the self from blameworthy qualities. It was then used figuratively for spending wealth for the sake of God, because the purpose of that wealth is the purification of the self, or because it increases the wealth of the giver. Thus the name of the cause was applied to the effect.

Its origin is the words of the Exalted: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them and cause them to grow﴾ [al-Tawbah: 103]. It was applied to the wealth spent itself by using the verbal noun for the object, since it is produced by it. This is the meaning specified here, by the indication of its being connected to (fa'ilun, "doers"), which requires that zakah be the object. As for the verbal noun in its own right, it cannot be an object of a verb derived from the root (f-'-l), because forming a verb from the root of that verbal noun makes unnecessary the use of a vague verb with its verbal noun in the accusative as its object. So if someone said, "I did a walking (fa'altu mashyan)" meaning "I walked," it would depart from the structure of Arabic, even if it conveyed meaning. But if someone said, "I did what you want (fa'altu mimma turiduhu)," the structure would be correct. God the Exalted said: ﴿Who did this to our gods?﴾ [al-Anbiya': 59], meaning: this which is witnessed of breaking and smashing, that is, this which resulted from the verbal noun. The intended meaning is not the verbal noun, because it cannot be pointed to, especially after the disappearance of its doer.

The verb intended here is the verb appropriate to this object, which is giving (al-iytha'). It is like His saying: ﴿and who give zakah﴾, so there is no need to estimate "performing zakah."

The more general term, (fa'ilun), was chosen here because the root (f-'-l) is famous for doing good. From it the form fa'al (with an open fa') is derived. Muhammad ibn Bashir al-Kharijī said:

If you spend wealth, or are burdened with its efforts, it will weigh upon you, and you will do beyond what has been done.

On this understanding came what is attributed to Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt:

Those who feed the food in the year of drought, and those who are active for the zakawat.

He recited it in al-Kashshaf. However, I have some doubt about the correctness of its attribution, because I think the use of zakah to mean wealth given for the sake of God is found only in the terminology of the Qur'an.

[Page 13]

So perhaps the verse is one of the poems falsely attributed to poets. Ibn Qutayba said in Kitab al-Shi'r wa al-Shu'ara': "Our scholars do not regard the poetry of Umayya as proof for the Book."

The lam in this case is the lam of reinforcement, because the governing word is weak by being derivative and by being placed after its object.

Abu Muslim and al-Raghib said: the lam is for causation, and they took zakah to mean the purification of the self. The meaning of (fa'ilun) is "doers of good deeds," and the object of (fa'ilun) was omitted, being indicated by its cause.

In al-Kashshaf, zakah here is a verbal noun meaning the act of the one who purifies, that is, giving zakah. This is what suits being connected to (fa'ilun), because every verbal noun can be expressed by the root fa'ala. Thus one says of the one who strikes, "doer of striking," and of the killer, "doer of killing." He attempted by this to establish an interpretation of the verse, so the side of verbal/lexical craft prevailed over the side of meaning. He also permitted the other possibility on condition of estimating a qualifying noun, but neither of these two considerations is binding.

He follows the mention of prayer with the mention of zakah because of the frequent pairing of the two in the verses of the Qur'an. He separated them here by turning away from idle talk, for the reason you have just heard.

This is among the etiquettes of dealing with the class of the needy, and it returns to the etiquettes of managing wealth. The discussion of repeating the relative pronoun and fronting the object is as was mentioned just before.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 23, verse 5–7:

﴿And those who guard their private parts,﴾ ﴿except from their wives or what their right hands possess, for then they are not blameworthy,﴾ ﴿but whoever seeks beyond that, it is those who are the transgressors.﴾

Al-hifz (الحِفْظ) is preservation and restraint. The guarding of the private part is well known, i.e., from intercourse. The exception in His saying "except from their wives..." etc. is an exception from the general scope of the objects of guarding that are indicated by the particle (عَلى, 'alā, "from/over"). That is, they guard them against everything they are to be guarded against, except the object that is their wives or what their right hands possess. So (حافِظُونَ, ḥāfiẓūn, "guarding") is construed to carry the sense of withholding/not giving up, as one says: "Keep the reins of my horse for me (iḥfaẓ ʿalayya ʿanān faraslī)," just as one says: "Hold on to me (amsik ʿalayya)," as in the verse ﴿Keep your wife for yourself (amsik ʿalayka zawjaka)﴾ [al-Ahzab: 37]. The meaning is the permissibility of these two categories from among the rest of the categories of women. This is a general statement (mujmal) whose details are clarified by the detailed rulings on the number of wives, what is lawful of them individually or in combination, and the details of circumstances, such as the state of lawful enjoyment or the state of the waiting period ('iddah). All of that is known to those addressed. Likewise regarding female slaves.

Referring to female slaves by the relative pronoun (مَا, "what") — which is mostly used for non-rational beings — goes against the usual practice, but it is a common usage that requires no interpretation.

His saying ﴿for then they are not blameworthy﴾ is an explicit statement of something beyond the ruling of the implied meaning of the exception, because the exception only indicates that not guarding against wives and owned slaves does not prevent success; so it is intended to add clarification that it also does not entail legal blame. Thus this indicates by implication that not guarding against anyone other than them entails legal blame, so that believers may beware of it.

The fa' (ف) in His saying (﴿فَإنَّهم غَيْرُ مَلُومِينَ﴾, "for then they are not blameworthy") is a consequence (تَفْرِيع) of the explicit statement upon the implied meaning of the exception, which is in the sense of a condition. Hence it resembles the consequence following the answer of a condition, so it was read with the fa' to affirm the conditionality.

This warning is further confirmed by following it with ﴿but whoever seeks beyond that, it is those who are the transgressors﴾, because the impulse of desire for the private part overpowering its guardian is a natural instinct, and it is feared that it may overcome the one who guards it. So the demonstrative "that" refers to what was mentioned in His saying ﴿except from their wives or what their right hands possess﴾, i.e., beyond the wives and the owned slaves, meaning other than those two categories.

The guarding of the private part is mentioned here as a continuation of turning away from idle talk, because turning away from idle talk includes, a fortiori, abandoning idle talk, as was mentioned just before; for the slip of the righteous may come from the uncontrolled use of one of these two organs due to the desire for their use that is placed in human nature. Therefore the Shari'ah regulated their use so that it is in righteous matters to which religion guides. In the hadith: "Whoever guarantees for me what is between his jaws and what is between his legs, I guarantee Paradise for him."

Blame (al-lawm, اللَّوْم) is reproach directed at another for an act or speech that is not fitting in the view of the one who is reasonable, and it is synonymous with 'adhl (reproach) and weaker than ta'nif (harsh censure).

(وراءَ, "beyond") is in the accusative as the object. The original meaning of wara' is a noun of place in the direction of the back, and it is applied to a thing that goes beyond a defined limit, by likening the one who exceeds the thing to something placed behind the back of that thing; because what a person values is placed before him and in his sight, whereas what is not so is cast behind the back. This imagery became so common in this usage that one says: "He is beyond the limit," even if he is facing it. Then it was extended to mean (غَيْرَ, "other than") or (ما عَدا, "except"), as here, i.e., whoever seeks with their private parts something other than wives and what their right hands possess.

The demonstrative (فَأُولَئِكَ هُمُ العادُونَ, "it is those who are the transgressors") was used to increase the distinction of those who have this blameworthy trait, so that their description as transgressors would be well known and established, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those are the righteous (ulā'ika humu al-muttaqun)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177] in Surah al-Baqarah. Al-'adi is the one who transgresses, i.e., the wrongdoer, because he has trespassed upon the command.

The placement of the pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl, هُمُ) is to strengthen the ruling, i.e., they are the ones who reach the utmost extent of transgression against the legal limits.

The discussion regarding the repetition of the relative pronoun and the fronting of the object is as previously discussed.

Al-'adi is the one who transgresses, i.e., the wrongdoer, because he has trespassed upon the command.

The placement of the pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl, هُمُ) is to strengthen the ruling, i.e., they are the ones who reach the utmost extent of transgression against the legal limits.

The discussion regarding the repetition of the relative pronoun and the fronting of the object is as previously discussed.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 23, verse 8:

﴿And those who are, for their trusts and their covenant, keepers.﴾ This is another of the noble attributes of the believers, which resolves into two virtues: the virtue of discharging the trust (amanah) that they are entrusted with, and the virtue of fulfilling the covenant (ʿahd).

Page 16
A trust is generally among the precious things whose owner fears for them to be lost, so he places them with one whom he thinks will guard them. Usually this takes place in private between the entrusting party and the trustee. Because of their preciousness, the trust may tempt the trustee not to return it and to deny to its owner that he has it. And because depositing it is usually free of witnesses, the love of it moves the trustee to hold on to it and not return it. Therefore God made returning it among the branches of faith.

It has come in a hadith from Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, who said: "The Messenger of God ﷺ told us that the trust descended into the root of men's hearts, then they learned from the Qur'an, then they learned from the Sunnah." And he told us about its removal, saying: "A man sleeps a sleep, and the trust is taken from his heart, and its trace remains like the trace of a mark (wakt), then he sleeps another sleep and it is taken, and its trace remains like a blister (majl), like a live coal you roll over your foot, so it blisters, and you see it swollen while there is nothing in it. People then begin to trade with one another, but hardly anyone discharges the trust. It is said: 'There is a trustworthy man among the family of so-and-so.' And it is said of a man: 'How intelligent he is, how witty he is, how strong he is,' while there is not in his heart the weight of a mustard seed of faith." Ended.

Al-wakt: a blackness that appears on the skin of a date. Al-majl: a swelling in thin skin, resembling the skin of a grape, arising from contact with fire or from much work with the hand. As for his saying, "the weight of a mustard seed of faith": it is a verbal noun from amanahu (to trust him), meaning: there is not in the depths of his soul the people's trust in him, so none trusts him except one who is deceived.

The discussion of the trust has already preceded in God's saying: ﴿Indeed, God commands you to render trusts to their owners﴾ [al-Nisa': 58] in Surat al-Nisa'.

He put "trusts" (al-amanat) in the plural, in consideration of the multiplicity of its kinds and the multiplicity of those who uphold it, as an explicit indication of generality.

Al-Jumhur read "li-amanatihim" in the plural form, while Ibn Kathir read "li-amanatihim" in the singular, considering it as a verbal noun, like ﴿those who are in their prayer humble﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 2].

Page 17
Al-ʿahd: a binding commitment between two or more parties to something by which each side deals with the other. It is called ʿahd because they swear by the covenant of God, that is, that God is a witness over them both in that matter, not escaping the accountability for failing it. It was mentioned earlier at His saying: ﴿Those who break the covenant of God after its confirmation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 27] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Fulfilling the covenant is among the greatest of noble characters, since it indicates nobility of soul and strength of resolve. For two parties may each bind themselves to the other to a great deed, and it may happen that the duty of fulfilling that commitment falls on one of them, so it becomes hard for him to undertake an act for the benefit of another without a return that benefits himself. His soul then tempts him to renege on the covenant out of stinginess or weakness of resolve. Therefore fulfilling the covenant was a sign of greatness of soul. God says: ﴿And fulfil the covenant; indeed, the covenant will be questioned about﴾ [al-Isra': 34].

Al-ra'y: watching over a thing by guarding it from perishing and by correcting what is corrupt in it. From it comes the herding of livestock (ra'y al-mashiyah), and from it the care of people (ra'y al-nas). From it the term al-muraʿah is used for what the one of good character deserves of good treatment. The one who performs the ra'y is ra'in (a keeper).

So guarding the trust (ra'y al-amanah) means preserving it. Since preservation is intended for the sake of its owner, returning it to him is better than keeping it.

Guarding the covenant (ra'y al-ʿahd) is a metaphor, meaning observing it on every occasion.

The discussion of the placement of ﴿li-amanatihim wa-ʿahdihim﴾ before "ra'un" is like the discussion of its similar earlier instances, and likewise the repetition of the relative pronoun.

The combination of guarding the trusts and guarding the covenant is because the covenant is like a trust: the one who made a covenant with you has entrusted you to fulfil what that covenant requires.

He mentioned them both right after the giving of zakat, because zakat is God's trust with those whom He has favoured with wealth. For this reason it was called: the right of God, the right of wealth, and the right of the needy.

[p. 18]

A praise of the believers for their preservation of the prayers (al-muhafazah 'ala al-salawat), that is, by not neglecting them or neglecting some of them. The form *al-muhafazah* is used for intensifying preservation, since the *mufa'alah* (the verbal form with the infix of mutual action) here is not literal, as in His saying: ﴿Preserve the prayers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 238]. The meaning of *hifz* (preservation) was mentioned shortly before.

The word *al-salawat* is used in the plural to indicate the preservation of all of its times and units, as an explicit statement of generality.

This was mentioned together with what preceded it, His saying: ﴿who are attentive in their prayer﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 2], because the mention of prayer there came as a complement to humility (khushu'). So it was intended to conclude the attributes of their praise with the attribute of their preservation of the prayers, so that this trait would be firmly fixed in the mind, since it is the last of these attributes to strike the hearing.

Through this, the mention of prayer was repeated as an emphasis upon it, and as *radd al-'ajuz 'ala al-sadr* (the return of the final part of a phrase to its beginning, a rhetorical embellishment), beautifying the speech in which these attributes were mentioned, so that the soul would be more receptive to hearing them and comprehending them, and would thus follow their example.

What is said regarding the repetition of the relative pronoun, the fronting of the object, and the attribution of the prayers to their pronoun is similar to what is said regarding its counterparts and their parallels.

The majority read *'ala salawatihim* in the plural form, while Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read *'ala salatihim* in the singular.

This verse has gathered the foundations of legal piety (al-taqwa al-shar'iyyah), because it addresses the most difficult things to which the soul is trained, of the actions of the heart and of the limbs.

It began with the description of faith, which is the foundation of piety, according to His saying: ﴿Then he became of those who believed﴾ [al-Balad: 17], and His saying: ﴿As for those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a level plain, which the thirsty one thinks to be water, until, when he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing﴾ [al-Nur: 39].

Then the prayer was mentioned, and it is the pillar of piety, and it is what forbids indecency and wrongdoing, because of the constant recollection of standing before Allah and conversing with Him.

[p. 19]

It also mentioned humility (khushu'), which is the completion of obedience, because a person may perform an act of obedience merely to discharge the obligation, without being mindful of humility before his Lord who assigned him the righteous deeds. When the believer adopts humility as a character trait, his watchfulness over his Lord intensifies, so he complies and refrains. These two are actions of the heart.

It mentioned turning away from idle talk (al-laghw), and idle talk is a bad moral conduct related to the tongue, which is difficult to restrain. When the believer adopts turning away from idle talk as a trait, it becomes easy for him to do what is less than that. Turning away from idle talk is also a discipline for the hearing, as you know.

It mentioned giving charity, and in it is a countering of the disease of miserliness: ﴿And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his own soul, those are the successful﴾ [al-Hashr: 9].

It mentioned the preservation of chastity (hifz al-farj). In this is the trait of resisting the constant pull of natural desire, by moderating and controlling it, and elevating oneself from its lowly level of resemblance to animals. Whoever adopts this has made the restraint of desire a faculty (malakah) and a character trait for himself.

It mentioned the fulfilment of trusts (ada' al-amanah), which is a manifestation of justice and of giving the rightful owner his right, and of overcoming the soul's desire for the goods of this world.

It mentioned the fulfilment of covenants (al-wafa' bi'l-'ahd), which is a manifestation of the trait of justice in dealings and of holding oneself to fairness, by giving one's brother what one loves for oneself of faithfulness.

It mentioned the preservation of the prayers (al-muhafazah 'ala al-salawat), which is the cultivation of care and the observance of the limits and the appointed times. This makes the orderliness of the affairs of both lives a firm faculty and character trait.

If you reflect upon these qualities, you will find that they return to the preservation of what the souls tend to neglect, such as the prayer, humility, abandoning idle talk, guarding chastity, and keeping covenants, and to the giving of what the souls tend to withhold, such as charity and the fulfilment of trusts.

Thus, in the totality of this there is the practice of the two faculties of doing and refraining in important matters, and these two are the source of virtuous morals for whoever pursues them.

[p. 20]

Al-Nasa'i narrated: "It was said to 'A'ishah: 'What was the character (khuluq) of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)?' She said: 'His character was the Qur'an.'" And she recited: ﴿Certainly the believers have succeeded﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1] until she reached His saying: ﴿and who are attentive to their prayers﴾.

The character of the people of pre-Islamic ignorance (ahl al-jahiliyyah) was the opposite of this, except for the keeping of covenants, generally. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Their prayer at the House was nothing but whistling and clapping﴾ [al-Anfal: 35]. And concerning the believers in their dealings with the disbelievers, He said: ﴿And when they hear idle talk, they turn away from it and say: "For us are our deeds and for you are your deeds; peace be upon you; we do not seek the ignorant"﴾ [al-Qasas: 55]. And He said: ﴿And woe to the polytheists who do not give zakah﴾ [Fussilat: 6]. And indeed, prostitution (al-bighda') and fornication (al-zina) were widespread in the pre-Islamic era.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 23, verses 10–11:

﴿Those are the inheritors,﴾ ﴿who will inherit the Paradise (al-Firdaws); therein they will abide forever.﴾

The demonstrative (ism al-ishara) was brought for them after the preceding attributes had been applied to them, so that the demonstrative indicates that their worthiness for what will be mentioned after the demonstrative resulted from their being characterized by those attributes. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5] after His saying: ﴿Guidance for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2] to the end of it, in Surat al-Baqarah. The meaning is: Those are the ones most deserving to be the inheritors of that.

The insertion of the pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl) serves to strengthen the predication about them. The object of (al-warithun) is omitted so that an ambiguity and generality arise, and the listener awaits its explanation; it is then explained by His saying: ﴿who will inherit the Paradise﴾, with the intention of magnifying this inheritance. The use, in the explanation, of the relative pronoun (ism al-mawsul), whose nature is that its meaning through its relative clause is known to the listener, is an indication that the definiteness of (al-warithun) is the definiteness of prior reference (ta'rif al-ahd), as if it were said: They are the people of this known attribute, known by it.

The word "inheritance" (al-wirath) is used metaphorically for established entitlement, because inheritance is the strongest cause for entitlement to property. He, exalted is He, says: ﴿And that is the Paradise which you have been made to inherit, because of what you used to do﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 72].

Page 21
Al-Firdaws is a name of Paradise in the terminology of the Qur'an, or one of the names of the most noble regions of the gardens. The root meaning of al-firdaws is a wide orchard comprising all kinds of fruit. In a hadith, the Prophet (ﷺ) said to the mother of Haritha ibn Suraqa, when an arrow of unknown origin struck him on the day of Badr and killed him, and his mother said: "If he is in Paradise, I will be patient and seek reward (from Allah)." He said to her: "Woe to you! Have you lost your senses? Is there only one Paradise? Indeed there are many gardens, and he is in al-Firdaws."

And regarding the virtue of these verses, it has been narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Ten verses have been revealed to me; whoever observes them will enter Paradise," then he recited ﴿Successful indeed are the believers﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1] until he finished ten verses. Ibn al-'Arabi said in al-'ARIDAH: His saying (﴿Who will inherit the Paradise﴾) is the tenth. Narrated by al-Tirmidhi, who authenticated it.

[Page 21]

﴿And We certainly created man from an extract of clay﴾ ﴿then We made him a drop [of semen] in a firm place﴾ ﴿then We made the drop a clinging clot, then We made the clot a lump of flesh, then We made the lump bones, then We clothed the bones with flesh; then We brought him forth as another creation. So blessed is Allah, the best of creators﴾. The waw here is conjunctive, joining one theme to another, which is called ʿatf al-qissa ʿala al-qissa (conjoining one narrative to another). Accordingly, the sentence has the status of isti'naf (a resumptive, new sentence), because it is conjoined to the sentence ﴿The believers have certainly prospered﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1], which is itself an independent sentence. This is the beginning of an argument for Allah's sole act of creation and for the immense power that no one shares with Him, and for the fact that man is a creature belonging to Allah alone. The reflection is upon what is in the creation of man and other things of the signs of power and of great blessing. Thus the purpose of it is to nullify shirk, for that is the fundamental root of the error of those who turn away from the Muhammadan call.

[Page 22]

This also includes a reminder of favour to people, that He brought them out from the humiliation of non-existence to the honour of existence. All of this is so that the difference may become evident between the group of believers, who in their faith act in a manner befitting the acknowledgment of this, and the group of polytheists, who followed a path that was not clear, and so they deviated from what gratitude requires by associating partners with Allah.

The emphasis of the statement by the lam of oath and the particle of confirmation (ḥarf al-taḥqīq) is intended as an indirect reproach directed at the polytheists, who are placed in the position of one who denies this statement, because they do not act in accordance with what knowledge requires.

Al-khalq (creation) means origination and fashioning. It was discussed previously in His saying: ﴿He said, "Thus Allah creates what He wills"﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 47] in Surat Ali 'Imran. The intended meaning of "al-insan" (man) may be the human species. Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid interpreted it in this way, so the definite article is for the genus. The pronoun in (jaʿalnāhu) refers back to al-insan.

Al-sulala is "that which is drawn out (al-maslūl)", i.e. that which is extracted from something else. It is said: "salaltu al-sayf" when I drew the sword out of its sheath. Thus al-sulala is an essence extracted from a thing. The pattern fuʿāla indicates smallness, like qulāma (parings) and ṣubāba (residue).

The "min" is ibtidāʾiyya (indicating origin), meaning: We created him separated and coming from an extract. On this reading, the sulala is the totality of the male's and female's fluid drawn out from their blood.

This sulala is what the digestive system produces from food when it becomes blood. When the male's blood passes over the reproductive glands (the two testicles), the two of them secrete from it a fatty, greasy substance which they retain, and it is this that turns into semen at the time of intercourse. That extract is thus drawn from clay, because it is from the foods whose origin is from the earth. As for the woman's blood, when it passes over the uterine tube it leaves in it very fine ova, which are the seed of embryos. From the joining of that fatty substance found in the testicles with an ovum from the ova in the uterine tube, the embryo comes into being. Therefore, it is indeed created from an extract of clay.

His saying: ﴿then We made him a drop [of semen] in a firm place﴾ is another stage of creation, which is the stage of the mixing of the two extracts in the womb. The male's extract was called nuṭfa (drop) because it is nuṭaf, i.e. dripped (quṭira) into the womb through a known channel; and the firm place (qarār makīn) is the womb.

[Page 23]

So "nuṭfatan" is in the accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative), and His saying "in a firm place" is the second object of "jaʿalnāhu". The "thumma" is for ordering by rank (al-tartīb al-rutbī), because that act of placing is greater than the creation of the extract. The pronoun in "jaʿalnāhu" refers to man in terms of his being from the extract. The meaning is: We placed the extract in a firm place, i.e. We set it there in order to preserve it. For this reason, the verse changed the expression from the verb of creation to the verb jaʿala (to place), transitive with "fī" in the sense of placing.

Al-qarār, originally, is the verbal noun of qarra, when something becomes settled in its place. Here the place itself is named by it. Al-makīn is that which is firmly fixed in a place such that it is not uprooted from it. Accordingly, the apparent rule is that the thing that is fixed in a place is described as makīn. Here, however, it is applied as an attribute of the place itself where the drop settled, in the manner of the rhetorical metaphor (al-majāz al-ʿaqlī) for emphasis; its reality is "makīn ḥāliluhu" (a firm place for what is in it). His exalted saying has previously been mentioned: ﴿Do you disbelieve in the One who created you from dust, then from a drop?﴾ [al-Kahf: 37] in Surat al-Kahf, and His saying: ﴿Indeed, We created you from dust, then from a drop﴾ [al-Hajj: 5] in Surat al-Hajj.

It is also possible that the intended meaning of "al-insan" in His saying "And We certainly created man" is Adam. Qatada held this view. Then the sulala would be the particular clay from which Allah formed Adam, namely the clay (ṣalṣāl) which He distinguished from the rest of the clay at the beginning of creation. That clay was drawn out in a special extraction from the clay so that a living being could be formed from it. On this basis, the pronoun in "jaʿalnāhu nuṭfatan" according to this view refers to man in terms of his being the offspring of Adam, and so there is istikhdām (a double reference) in the pronoun. The meaning of this verse is like the meaning of His exalted saying: ﴿And He began the creation of man from clay﴾ [al-Sajda: 7], ﴿then He made his offspring from an extract of worthless fluid﴾ [al-Sajda: 8].

The particle "thumma" in His exalted saying: ﴿then We made the drop a clinging clot﴾ is for ordering by rank, since the making of the drop into a clot is more wondrous than the making of the drop, as it transforms liquid water into solid blood, changing by thickness and altering in colour, due to factors that Allah placed in the womb.

Among the scientific miracles of the Qur'an is the naming of this being by the name "ʿalaqa" (clot), for it is an excellent designation for it, since it has been established in the science of anatomy that this part into which the drop was transformed is a living being which has the power to absorb its nourishment from the mother's blood, by virtue of its attachment to veins in the womb that convey the force of the blood to it. The ʿalaqa is a piece of coagulated blood.

[Page 24]

The muḍgha (lump) is a small piece of flesh, the amount of a mouthful that is chewed. The manner of the embryo's formation was discussed previously at the beginning of Surat al-Hajj.

The making of the clot into a lump is conjoined with the fāʾ (so/then), because the transition from the clot to the lump resembles one thing following upon another, since flesh and solid blood are close to each other, so their development is near, even though the duration of each stage may be a long period.

The creation of the lump into bones is the formation of the bones inside that lump, and that is the beginning of the formation of the human framework from bone and flesh. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿then We clothed the bones with flesh﴾, with the fāʾ of consequence (tafrīʿ), in accordance with the manner established in the conjunction "fa-khalaqnā al-muḍgha" with fāʾ.

So the meaning of "fa-kasawnā" (then We clothed) is that the flesh was like a garment for the bones, and this does not necessarily mean that the bones remained for a period without being clothed. In the authentic hadith: "Indeed, one of you is gathered in the womb of his mother as a drop for forty days, then he becomes a clot for a similar period, then he becomes a lump for a similar period, then an angel is sent to him and he breathes the spirit into him," the hadith [continues]. When the spirit is breathed into him, he has become prepared for life and growth, and that is what is referred to by His exalted saying: ﴿then We brought him forth as another creation﴾, because the creation mentioned before it was without life. Then the creation of life arose in it, and that is another state which came upon it, which He expressed by the term "in-shāʾ" (bringing forth). To indicate the difference in rank between the two creations, He conjoined this bringing forth with "thumma", which denotes the basic sense of ordering in the conjunction of sentences with "thumma".

These stages which the verse addressed are seven stages; when they are completed, the one being formed has become living. In the commentary on the Muwatta': Two men were conversing in the assembly of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab while ʿAli was present. ʿUmar said to them: "What is this private conversation?" One of them said: "The Jews claim that ʿazl (coitus interruptus) is the lesser burying alive (al-mawʾūda al-ṣughrā)." ʿAli said: "It is not a burying alive until there pass over it the seven stages, [quoting] ﴿And We certainly created man from an extract of clay﴾ the verse." ʿUmar said to ʿAli: "You have spoken truly, may Allah prolong your life." It is said: ʿUmar was the first to invoke with the phrase "may Allah prolong your life."

[Page 25]

The majority of readers recited ﴿then We made the lump bones, then We clothed the bones﴾ with the plural form "al-ʿiẓām" in both places. Ibn ʿAmir and Abu Bakr from ʿAsim recited it ("ʿaẓman… wal-ʿaẓma") in the singular form.

Following upon the narration of this marvellous creation comes the declaration of praise for Allah, the Exalted, that He is "aḥsan al-khāliqīn" (the best of creators), i.e. the best of those who bring things into being in origination, because He originated what no one else is able to originate.

Since the indication of the creation of man upon the magnitude of power is more immediate to the consideration of the one who reflects, the praise that follows it is praise for the wondrous power of the Creator, derived from "al-barakah" (blessing), which means increase.

The form tafāʿala is originally a form of muṭāwaʿa (acceptance/reflexivity). The essence of muṭāwaʿa is the acceptance of the effect of the act, and it is used for its consequence, namely the state of being firmly characterised by the meaning of the act; for it is the nature of muṭāwaʿa to occur after the act has been applied, so it requires the impression of the meaning of the act upon the object that receives it, until that object itself becomes an agent. Thus it is said: "I broke it, so it broke." For this reason, tafāʿala when it comes with the meaning of faʿala indicates emphasis, as al-Radi stated in his commentary on al-Shafiya. Accordingly, the forms of muṭāwaʿa and the forms of taklīf (effort/affectation) generally coincide in examples such as: tathannā (to bend), takabbara (to be arrogant), tashāmakha (to be haughty), taqāʿasa (to be slack). So the meaning of ﴿Blessed be Allah﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 54] is that He is described as possessing greatness in goodness, i.e. the greatness of the good that He decrees for people and the righteousness for them.

On this understanding, the sentence is a tadhyīl (concluding appendage), because "tabāraka", when its object is omitted, is general, so it encompasses the greatness of goodness in the creation and in other than it. Likewise, the omission of the object of "al-khāliqīn" (the creators) encompasses the creation of man and the creation of others, such as the mountains and the heavens.

[Page 21]

﴿And We certainly created man from an extract of clay﴾ ﴿then We made him a drop [of semen] in a firm place﴾ ﴿then We made the drop a clinging clot, then We made the clot a lump of flesh, then We made the lump bones, then We clothed the bones with flesh; then We brought him forth as another creation. So blessed is Allah, the best of creators﴾. The waw here is conjunctive, joining one theme to another, which is called ʿatf al-qissa ʿala al-qissa (conjoining one narrative to another). Accordingly, the sentence has the status of isti'naf (a resumptive, new sentence), because it is conjoined to the sentence ﴿The believers have certainly prospered﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1], which is itself an independent sentence. This is the beginning of an argument for Allah's sole act of creation and for the immense power that no one shares with Him, and for the fact that man is a creature belonging to Allah alone. The reflection is upon what is in the creation of man and other things of the signs of power and of great blessing. Thus the purpose of it is to nullify shirk, for that is the fundamental root of the error of those who turn away from the Muhammadan call.

[Page 22]

This also includes a reminder of favour to people, that He brought them out from the humiliation of non-existence to the honour of existence. All of this is so that the difference may become evident between the group of believers, who in their faith act in a manner befitting the acknowledgment of this, and the group of polytheists, who followed a path that was not clear, and so they deviated from what gratitude requires by associating partners with Allah.

The emphasis of the statement by the lam of oath and the particle of confirmation (ḥarf al-taḥqīq) is intended as an indirect reproach directed at the polytheists, who are placed in the position of one who denies this statement, because they do not act in accordance with what knowledge requires.

Al-khalq (creation) means origination and fashioning. It was discussed previously in His saying: ﴿He said, "Thus Allah creates what He wills"﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 47] in Surat Ali 'Imran. The intended meaning of "al-insan" (man) may be the human species. Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid interpreted it in this way, so the definite article is for the genus. The pronoun in (jaʿalnāhu) refers back to al-insan.

Al-sulala is "that which is drawn out (al-maslūl)", i.e. that which is extracted from something else. It is said: "salaltu al-sayf" when I drew the sword out of its sheath. Thus al-sulala is an essence extracted from a thing. The pattern fuʿāla indicates smallness, like qulāma (parings) and ṣubāba (residue).

The "min" is ibtidāʾiyya (indicating origin), meaning: We created him separated and coming from an extract. On this reading, the sulala is the totality of the male's and female's fluid drawn out from their blood.

This sulala is what the digestive system produces from food when it becomes blood. When the male's blood passes over the reproductive glands (the two testicles), the two of them secrete from it a fatty, greasy substance which they retain, and it is this that turns into semen at the time of intercourse. That extract is thus drawn from clay, because it is from the foods whose origin is from the earth. As for the woman's blood, when it passes over the uterine tube it leaves in it very fine ova, which are the seed of embryos. From the joining of that fatty substance found in the testicles with an ovum from the ova in the uterine tube, the embryo comes into being. Therefore, it is indeed created from an extract of clay.

His saying: ﴿then We made him a drop [of semen] in a firm place﴾ is another stage of creation, which is the stage of the mixing of the two extracts in the womb. The male's extract was called nuṭfa (drop) because it is nuṭaf, i.e. dripped (quṭira) into the womb through a known channel; and the firm place (qarār makīn) is the womb.

[Page 23]

So "nuṭfatan" is in the accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative), and His saying "in a firm place" is the second object of "jaʿalnāhu". The "thumma" is for ordering by rank (al-tartīb al-rutbī), because that act of placing is greater than the creation of the extract. The pronoun in "jaʿalnāhu" refers to man in terms of his being from the extract. The meaning is: We placed the extract in a firm place, i.e. We set it there in order to preserve it. For this reason, the verse changed the expression from the verb of creation to the verb jaʿala (to place), transitive with "fī" in the sense of placing.

Al-qarār, originally, is the verbal noun of qarra, when something becomes settled in its place. Here the place itself is named by it. Al-makīn is that which is firmly fixed in a place such that it is not uprooted from it. Accordingly, the apparent rule is that the thing that is fixed in a place is described as makīn. Here, however, it is applied as an attribute of the place itself where the drop settled, in the manner of the rhetorical metaphor (al-majāz al-ʿaqlī) for emphasis; its reality is "makīn ḥāliluhu" (a firm place for what is in it). His exalted saying has previously been mentioned: ﴿Do you disbelieve in the One who created you from dust, then from a drop?﴾ [al-Kahf: 37] in Surat al-Kahf, and His saying: ﴿Indeed, We created you from dust, then from a drop﴾ [al-Hajj: 5] in Surat al-Hajj.

It is also possible that the intended meaning of "al-insan" in His saying "And We certainly created man" is Adam. Qatada held this view. Then the sulala would be the particular clay from which Allah formed Adam, namely the clay (ṣalṣāl) which He distinguished from the rest of the clay at the beginning of creation. That clay was drawn out in a special extraction from the clay so that a living being could be formed from it. On this basis, the pronoun in "jaʿalnāhu nuṭfatan" according to this view refers to man in terms of his being the offspring of Adam, and so there is istikhdām (a double reference) in the pronoun. The meaning of this verse is like the meaning of His exalted saying: ﴿And He began the creation of man from clay﴾ [al-Sajda: 7], ﴿then He made his offspring from an extract of worthless fluid﴾ [al-Sajda: 8].

The particle "thumma" in His exalted saying: ﴿then We made the drop a clinging clot﴾ is for ordering by rank, since the making of the drop into a clot is more wondrous than the making of the drop, as it transforms liquid water into solid blood, changing by thickness and altering in colour, due to factors that Allah placed in the womb.

Among the scientific miracles of the Qur'an is the naming of this being by the name "ʿalaqa" (clot), for it is an excellent designation for it, since it has been established in the science of anatomy that this part into which the drop was transformed is a living being which has the power to absorb its nourishment from the mother's blood, by virtue of its attachment to veins in the womb that convey the force of the blood to it. The ʿalaqa is a piece of coagulated blood.

[Page 24]

The muḍgha (lump) is a small piece of flesh, the amount of a mouthful that is chewed. The manner of the embryo's formation was discussed previously at the beginning of Surat al-Hajj.

The making of the clot into a lump is conjoined with the fāʾ (so/then), because the transition from the clot to the lump resembles one thing following upon another, since flesh and solid blood are close to each other, so their development is near, even though the duration of each stage may be a long period.

The creation of the lump into bones is the formation of the bones inside that lump, and that is the beginning of the formation of the human framework from bone and flesh. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿then We clothed the bones with flesh﴾, with the fāʾ of consequence (tafrīʿ), in accordance with the manner established in the conjunction "fa-khalaqnā al-muḍgha" with fāʾ.

So the meaning of "fa-kasawnā" (then We clothed) is that the flesh was like a garment for the bones, and this does not necessarily mean that the bones remained for a period without being clothed. In the authentic hadith: "Indeed, one of you is gathered in the womb of his mother as a drop for forty days, then he becomes a clot for a similar period, then he becomes a lump for a similar period, then an angel is sent to him and he breathes the spirit into him," the hadith [continues]. When the spirit is breathed into him, he has become prepared for life and growth, and that is what is referred to by His exalted saying: ﴿then We brought him forth as another creation﴾, because the creation mentioned before it was without life. Then the creation of life arose in it, and that is another state which came upon it, which He expressed by the term "in-shāʾ" (bringing forth). To indicate the difference in rank between the two creations, He conjoined this bringing forth with "thumma", which denotes the basic sense of ordering in the conjunction of sentences with "thumma".

These stages which the verse addressed are seven stages; when they are completed, the one being formed has become living. In the commentary on the Muwatta': Two men were conversing in the assembly of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab while ʿAli was present. ʿUmar said to them: "What is this private conversation?" One of them said: "The Jews claim that ʿazl (coitus interruptus) is the lesser burying alive (al-mawʾūda al-ṣughrā)." ʿAli said: "It is not a burying alive until there pass over it the seven stages, [quoting] ﴿And We certainly created man from an extract of clay﴾ the verse." ʿUmar said to ʿAli: "You have spoken truly, may Allah prolong your life." It is said: ʿUmar was the first to invoke with the phrase "may Allah prolong your life."

[Page 25]

The majority of readers recited ﴿then We made the lump bones, then We clothed the bones﴾ with the plural form "al-ʿiẓām" in both places. Ibn ʿAmir and Abu Bakr from ʿAsim recited it ("ʿaẓman… wal-ʿaẓma") in the singular form.

Following upon the narration of this marvellous creation comes the declaration of praise for Allah, the Exalted, that He is "aḥsan al-khāliqīn" (the best of creators), i.e. the best of those who bring things into being in origination, because He originated what no one else is able to originate.

Since the indication of the creation of man upon the magnitude of power is more immediate to the consideration of the one who reflects, the praise that follows it is praise for the wondrous power of the Creator, derived from "al-barakah" (blessing), which means increase.

The form tafāʿala is originally a form of muṭāwaʿa (acceptance/reflexivity). The essence of muṭāwaʿa is the acceptance of the effect of the act, and it is used for its consequence, namely the state of being firmly characterised by the meaning of the act; for it is the nature of muṭāwaʿa to occur after the act has been applied, so it requires the impression of the meaning of the act upon the object that receives it, until that object itself becomes an agent. Thus it is said: "I broke it, so it broke." For this reason, tafāʿala when it comes with the meaning of faʿala indicates emphasis, as al-Radi stated in his commentary on al-Shafiya. Accordingly, the forms of muṭāwaʿa and the forms of taklīf (effort/affectation) generally coincide in examples such as: tathannā (to bend), takabbara (to be arrogant), tashāmakha (to be haughty), taqāʿasa (to be slack). So the meaning of ﴿Blessed be Allah﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 54] is that He is described as possessing greatness in goodness, i.e. the greatness of the good that He decrees for people and the righteousness for them.

On this understanding, the sentence is a tadhyīl (concluding appendage), because "tabāraka", when its object is omitted, is general, so it encompasses the greatness of goodness in the creation and in other than it. Likewise, the omission of the object of "al-khāliqīn" (the creators) encompasses the creation of man and the creation of others, such as the mountains and the heavens.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 23, verses 15–16:

﴿Then indeed, after that, you will surely die.﴾ ﴿Then indeed, on the Day of Resurrection, you will be raised up.﴾

Page 26
This is an incidental insertion (idmaj) within the enumeration of the proofs of God's sole creative power over the varied kinds of created beings, aimed at refuting polytheism. The "then" (thumma) here indicates a ranking sequence (al-tartib al-rutbi), because the importance of reminding of death in this context is stronger than the importance of mentioning creation. This is because informing them of their death serves as a preparation (tawti'ah) for the sentence that follows it, which is His saying: ﴿Then indeed, on the Day of Resurrection, you will be raised up,﴾ and this is the intended purpose. It is like His saying: ﴿He who created death and life that He might test you as to which of you is best in deed﴾ [al-Mulk: 2]. This sentence has the status of an independent sentence (jumla ibtida'iyya), and it is parenthetical between the sentence preceding it and the sentence ﴿And We have certainly created above you seven paths﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 17]. Since "then" (thumma) does not here convey a lapse of time, He explicitly stated the interval in His saying "after that" (ba'da dhalika). The reference to the creation explained just before is intended: that is, after that marvelous formation and perfectly ordered growth, you are heading toward death, which is the cessation of the effect of that origination, and then its ultimate fate is decay and dissolution. He emphasized this report with "indeed" (inna) and the lam, even though they do not doubt it, because when they turned away from reflecting on what comes after this life, they were in the position of those who deny that they will die.

The emphasis on the report "Then indeed, on the Day of Resurrection, you will be raised up" is because they deny resurrection. What was mentioned before it of the first creation serves as evidence for the possibility of the second creation, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Did We then fail with the first creation? Nay, but they are in doubt about a new creation﴾ [Qaf: 15]. Therefore, there was no need to strengthen the emphasis with more than one emphasizing particle, even though their denial of resurrection is strong.

The discourse shifts from the third person (ghayba) to the second person (khitab) by way of iltifat (shift in grammatical person). The point (nukta) here is that the purpose is to remind of death and what follows it, in a manner of indirect allusion (ta'rid) with intimidation, and the second person is what suits this.
