﴿And We have certainly created above you seven heavens/paths, and We have never been unmindful of creation.﴾

This is a transition from reasoning by the creation of man to reasoning by the creation of the upper worlds, because their matter is more wondrous, even though man is closer to his own likeness. Thus the sentence is coordinated (ʿatf) to the sentence ﴿And We certainly created man from an extract of clay﴾ [al-Muʾminun: 12]. This was mentioned right after His saying: ﴿Then indeed you, on the Day of Resurrection, will be resurrected﴾ [al-Muʾminun: 16], to draw attention to the fact that He who created this upper world created it only for a purpose, that the Wise does not neglect the reward of the righteous for their good deeds, nor the punishment of the evildoers for their bad deeds, and that His placing those paths above us, in a position where we see them, indicates that they have a connection with us, because the world of recompense exists within them and His creatures are settled in them. So the indication by this arrangement is like the indication by its reverse in His saying: ﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play﴾ [al-Dukhan: 38], ﴿We did not create them except with truth, but most of them do not know﴾ [al-Dukhan: 39], ﴿Indeed, the Day of Judgment is the appointed time for them all﴾ [al-Dukhan: 40].

Al-tara'iq (the paths) is the plural of ṭarīqah, which is a noun for a road, and it is both masculine and feminine. What is meant here is the paths of the motion of the seven planets, namely their orbits, i.e., the hypothetical lines by which people have measured the courses of the planets' motion. The name al-ṭāriq has been applied to a star in His saying: ﴿By the sky and the ṭāriq﴾ [al-Tariq: 1], because it moves along a course called a ṭarīqah; the traveller on a road is called ṭāriq, and there is no doubt that the paths necessitate travellers in them. So the meaning is: We created travelling bodies and their paths.

Mentioning (above you) draws attention to the obligation to reflect upon their conditions in order to infer from them the power of the Creator who made them, for they are in a state where they can be looked at and contemplated.

And because their being above people has facilitated their benefit from them in timekeeping, for this reason He followed it with the sentence ﴿and We have never been unmindful of creation﴾, which suggests that in this there is kindness to creation and facilitation for them in the affairs of their lives, and this is a favour. Thus the waw in ﴿and We have never been unmindful of creation﴾ is for the circumstantial (ḥāl), and the sentence is in the position of a circumstantial clause. In it there is also an indication to reflect that the world of recompense exists among those worlds. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And in the sky is your provision and what you are promised﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 22].

Al-khalq (creation) is a maf'ul (object) named by the verbal noun, i.e., We have never been unmindful of the needs of Our creatures, meaning mankind. Negation of heedlessness is a kinayah (metonymy) for care and attention, and this conveys that in the creation of the heavenly paths, for what they were created for, there is also kindness to people, since the system of their creation is suitable for people's benefit in their timekeeping and their journeys on land and sea, as He said: ﴿And it is He who placed for you the stars that you may be guided by them in the darknesses of land and sea﴾ [al-An'am: 97]. The greatest of those paths is the path of the sun, together with the benefit it adds through illumination and the improvement of the earth and of bodies. So the meaning becomes: We created above you seven paths for a wisdom you do not know, and in their creation We did not neglect to attend to your interests also.

The shift from the pronoun (ḍamīr) to the explicit noun in His saying ﴿and We have never been unmindful of creation﴾, rather than saying "and We have never been unmindful of you", is because of what the derived form conveys of the meaning of causation, i.e., We have never been unmindful of you because you are Our creatures, so We treat you by the attribute of lordship. In this there is an indication of the obligation of gratitude and of abandoning disbelief.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 23, verse 18–20 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And We sent down water from the sky in a measured amount, and We lodged it in the earth; and indeed, We are able to take it away.﴾ ﴿Then We produced for you thereby gardens of date palms and grapevines, in which you have abundant fruits, and from which you eat.﴾ ﴿And a tree that springs from Mount Sinai, which grows with oil and a relish for those who eat.﴾

The occasion for connecting the sending down of rain water to the sentence ﴿And We created above you seven paths﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 17] is that rain water descends from the direction of the sky, i.e., from the side of the sky.

In the sending down of rain water there is a proof of the breadth of knowledge and the subtlety of power, and in it also is a favour upon creation. So the speech is a call to reflection and an expression of favour, from His saying ﴿We produced for you thereby gardens﴾ to the end of it. The meaning of this verse has already been explained in Surat al-An'am, Surat al-Ra'd and Surat al-Nahl.

The sending down of water is its dropping from the clouds as water, snow and hail upon the plains and the mountains.

صفحة ٢٩

The word qadar (measure) here means determination and specification of a quantity, both in amount and in its timing. It may therefore be taken in its plain sense, i.e., in a specific measure suited to the bounty of it; for when it is sent down in this way, irrigation and continuity are achieved by it, and likewise the melting of the falling snow. It is also permissible that, alongside this, the meaning intended is a metaphor for precision and perfection. The meaning of qadar here is not the sense found in the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "And that you believe in qadar, its good and its evil."

The word iskan (lodging) means placing a thing in a dwelling, and the maskan is the place of settling; it is a maf'al, a noun of place derived from sukun (rest). Lodging is used figuratively for settling in the earth. This settling is of two kinds: a short settling, like the settling of rain water in the outer crust of the earth immediately after the rains fall, according to what the abundance of the rain, the softness of the earth, and the intensity of heat or cold require. By it plants grow in the cultivated land and herbage in spring, and trees draw from it through their roots and so bear their fruit, and the roots and bases of trees emerge from the seeds that are in the earth.

The other kind is a long settling, which is the settling of waters that fall as rain and from the melting of falling snow, which seep into the inner parts of the earth, from which springs arise that gush forth by themselves, or are made to flow as wells by digging.

The clause ﴿And indeed, We are able to take it away﴾ is an interposed sentence between the preceding sentence and what branches from it; in this there is a reminder that the power of God the Exalted is capable of bringing into being and of annihilating.

The indefiniteness of (dhahab) is for magnification and exaltation; the meaning of exaltation here is the multiplicity of the states of its being taken away: from its sinking into the depths of the earth through a splitting of the earth by an earthquake or the like, and from its drying up through intense heat, and from the withholding of its sending down for a long time.

Its meaning is found in His exalted saying: ﴿Say: Have you considered, if your water should become sunken, who would bring you clear water?﴾ [al-Mulk: 30]. In al-Kashshaf: (It — i.e., what is in this verse — is more emphatic in threat than His saying: ﴿Say: Have you considered, if your water should become sunken, who would bring you clear water?﴾ [al-Mulk: 30]) end.

Then the author of al-Taqrib for the Eloquence (al-Taqrib lil-Ablagiyya) explained eighteen aspects of its greater eloquence:

The first: that this is on the basis of supposition and estimation, whereas that is in the form of a categorical assertion, in the sense that it is more indicative of the realisation of what is threatened even if it has not occurred.

The second: the emphasis with (inna).

The third: the lam in the predicate.

The fourth: that this one concerns water in general sent down from the sky, whereas that one concerns water attributed to them.

The fifth: that the sunken water may remain, unlike the departed water.

The sixth: what is in the indefiniteness of (dhahab) of exaggeration.

The seventh: its attribution here to one who causes it to depart, unlike there where (sunken) is said.

The eighth: what is in the self-referential form of the Exalted, of awe.

The ninth: what is in (qadirun) of indication of power over it, and the act proceeding from the one who is capable is more eloquent.

The tenth: what is in its plural form.

The eleventh: what is in the word (bihi) of indication that whatever He withholds, there is no sender of it.

The twelfth: its freedom from being followed by a hope-inspiring expression, whereas there the arrival (of water) is mentioned, which is a hope-giving expression.

The thirteenth: the placing first of what is in the threat, which is the departing, before what is, as it were, its complement or its object, according to the Basran and Kufan schools.

The fourteenth: the difference between the nominal and verbal sentences in stability and otherwise.

The fifteenth: what is in the word asbaha of indication of transition and becoming.

The sixteenth: that the taking away here is stated explicitly, whereas there it is understood from the context of the interrogation.

The seventeenth: that there is the negation of a specific water, namely clear water, unlike here.

The eighteenth: the consideration of all these matters together, each of which suffices as an emphasis.

Al-Alusi added in his tafsir, saying:

The nineteenth: God's own report of it without commanding another here, unlike there, where He, glorified be He, commanded His Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace, to say that.

The twentieth: the non-specification of an addressee here, and the specification of the disbelievers with the address there.

The twenty-first: the simile derived from making the sentence a circumstantial clause, for it establishes the realisation of power, and there is no simile there.

The twenty-second: the attribution of power to Him, the Exalted, twice.

Al-Alusi also transmitted from his contemporary, Mawla Muhammad al-Zahawi, aspects which are these:

The twenty-third: the implicit inclusion here of the threat of their being removed far from the mercy of God the Exalted; for (dhahaba bihi) implies the companionship of the agent with the object, and the departure of God the Exalted from them along with the water means the departure of His mercy, glorified be He, from them, and their being cursed and driven away from it; and this is not the case there.

The twenty-fourth: that the time of the departing is not specified here, unlike in (in asbaha), for from it is understood that the becoming occurs in the morning, according to one of the usages of asbaha as a defective verb.

The twenty-fifth: that the direction of the taking away is not specified here as being downward (i.e., what is indicated by the word ghawran).

The twenty-sixth: that the threat here is with what they have never been tested with, unlike what is there.

The twenty-seventh: that the thing threatened here, if it occurs, they are certainly destroyed.

The twenty-eighth: that there remains here for them no clinging, even weak, to a supposition of the impossibility of the threatened thing, whereas there, where the morning is attributed to the water as ghawran, and it is known that water does not become sunken by itself, as the verification of the view of the Wise man holds; also it was possible that the conditional might be imagined, while true, to be of impossible antecedent, so that they would feel secure from its occurrence.

The twenty-ninth: that the thing threatened here may at first glance be thought to occur immediately, unlike there, for the future is definite for its occurrence because of (in). It is evident that a threat with what may occur at once is more terrifying, and a threat with what is definitely to occur in the future is less so.

The thirtieth: that what is here admits only of threat, unlike there, for it admits of, even if remotely, the meaning of favour: "If your water becomes sunken, no one but God the Exalted will bring you clear water."

I say: These scholars took pains to explain the difference between the two verses, but none of them undertook to uncover the reason why these features are gathered in this verse and not in the other parallel verse; and this is not because the verse is void of the points of inimitability, nor because those who reflect are unable to extract their like. Rather, what is set forth of the rhetorical features of the Qur'an, its explainer does not mean that what has occurred to him and what he has been granted success in is the utmost of what God placed in the arrangement of the Qur'an of features and meanings; rather he conveys what has struck the eye of the reflecting observer, and scholars differ in uncovering it according to the measure of their talents and understandings. A person may be granted the perception of rhetorical features in some verses and not be granted the like of it, or the like of it in others. The people of meanings intend, in extended discourse on some verses, that they be a model for extracting the like of those features in other verses. As al-Sakkaki did in explaining the features of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And it was said: O earth, swallow your water﴾ [Hud: 44], the verse, in the section on fluency and eloquence from al-Miftah; and he said at the end of his speech: (Do not suppose that the verse is confined to what I have mentioned, for perhaps what I left out is more than what I mentioned; for the aim was only to guide to the manner of gathering the fruits of the two sciences of meanings and expression.)

صفحة ٣٣

And we may say: the verse of Surat al-Mu'minun is intended for warning and threat of the removal of that great blessing, whereas the verse of Surat al-Mulk is intended for taking lesson from God the Exalted's power to remove it. The difference of the two contexts has an effect on the difference of the requirements; so the verse of Surat al-Mu'minun was more suited, with an abundance of features appropriate to the context of warning and threat, without neglecting the extraction of features in it, which we may touch upon when we reach it.

Moreover, Surat al-Mulk was revealed directly after Surat al-Mu'minun, and the revelation of some of it may overlap with the revelation of part of Surat al-Mu'minun. So when the verse of Surat al-Mu'minun was fully elaborated with the particulars that the context required, it sufficed without the like of it in its counterpart in Surat al-Mulk; so in the second it took the path of brevity, due to the closeness of its time to its counterpart.

The making of the gardens is from the handiwork of God the Exalted: first the growing of gardens on the earth; and after that gardens were grown by human planting; and that too is from the handiwork of God, through what He placed in minds of knowledge of planting, sowing, watering, channelling water and bringing it from afar. So all this making is from God the Exalted.

And the garden (jannah) is a place with trees. Its usage is mostly applied to what contains date palms and vines. It has already been mentioned at His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Like a garden on a height﴾ [al-Baqarah: 265], the verse, in Surat al-Baqarah.

What is mentioned here of the three kinds of trees is the most noble of trees and the most beneficial in fruit: they are the date palm, the grapevine and the olive; and the discussion of date palms, grapevines and olives has already preceded in Surat al-An'am and in Surat al-Nahl.

Fawakih is the plural of fakihah, which is food by which one enjoys oneself through eating, i.e., is delighted by its taste without intending sustenance; if it is intended as sustenance, it is called ta'am (food). Among foods there is that which is both fakihah and ta'am, like dates and grapes, for they are eaten fresh and dried; and among them is that which is fakihah but not ta'am, like almonds and pears; and among them is that which is ta'am but not fakihah, like the olive. For this reason the mention of the olive tree was put after its two siblings, because what is intended is the favour of what is in their fruit of enjoyment and sustenance; so it is a favour concerning the needful and the embellishing.

صفحة ٣٤

He described the fawakih as ﴿abundant﴾ in view of the difference of kinds, such as unripe dates, ripe dates and dried dates, and such as olive oil and fresh grapes; and also in view of the abundance of fruiting of these two trees.

(And a tree) is conjoined to (gardens), i.e., And We brought forth for you thereby a tree that springs from Mount Sinai, and it is the olive tree; and the clause (springs) is an attribute of (a tree).

Its specification by mention, together with the implicit fact that people eat from it, is an honouring of its status and a hint at the abundance of its benefits; for from its fruit come food, remedy and healing, and from its wood fuel and other things. In a hadith: "Eat the oil and anoint yourselves with it, for it comes from a blessed tree."

Tur Sina' is a mountain in the desert of Sinai, which lies between the Gulf of Aqaba and Egypt, and which in ancient times was among the lands of Palestine; and upon it Moses communed with his Lord, the Exalted. Its discussion has already preceded in Surat al-A'raf at His saying: ﴿But look upon the mountain﴾ [al-A'raf: 143]. The name Tur came to be dominant without an addition, and it is Tur Sina' or Tur Sinin. The meaning of tur is the mountain. Sina' is said to be the name of a tree that abounds there; and it is said to be the name of stones; and it is said to be the name of that place. It is said to be a Nabataean name, and it is said to be an Abyssinian name, but this is not correct. Those who said it were deceived only by the resemblance of this name to the attribute of beauty in the Abyssinian language, which is the word: sanah. Such resemblance has given rise to errors.

Ya' of "Sayna'" (سَيْناءَ) was given dead sukun, and this is how the majority (al-Jumhur) read it. It is also permissible to pronounce it with a fatha and with a living sukun on the ya', and this is how Ibn Kathir, 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it. In both readings it is diptote (mamnu' min al-sarf). In the reading with kasra, it is said to be diptote because of its being a proper noun (al-'alamiyyah) and its being non-Arabic (al-'ujmah), since the pattern fa'ila' (فَعِلاءَ), when its middle radical is original, does not have its alif as the feminine marker but as an extension (lil-ilhaq), and the alif of extension does not prevent declension. In the reading with fatha, its prohibition from declension is due to the alif of feminine marking, since the pattern fa'alaa' (فَعَلاءَ) is one of the patterns of the feminine alif.

His words, "﴿comes forth from Mount Sinai﴾," imply that it has a special connection with Mount Sinai, and the reason for this has been obscure. What I consider to be the case is that "coming forth" (al-khuruj) is used with the meaning of coming into being and taking form, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then We brought forth with it pairs of various plants﴾ [Ta-Ha: 53], and His saying: ﴿He brings forth with it crops of varying colours﴾ [az-Zumar: 21]. This is because the true meaning of khuruj is emerging from a place. Since every created thing emerges after non-existence, and since a place is necessary for every newly come-into-being thing, the appearance of a thing after it was non-existent was likened to the emergence of a thing from the place in which it had been hidden. This is a widespread metaphor in the Qur'an.

So it appears that the meaning is that God created the first olive tree in Mount Sinai. This is because the kinds and species existing on the terrestrial globe must have places where their existence first began, prior to their existence elsewhere, since some places are more favourable for the origin of some existing things than others, owing to a suitability between the nature of the place and the nature of the thing existing in it, whether heat, cold or moderateness. Likewise the seasons of the year: spring suits some animals, winter others, and summer others. God brings existing things into being in the conditions suited to them, and animals and plants all proceed according to this law.

Then, when people transport an animal or plant from one land to another, or wish to benefit from it in a season other than its own, and they see that the place or time to which it has been moved is unsuitable, they resort to means that make up for its deficiency, such as warming it in severe cold or cooling it by bathing in water during intense heat, so that the propagation of that transported thing is not impeded in a place other than its own. Just as some animals or plants do not live long in some regions unsuited to their natures, such as the gazelle in lands of snow, so too some places within a suitable region may be more fitting for an animal or plant than other parts of that region. Perhaps the climate of Mount Sinai, by its being midway between the extreme regions of heat and cold, and by the middling height of its elevation between highlands and plains, is more favourable to the nature of the olive family, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿an olive tree neither of the east nor of the west﴾ [an-Nur: 35]. So God, exalted is He, prepared that place for its creation when He willed to create it, just as He prepared a special clay for the creation of Adam, when He said: ﴿He created man from clay like pottery﴾ [ar-Rahman: 14]. Then the olive tree was transported from the first place where it appeared to other places to which its inhabitants carried it for benefit. It succeeded in some of them and did not succeed in others.

It is established in the Torah that the olive tree existed before the Flood and after it. In Chapter 8 of the Book of Genesis: Noah sent out a dove seeking a place from which the waters of the Flood had receded, and the dove returned in the evening carrying in its beak a fresh olive leaf, so Noah knew that the water had begun to recede from the earth.

It is known that the first receding of the water is revealed on the summits of the mountains, so perhaps the olive leaf that the dove carried was from a tree in Mount Sinai.

Whatever the case, Noah recognised the olive leaf, which indicates that they knew this tree before the Flood. However, no mention is found of the use of olive oil in food in ancient history except in the time of Moses, peace be upon him, when the Children of Israel were around Mount Sinai. Oil was used to light the Tent of Meeting by God's revelation to Moses, and Moses poured the anointing oil upon the head of his brother Aaron when he appointed him priest over the Children of Israel.

It is also possible that the meaning of "comes forth" is "appears and becomes known," so that the first human awareness of the benefits of this tree and its transport came from the olive tree that is in Mount Sinai. This is like how we in our country call the turkey "the Indian hen," because people knew it from the lands of India; and as some swords in the lands of the Arabs are called "al-Mashrafiyyah," because they were known from the outskirts of Syria (mashariq al-Sham); and some spears are called "al-Khattiyyah," because they came to the lands of the Arabs from a port called al-Khatt; and some swords are called "al-Muhannad," because they are brought from India. Oil was brought to the lands of the Arabs from Syria and from Palestine.

Whatever the case, the purpose of mentioning that it comes forth from Mount Sinai is only to point out that this is its original place of growth. Otherwise, the favour of it was not then directed to the inhabitants of Mount Sinai. This indication was only to highlight the nobility of its place of origin and the generosity of the land in which it appeared. The olive tree has remained famous for blessing among people. I have seen in Lisan al-'Arab, from al-Asma'i, from 'Abd al-Malik ibn Salih: that every olive tree in Palestine is planted by peoples called the Greeks (al-Yunaniyyun), end quote. The apparent meaning is that he means by it the olive trees of their time, which they had replaced with ancient trees that had perished.

In Greek myths (mythology) it is said that Minerva and Neptune (the two gods in Greek belief) disputed over which of them would name a city that they had founded (Cecrops). The gods judged between them that this honour would be attained only by whoever produces the most useful thing. As for Neptune, he produced a great and powerful sea-horse; as for Minerva, she produced the olive tree with its fruit. So the gods ruled that she was more deserving, and therefore they named the city Athens, which is the name of Minerva. They also claimed that Hercules, when he returned from some of his expeditions, brought with him branches of olive, and planted them on the mountain of Olympus, which in their belief was the dwelling of their gods.

Olive oil was used among the Greeks from the time of Homer, for he mentioned in the Iliad that Achilles poured oil over the body of Patroclus and the body of Hector.

Oil was rare in most of the lands of the Arabs, as it was brought to the lands of the Arabs from Syria.

God has also used the olive tree's oil as a parable for His light, in His saying: ﴿The parable of His light is like a niche within which is a lamp, the lamp is in a glass, the glass as if it were a pearly star, lit from a blessed olive tree, neither of the east nor of the west, whose oil would almost glow even if no fire touched it. Light upon light﴾ [an-Nur: 35].

The use of the present tense in His saying, "﴿comes forth from Mount Sinai﴾," is to call to mind the wondrous and important image in which that tree was formed at the beginning of its creation, so that the hearer almost sees it coming forth with vegetation at Mount Sinai. This is like His saying: ﴿And when you shape from clay the likeness of a bird﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 110]. This is more suited to the first interpretation of the meaning of "comes forth from Mount Sinai."

The meaning of "﴿grows with oil﴾" is that it grows accompanied by oil, so the ba' is for accompaniment (al-mulabasah).

This verse is an example of the ba' of accompaniment, and accompaniment is a broad meaning. The accompaniment of the olive tree's growth with oil and seasoning is an accompaniment through the accompaniment of its fruit with oil and seasoning, for its fruit contains the oil, which constitutes both grease and condiment for those who eat. As for its being grease, people anoint their bodies with it, comb their hair with it, and put perfumes in it, so they comb their hair with it; and the Prophet ﷺ used to anoint his head with oil.

"Duhn" with a damma on the dal is the name of what is applied to something, i.e. with which something is smeared, and "duhn" is applied to oil in view of its being smeared on the body for treatment and on the hair for combing.

"Sibgh," with a kasra on the sad, is what something is dyed with, i.e. what changes the colour by it. Then its use was extended to every liquid with which the outer surface of some body is smeared; from this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the dye of God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 138]. Oil was called "sibgh" because bread is dipped (yusbagh) in it. The coordination of "sibgh" with "duhn" is in view of the difference in what the derivation of the descriptive term indicates: "sibgh" is what something is dipped in, and "duhn" is what something is smeared with. "Sibgh" is more specific; so it is of the type of coordinating the specific with the general for emphasis. They used to dip their food in it, and that is a condiment for food. At-Tirmidhi related in his Sunan from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and from Abu Usayd that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Eat the oil and anoint yourselves with it, for it is from a blessed tree."

The majority read "tanbutu" with a fatha on the ta' and a damma on the ba' (تَنْبُتُ), while Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ruways and Ya'qub read it with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the ba' (تُنْبِتُ), according to the dialect of those who say anbata meaning nabata, or with the object omitted, i.e. it (the tree) produces its fruit, meaning it brings it forth.

﴿And We sent down water from the sky in a measured amount, and We lodged it in the earth; and indeed, We are able to take it away.﴾ ﴿Then We produced for you thereby gardens of date palms and grapevines, in which you have abundant fruits, and from which you eat.﴾ ﴿And a tree that springs from Mount Sinai, which grows with oil and a relish for those who eat.﴾

The sending down of water is its dropping from the clouds as water, snow and hail upon the plains and the mountains.

صفحة ٢٩

The meaning of qadar here is not the sense found in the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "And that you believe in qadar, its good and its evil."

The word iskan (lodging) means placing a thing in a dwelling, and the maskan is the place of settling; it is a maf'al, a noun of place derived from sukun (rest). The other kind is a long settling, which is the settling of waters that fall as rain and from the melting of falling snow, which seep into the inner parts of the earth, from which springs arise that gush forth by themselves, or are made to flow as wells by digging.

The clause ﴿And indeed, We are able to take it away﴾ is an interposed sentence between the preceding sentence and what branches from it; in this there is a reminder that the power of God the Exalted is capable of bringing into being and of annihilating.

The indefiniteness of (dhahab) is for magnification and exaltation; the meaning of exaltation here is the multiplicity of the states of its being taken away: from its sinking into the depths of the earth through a splitting of the earth by an earthquake or the like, and from its drying up through intense heat, and from the withholding of its sending down for a long time.

Its meaning is found in His exalted saying: ﴿Say: Have you considered, if your water should become sunken, who would bring you clear water?﴾ [al-Mulk: 30]. In al-Kashshaf: (It — i.e., what is in this verse — is more emphatic in threat than His saying: ﴿Say: Have you considered, if your water should become sunken, who would bring you clear water?﴾ [al-Mulk: 30]) end.

Then the author of al-Taqrib for the Eloquence (al-Taqrib lil-Ablagiyya) explained eighteen aspects of its greater eloquence:

The first: that this is on the basis of supposition and estimation, whereas that is in the form of a categorical assertion, in the sense that it is more indicative of the realisation of what is threatened even if it has not occurred.

The second: the emphasis with (inna).

The third: the lam in the predicate.

The fourth: that this one concerns water in general sent down from the sky, whereas that one concerns water attributed to them.

The fifth: that the sunken water may remain, unlike the departed water.

The sixth: what is in the indefiniteness of (dhahab) of exaggeration.

The seventh: its attribution here to one who causes it to depart, unlike there where (sunken) is said.

The eighth: what is in the self-referential form of the Exalted, of awe.

The ninth: what is in (qadirun) of indication of power over it, and the act proceeding from the one who is capable is more eloquent.

The tenth: what is in its plural form.

The eleventh: what is in the word (bihi) of indication that whatever He withholds, there is no sender of it.

The twelfth: its freedom from being followed by a hope-inspiring expression, whereas there the arrival (of water) is mentioned, which is a hope-giving expression.

The thirteenth: the placing first of what is in the threat, which is the departing, before what is, as it were, its complement or its object, according to the Basran and Kufan schools.

The fourteenth: the difference between the nominal and verbal sentences in stability and otherwise.

The fifteenth: what is in the word asbaha of indication of transition and becoming.

The sixteenth: that the taking away here is stated explicitly, whereas there it is understood from the context of the interrogation.

The seventeenth: that there is the negation of a specific water, namely clear water, unlike here.

The eighteenth: the consideration of all these matters together, each of which suffices as an emphasis.

Al-Alusi added in his tafsir, saying:

The nineteenth: God's own report of it without commanding another here, unlike there, where He, glorified be He, commanded His Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace, to say that.

The twentieth: the non-specification of an addressee here, and the specification of the disbelievers with the address there.

The twenty-first: the simile derived from making the sentence a circumstantial clause, for it establishes the realisation of power, and there is no simile there.

The twenty-second: the attribution of power to Him, the Exalted, twice.

Al-Alusi also transmitted from his contemporary, Mawla Muhammad al-Zahawi, aspects which are these:

The twenty-third: the implicit inclusion here of the threat of their being removed far from the mercy of God the Exalted; for (dhahaba bihi) implies the companionship of the agent with the object, and the departure of God the Exalted from them along with the water means the departure of His mercy, glorified be He, from them, and their being cursed and driven away from it; and this is not the case there.

The twenty-fourth: that the time of the departing is not specified here, unlike in (in asbaha), for from it is understood that the becoming occurs in the morning, according to one of the usages of asbaha as a defective verb.

The twenty-fifth: that the direction of the taking away is not specified here as being downward (i.e., what is indicated by the word ghawran).

The twenty-sixth: that the threat here is with what they have never been tested with, unlike what is there.

The twenty-seventh: that the thing threatened here, if it occurs, they are certainly destroyed.

The twenty-eighth: that there remains here for them no clinging, even weak, to a supposition of the impossibility of the threatened thing, whereas there, where the morning is attributed to the water as ghawran, and it is known that water does not become sunken by itself, as the verification of the view of the Wise man holds; also it was possible that the conditional might be imagined, while true, to be of impossible antecedent, so that they would feel secure from its occurrence.

The twenty-ninth: that the thing threatened here may at first glance be thought to occur immediately, unlike there, for the future is definite for its occurrence because of (in). It is evident that a threat with what may occur at once is more terrifying, and a threat with what is definitely to occur in the future is less so.

The thirtieth: that what is here admits only of threat, unlike there, for it admits of, even if remotely, the meaning of favour: "If your water becomes sunken, no one but God the Exalted will bring you clear water."

I say: These scholars took pains to explain the difference between the two verses, but none of them undertook to uncover the reason why these features are gathered in this verse and not in the other parallel verse; and this is not because the verse is void of the points of inimitability, nor because those who reflect are unable to extract their like. Rather, what is set forth of the rhetorical features of the Qur'an, its explainer does not mean that what has occurred to him and what he has been granted success in is the utmost of what God placed in the arrangement of the Qur'an of features and meanings; rather he conveys what has struck the eye of the reflecting observer, and scholars differ in uncovering it according to the measure of their talents and understandings. A person may be granted the perception of rhetorical features in some verses and not be granted the like of it, or the like of it in others. The people of meanings intend, in extended discourse on some verses, that they be a model for extracting the like of those features in other verses. As al-Sakkaki did in explaining the features of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And it was said: O earth, swallow your water﴾ [Hud: 44], the verse, in the section on fluency and eloquence from al-Miftah; and he said at the end of his speech: (Do not suppose that the verse is confined to what I have mentioned, for perhaps what I left out is more than what I mentioned; for the aim was only to guide to the manner of gathering the fruits of the two sciences of meanings and expression.)

صفحة ٣٣

And we may say: the verse of Surat al-Mu'minun is intended for warning and threat of the removal of that great blessing, whereas the verse of Surat al-Mulk is intended for taking lesson from God the Exalted's power to remove it. The difference of the two contexts has an effect on the difference of the requirements; so the verse of Surat al-Mu'minun was more suited, with an abundance of features appropriate to the context of warning and threat, without neglecting the extraction of features in it, which we may touch upon when we reach it.

Moreover, Surat al-Mulk was revealed directly after Surat al-Mu'minun, and the revelation of some of it may overlap with the revelation of part of Surat al-Mu'minun. So when the verse of Surat al-Mu'minun was fully elaborated with the particulars that the context required, it sufficed without the like of it in its counterpart in Surat al-Mulk; so in the second it took the path of brevity, due to the closeness of its time to its counterpart.

The making of the gardens is from the handiwork of God the Exalted: first the growing of gardens on the earth; and after that gardens were grown by human planting; and that too is from the handiwork of God, through what He placed in minds of knowledge of planting, sowing, watering, channelling water and bringing it from afar. So all this making is from God the Exalted.

And the garden (jannah) is a place with trees. Its usage is mostly applied to what contains date palms and vines. It has already been mentioned at His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Like a garden on a height﴾ [al-Baqarah: 265], the verse, in Surat al-Baqarah.

What is mentioned here of the three kinds of trees is the most noble of trees and the most beneficial in fruit: they are the date palm, the grapevine and the olive; and the discussion of date palms, grapevines and olives has already preceded in Surat al-An'am and in Surat al-Nahl.

Fawakih is the plural of fakihah, which is food by which one enjoys oneself through eating, i.e., is delighted by its taste without intending sustenance; if it is intended as sustenance, it is called ta'am (food). Among foods there is that which is both fakihah and ta'am, like dates and grapes, for they are eaten fresh and dried; and among them is that which is fakihah but not ta'am, like almonds and pears; and among them is that which is ta'am but not fakihah, like the olive. For this reason the mention of the olive tree was put after its two siblings, because what is intended is the favour of what is in their fruit of enjoyment and sustenance; so it is a favour concerning the needful and the embellishing.

صفحة ٣٤

He described the fawakih as ﴿abundant﴾ in view of the difference of kinds, such as unripe dates, ripe dates and dried dates, and such as olive oil and fresh grapes; and also in view of the abundance of fruiting of these two trees.

(And a tree) is conjoined to (gardens), i.e., And We brought forth for you thereby a tree that springs from Mount Sinai, and it is the olive tree; and the clause (springs) is an attribute of (a tree).

Its specification by mention, together with the implicit fact that people eat from it, is an honouring of its status and a hint at the abundance of its benefits; for from its fruit come food, remedy and healing, and from its wood fuel and other things. In a hadith: "Eat the oil and anoint yourselves with it, for it comes from a blessed tree."

Tur Sina' is a mountain in the desert of Sinai, which lies between the Gulf of Aqaba and Egypt, and which in ancient times was among the lands of Palestine; and upon it Moses communed with his Lord, the Exalted. Its discussion has already preceded in Surat al-A'raf at His saying: ﴿But look upon the mountain﴾ [al-A'raf: 143]. The name Tur came to be dominant without an addition, and it is Tur Sina' or Tur Sinin. The meaning of tur is the mountain. Sina' is said to be the name of a tree that abounds there; and it is said to be the name of stones; and it is said to be the name of that place. It is said to be a Nabataean name, and it is said to be an Abyssinian name, but this is not correct. Those who said it were deceived only by the resemblance of this name to the attribute of beauty in the Abyssinian language, which is the word: sanah. Such resemblance has given rise to errors.

Ya' of "Sayna'" (سَيْناءَ) was given dead sukun, and this is how the majority (al-Jumhur) read it. It is also permissible to pronounce it with a fatha and with a living sukun on the ya', and this is how Ibn Kathir, 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it. In both readings it is diptote (mamnu' min al-sarf). In the reading with kasra, it is said to be diptote because of its being a proper noun (al-'alamiyyah) and its being non-Arabic (al-'ujmah), since the pattern fa'ila' (فَعِلاءَ), when its middle radical is original, does not have its alif as the feminine marker but as an extension (lil-ilhaq), and the alif of extension does not prevent declension. In the reading with fatha, its prohibition from declension is due to the alif of feminine marking, since the pattern fa'alaa' (فَعَلاءَ) is one of the patterns of the feminine alif.

His words, "﴿comes forth from Mount Sinai﴾," imply that it has a special connection with Mount Sinai, and the reason for this has been obscure. What I consider to be the case is that "coming forth" (al-khuruj) is used with the meaning of coming into being and taking form, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then We brought forth with it pairs of various plants﴾ [Ta-Ha: 53], and His saying: ﴿He brings forth with it crops of varying colours﴾ [az-Zumar: 21]. This is because the true meaning of khuruj is emerging from a place. Since every created thing emerges after non-existence, and since a place is necessary for every newly come-into-being thing, the appearance of a thing after it was non-existent was likened to the emergence of a thing from the place in which it had been hidden. This is a widespread metaphor in the Qur'an.

So it appears that the meaning is that God created the first olive tree in Mount Sinai. This is because the kinds and species existing on the terrestrial globe must have places where their existence first began, prior to their existence elsewhere, since some places are more favourable for the origin of some existing things than others, owing to a suitability between the nature of the place and the nature of the thing existing in it, whether heat, cold or moderateness. Likewise the seasons of the year: spring suits some animals, winter others, and summer others. God brings existing things into being in the conditions suited to them, and animals and plants all proceed according to this law.

Then, when people transport an animal or plant from one land to another, or wish to benefit from it in a season other than its own, and they see that the place or time to which it has been moved is unsuitable, they resort to means that make up for its deficiency, such as warming it in severe cold or cooling it by bathing in water during intense heat, so that the propagation of that transported thing is not impeded in a place other than its own. Just as some animals or plants do not live long in some regions unsuited to their natures, such as the gazelle in lands of snow, so too some places within a suitable region may be more fitting for an animal or plant than other parts of that region. Perhaps the climate of Mount Sinai, by its being midway between the extreme regions of heat and cold, and by the middling height of its elevation between highlands and plains, is more favourable to the nature of the olive family, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿an olive tree neither of the east nor of the west﴾ [an-Nur: 35]. So God, exalted is He, prepared that place for its creation when He willed to create it, just as He prepared a special clay for the creation of Adam, when He said: ﴿He created man from clay like pottery﴾ [ar-Rahman: 14]. Then the olive tree was transported from the first place where it appeared to other places to which its inhabitants carried it for benefit. It succeeded in some of them and did not succeed in others.

It is established in the Torah that the olive tree existed before the Flood and after it. In Chapter 8 of the Book of Genesis: Noah sent out a dove seeking a place from which the waters of the Flood had receded, and the dove returned in the evening carrying in its beak a fresh olive leaf, so Noah knew that the water had begun to recede from the earth.

It is known that the first receding of the water is revealed on the summits of the mountains, so perhaps the olive leaf that the dove carried was from a tree in Mount Sinai.

Whatever the case, Noah recognised the olive leaf, which indicates that they knew this tree before the Flood. However, no mention is found of the use of olive oil in food in ancient history except in the time of Moses, peace be upon him, when the Children of Israel were around Mount Sinai. Oil was used to light the Tent of Meeting by God's revelation to Moses, and Moses poured the anointing oil upon the head of his brother Aaron when he appointed him priest over the Children of Israel.

It is also possible that the meaning of "comes forth" is "appears and becomes known," so that the first human awareness of the benefits of this tree and its transport came from the olive tree that is in Mount Sinai. This is like how we in our country call the turkey "the Indian hen," because people knew it from the lands of India; and as some swords in the lands of the Arabs are called "al-Mashrafiyyah," because they were known from the outskirts of Syria (mashariq al-Sham); and some spears are called "al-Khattiyyah," because they came to the lands of the Arabs from a port called al-Khatt; and some swords are called "al-Muhannad," because they are brought from India. Oil was brought to the lands of the Arabs from Syria and from Palestine.

Whatever the case, the purpose of mentioning that it comes forth from Mount Sinai is only to point out that this is its original place of growth. Otherwise, the favour of it was not then directed to the inhabitants of Mount Sinai. This indication was only to highlight the nobility of its place of origin and the generosity of the land in which it appeared. The olive tree has remained famous for blessing among people. I have seen in Lisan al-'Arab, from al-Asma'i, from 'Abd al-Malik ibn Salih: that every olive tree in Palestine is planted by peoples called the Greeks (al-Yunaniyyun), end quote. The apparent meaning is that he means by it the olive trees of their time, which they had replaced with ancient trees that had perished.

In Greek myths (mythology) it is said that Minerva and Neptune (the two gods in Greek belief) disputed over which of them would name a city that they had founded (Cecrops). The gods judged between them that this honour would be attained only by whoever produces the most useful thing. As for Neptune, he produced a great and powerful sea-horse; as for Minerva, she produced the olive tree with its fruit. So the gods ruled that she was more deserving, and therefore they named the city Athens, which is the name of Minerva. They also claimed that Hercules, when he returned from some of his expeditions, brought with him branches of olive, and planted them on the mountain of Olympus, which in their belief was the dwelling of their gods.

Olive oil was used among the Greeks from the time of Homer, for he mentioned in the Iliad that Achilles poured oil over the body of Patroclus and the body of Hector.

Oil was rare in most of the lands of the Arabs, as it was brought to the lands of the Arabs from Syria.

God has also used the olive tree's oil as a parable for His light, in His saying: ﴿The parable of His light is like a niche within which is a lamp, the lamp is in a glass, the glass as if it were a pearly star, lit from a blessed olive tree, neither of the east nor of the west, whose oil would almost glow even if no fire touched it. Light upon light﴾ [an-Nur: 35].

The use of the present tense in His saying, "﴿comes forth from Mount Sinai﴾," is to call to mind the wondrous and important image in which that tree was formed at the beginning of its creation, so that the hearer almost sees it coming forth with vegetation at Mount Sinai. This is like His saying: ﴿And when you shape from clay the likeness of a bird﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 110]. This is more suited to the first interpretation of the meaning of "comes forth from Mount Sinai."

The meaning of "﴿grows with oil﴾" is that it grows accompanied by oil, so the ba' is for accompaniment (al-mulabasah).

This verse is an example of the ba' of accompaniment, and accompaniment is a broad meaning. The accompaniment of the olive tree's growth with oil and seasoning is an accompaniment through the accompaniment of its fruit with oil and seasoning, for its fruit contains the oil, which constitutes both grease and condiment for those who eat. As for its being grease, people anoint their bodies with it, comb their hair with it, and put perfumes in it, so they comb their hair with it; and the Prophet ﷺ used to anoint his head with oil.

"Duhn" with a damma on the dal is the name of what is applied to something, i.e. with which something is smeared, and "duhn" is applied to oil in view of its being smeared on the body for treatment and on the hair for combing.

"Sibgh," with a kasra on the sad, is what something is dyed with, i.e. what changes the colour by it. Then its use was extended to every liquid with which the outer surface of some body is smeared; from this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the dye of God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 138]. Oil was called "sibgh" because bread is dipped (yusbagh) in it. The coordination of "sibgh" with "duhn" is in view of the difference in what the derivation of the descriptive term indicates: "sibgh" is what something is dipped in, and "duhn" is what something is smeared with. "Sibgh" is more specific; so it is of the type of coordinating the specific with the general for emphasis. They used to dip their food in it, and that is a condiment for food. At-Tirmidhi related in his Sunan from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and from Abu Usayd that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Eat the oil and anoint yourselves with it, for it is from a blessed tree."

The majority read "tanbutu" with a fatha on the ta' and a damma on the ba' (تَنْبُتُ), while Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ruways and Ya'qub read it with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the ba' (تُنْبِتُ), according to the dialect of those who say anbata meaning nabata, or with the object omitted, i.e. it (the tree) produces its fruit, meaning it brings it forth.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 23, verse 18–20 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And We sent down water from the sky in a measured amount, and We lodged it in the earth; and indeed, We are able to take it away.﴾ ﴿Then We produced for you thereby gardens of date palms and grapevines, in which you have abundant fruits, and from which you eat.﴾ ﴿And a tree that springs from Mount Sinai, which grows with oil and a relish for those who eat.﴾

The occasion for connecting the sending down of rain water to the sentence ﴿And We created above you seven paths﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 17] is that rain water descends from the direction of the sky, i.e., from the side of the sky.

In the sending down of rain water there is a proof of the breadth of knowledge and the subtlety of power, and in it also is a favour upon creation. So the speech is a call to reflection and an expression of favour, from His saying ﴿We produced for you thereby gardens﴾ to the end of it. The meaning of this verse has already been explained in Surat al-An'am, Surat al-Ra'd and Surat al-Nahl.

The sending down of water is its dropping from the clouds as water, snow and hail upon the plains and the mountains.

صفحة ٢٩

The word qadar (measure) here means determination and specification of a quantity, both in amount and in its timing. It may therefore be taken in its plain sense, i.e., in a specific measure suited to the bounty of it; for when it is sent down in this way, irrigation and continuity are achieved by it, and likewise the melting of the falling snow. It is also permissible that, alongside this, the meaning intended is a metaphor for precision and perfection. The meaning of qadar here is not the sense found in the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "And that you believe in qadar, its good and its evil."

The word iskan (lodging) means placing a thing in a dwelling, and the maskan is the place of settling; it is a maf'al, a noun of place derived from sukun (rest). Lodging is used figuratively for settling in the earth. This settling is of two kinds: a short settling, like the settling of rain water in the outer crust of the earth immediately after the rains fall, according to what the abundance of the rain, the softness of the earth, and the intensity of heat or cold require. By it plants grow in the cultivated land and herbage in spring, and trees draw from it through their roots and so bear their fruit, and the roots and bases of trees emerge from the seeds that are in the earth.

The other kind is a long settling, which is the settling of waters that fall as rain and from the melting of falling snow, which seep into the inner parts of the earth, from which springs arise that gush forth by themselves, or are made to flow as wells by digging.

The clause ﴿And indeed, We are able to take it away﴾ is an interposed sentence between the preceding sentence and what branches from it; in this there is a reminder that the power of God the Exalted is capable of bringing into being and of annihilating.

In al-Kashshaf: (It — i.e., what is in this verse — is more emphatic in threat than His saying: ﴿Say: Have you considered, if your water should become sunken, who would bring you clear water?﴾ [al-Mulk: 30]) end.

As al-Sakkaki did in explaining the features of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And it was said: O earth, swallow your water﴾ [Hud: 44], the verse, in the section on fluency and eloquence from al-Miftah; and he said at the end of his speech: (Do not suppose that the verse is confined to what I have mentioned, for perhaps what I left out is more than what I mentioned; for the aim was only to guide to the manner of gathering the fruits of the two sciences of meanings and expression.)

صفحة ٣٣

And we may say: the verse of Surat al-Mu'minun is intended for warning and threat of the removal of that great blessing, whereas the verse of Surat al-Mulk is intended for taking lesson from God the Exalted's power to remove it. The difference of the two contexts has an effect on the difference of the requirements; so the verse of Surat al-Mu'minun was more suited, with an abundance of features appropriate to the context of warning and threat, without neglecting the extraction of features in it, which we may touch upon when we reach it.

Moreover, Surat al-Mulk was revealed directly after Surat al-Mu'minun, and the revelation of some of it may overlap with the revelation of part of Surat al-Mu'minun. So when the verse of Surat al-Mu'minun was fully elaborated with the particulars that the context required, it sufficed without the like of it in its counterpart in Surat al-Mulk; so in the second it took the path of brevity, due to the closeness of its time to its counterpart.

The making of the gardens is from the handiwork of God the Exalted: first the growing of gardens on the earth; and after that gardens were grown by human planting; and that too is from the handiwork of God, through what He placed in minds of knowledge of planting, sowing, watering, channelling water and bringing it from afar. So all this making is from God the Exalted.

And the garden (jannah) is a place with trees. Its usage is mostly applied to what contains date palms and vines. It has already been mentioned at His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Like a garden on a height﴾ [al-Baqarah: 265], the verse, in Surat al-Baqarah.

What is mentioned here of the three kinds of trees is the most noble of trees and the most beneficial in fruit: they are the date palm, the grapevine and the olive; and the discussion of date palms, grapevines and olives has already preceded in Surat al-An'am and in Surat al-Nahl.

Fawakih is the plural of fakihah, which is food by which one enjoys oneself through eating, i.e., is delighted by its taste without intending sustenance; if it is intended as sustenance, it is called ta'am (food). Among foods there is that which is both fakihah and ta'am, like dates and grapes, for they are eaten fresh and dried; and among them is that which is fakihah but not ta'am, like almonds and pears; and among them is that which is ta'am but not fakihah, like the olive. For this reason the mention of the olive tree was put after its two siblings, because what is intended is the favour of what is in their fruit of enjoyment and sustenance; so it is a favour concerning the needful and the embellishing.

صفحة ٣٤

He described the fawakih as ﴿abundant﴾ in view of the difference of kinds, such as unripe dates, ripe dates and dried dates, and such as olive oil and fresh grapes; and also in view of the abundance of fruiting of these two trees.

(And a tree) is conjoined to (gardens), i.e., And We brought forth for you thereby a tree that springs from Mount Sinai, and it is the olive tree; and the clause (springs) is an attribute of (a tree).

Its specification by mention, together with the implicit fact that people eat from it, is an honouring of its status and a hint at the abundance of its benefits; for from its fruit come food, remedy and healing, and from its wood fuel and other things. In a hadith: "Eat the oil and anoint yourselves with it, for it comes from a blessed tree."

Tur Sina' is a mountain in the desert of Sinai, which lies between the Gulf of Aqaba and Egypt, and which in ancient times was among the lands of Palestine; and upon it Moses communed with his Lord, the Exalted. Its discussion has already preceded in Surat al-A'raf at His saying: ﴿But look upon the mountain﴾ [al-A'raf: 143]. The name Tur came to be dominant without an addition, and it is Tur Sina' or Tur Sinin. The meaning of tur is the mountain. Sina' is said to be the name of a tree that abounds there; and it is said to be the name of stones; and it is said to be the name of that place. It is said to be a Nabataean name, and it is said to be an Abyssinian name, but this is not correct. Those who said it were deceived only by the resemblance of this name to the attribute of beauty in the Abyssinian language, which is the word: sanah. Such resemblance has given rise to errors.

Ya' of "Sayna'" (سَيْناءَ) was given dead sukun, and this is how the majority (al-Jumhur) read it. It is also permissible to pronounce it with a fatha and with a living sukun on the ya', and this is how Ibn Kathir, 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it. In both readings it is diptote (mamnu' min al-sarf). In the reading with kasra, it is said to be diptote because of its being a proper noun (al-'alamiyyah) and its being non-Arabic (al-'ujmah), since the pattern fa'ila' (فَعِلاءَ), when its middle radical is original, does not have its alif as the feminine marker but as an extension (lil-ilhaq), and the alif of extension does not prevent declension. In the reading with fatha, its prohibition from declension is due to the alif of feminine marking, since the pattern fa'alaa' (فَعَلاءَ) is one of the patterns of the feminine alif.

His words, "﴿comes forth from Mount Sinai﴾," imply that it has a special connection with Mount Sinai, and the reason for this has been obscure. What I consider to be the case is that "coming forth" (al-khuruj) is used with the meaning of coming into being and taking form, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then We brought forth with it pairs of various plants﴾ [Ta-Ha: 53], and His saying: ﴿He brings forth with it crops of varying colours﴾ [az-Zumar: 21]. This is because the true meaning of khuruj is emerging from a place. Since every created thing emerges after non-existence, and since a place is necessary for every newly come-into-being thing, the appearance of a thing after it was non-existent was likened to the emergence of a thing from the place in which it had been hidden. This is a widespread metaphor in the Qur'an.

So it appears that the meaning is that God created the first olive tree in Mount Sinai. This is because the kinds and species existing on the terrestrial globe must have places where their existence first began, prior to their existence elsewhere, since some places are more favourable for the origin of some existing things than others, owing to a suitability between the nature of the place and the nature of the thing existing in it, whether heat, cold or moderateness. Likewise the seasons of the year: spring suits some animals, winter others, and summer others. God brings existing things into being in the conditions suited to them, and animals and plants all proceed according to this law.

Then, when people transport an animal or plant from one land to another, or wish to benefit from it in a season other than its own, and they see that the place or time to which it has been moved is unsuitable, they resort to means that make up for its deficiency, such as warming it in severe cold or cooling it by bathing in water during intense heat, so that the propagation of that transported thing is not impeded in a place other than its own. Just as some animals or plants do not live long in some regions unsuited to their natures, such as the gazelle in lands of snow, so too some places within a suitable region may be more fitting for an animal or plant than other parts of that region. Perhaps the climate of Mount Sinai, by its being midway between the extreme regions of heat and cold, and by the middling height of its elevation between highlands and plains, is more favourable to the nature of the olive family, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿an olive tree neither of the east nor of the west﴾ [an-Nur: 35]. So God, exalted is He, prepared that place for its creation when He willed to create it, just as He prepared a special clay for the creation of Adam, when He said: ﴿He created man from clay like pottery﴾ [ar-Rahman: 14]. Then the olive tree was transported from the first place where it appeared to other places to which its inhabitants carried it for benefit. It succeeded in some of them and did not succeed in others.

It is established in the Torah that the olive tree existed before the Flood and after it. In Chapter 8 of the Book of Genesis: Noah sent out a dove seeking a place from which the waters of the Flood had receded, and the dove returned in the evening carrying in its beak a fresh olive leaf, so Noah knew that the water had begun to recede from the earth.

It is known that the first receding of the water is revealed on the summits of the mountains, so perhaps the olive leaf that the dove carried was from a tree in Mount Sinai.

Whatever the case, Noah recognised the olive leaf, which indicates that they knew this tree before the Flood. However, no mention is found of the use of olive oil in food in ancient history except in the time of Moses, peace be upon him, when the Children of Israel were around Mount Sinai. Oil was used to light the Tent of Meeting by God's revelation to Moses, and Moses poured the anointing oil upon the head of his brother Aaron when he appointed him priest over the Children of Israel.

It is also possible that the meaning of "comes forth" is "appears and becomes known," so that the first human awareness of the benefits of this tree and its transport came from the olive tree that is in Mount Sinai. This is like how we in our country call the turkey "the Indian hen," because people knew it from the lands of India; and as some swords in the lands of the Arabs are called "al-Mashrafiyyah," because they were known from the outskirts of Syria (mashariq al-Sham); and some spears are called "al-Khattiyyah," because they came to the lands of the Arabs from a port called al-Khatt; and some swords are called "al-Muhannad," because they are brought from India. Oil was brought to the lands of the Arabs from Syria and from Palestine.

Whatever the case, the purpose of mentioning that it comes forth from Mount Sinai is only to point out that this is its original place of growth. Otherwise, the favour of it was not then directed to the inhabitants of Mount Sinai. This indication was only to highlight the nobility of its place of origin and the generosity of the land in which it appeared. The olive tree has remained famous for blessing among people. I have seen in Lisan al-'Arab, from al-Asma'i, from 'Abd al-Malik ibn Salih: that every olive tree in Palestine is planted by peoples called the Greeks (al-Yunaniyyun), end quote. The apparent meaning is that he means by it the olive trees of their time, which they had replaced with ancient trees that had perished.

In Greek myths (mythology) it is said that Minerva and Neptune (the two gods in Greek belief) disputed over which of them would name a city that they had founded (Cecrops). The gods judged between them that this honour would be attained only by whoever produces the most useful thing. As for Neptune, he produced a great and powerful sea-horse; as for Minerva, she produced the olive tree with its fruit. So the gods ruled that she was more deserving, and therefore they named the city Athens, which is the name of Minerva. They also claimed that Hercules, when he returned from some of his expeditions, brought with him branches of olive, and planted them on the mountain of Olympus, which in their belief was the dwelling of their gods.

Olive oil was used among the Greeks from the time of Homer, for he mentioned in the Iliad that Achilles poured oil over the body of Patroclus and the body of Hector.

Oil was rare in most of the lands of the Arabs, as it was brought to the lands of the Arabs from Syria.

God has also used the olive tree's oil as a parable for His light, in His saying: ﴿The parable of His light is like a niche within which is a lamp, the lamp is in a glass, the glass as if it were a pearly star, lit from a blessed olive tree, neither of the east nor of the west, whose oil would almost glow even if no fire touched it. Light upon light﴾ [an-Nur: 35].

The use of the present tense in His saying, "﴿comes forth from Mount Sinai﴾," is to call to mind the wondrous and important image in which that tree was formed at the beginning of its creation, so that the hearer almost sees it coming forth with vegetation at Mount Sinai. This is like His saying: ﴿And when you shape from clay the likeness of a bird﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 110]. This is more suited to the first interpretation of the meaning of "comes forth from Mount Sinai."

The meaning of "﴿grows with oil﴾" is that it grows accompanied by oil, so the ba' is for accompaniment (al-mulabasah).

This verse is an example of the ba' of accompaniment, and accompaniment is a broad meaning. The accompaniment of the olive tree's growth with oil and seasoning is an accompaniment through the accompaniment of its fruit with oil and seasoning, for its fruit contains the oil, which constitutes both grease and condiment for those who eat. As for its being grease, people anoint their bodies with it, comb their hair with it, and put perfumes in it, so they comb their hair with it; and the Prophet ﷺ used to anoint his head with oil.

"Duhn" with a damma on the dal is the name of what is applied to something, i.e. with which something is smeared, and "duhn" is applied to oil in view of its being smeared on the body for treatment and on the hair for combing.

"Sibgh," with a kasra on the sad, is what something is dyed with, i.e. what changes the colour by it. Then its use was extended to every liquid with which the outer surface of some body is smeared; from this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the dye of God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 138]. Oil was called "sibgh" because bread is dipped (yusbagh) in it. The coordination of "sibgh" with "duhn" is in view of the difference in what the derivation of the descriptive term indicates: "sibgh" is what something is dipped in, and "duhn" is what something is smeared with. "Sibgh" is more specific; so it is of the type of coordinating the specific with the general for emphasis. They used to dip their food in it, and that is a condiment for food. At-Tirmidhi related in his Sunan from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and from Abu Usayd that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Eat the oil and anoint yourselves with it, for it is from a blessed tree."

The majority read "tanbutu" with a fatha on the ta' and a damma on the ba' (تَنْبُتُ), while Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ruways and Ya'qub read it with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the ba' (تُنْبِتُ), according to the dialect of those who say anbata meaning nabata, or with the object omitted, i.e. it (the tree) produces its fruit, meaning it brings it forth.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 23, verses 21–22:**

﴿And indeed, in the cattle there is a lesson for you. We give you to drink from what is in their bellies, and for you in them are many benefits, and from them you eat.﴾ ﴿And upon them and upon the ship you are carried.﴾

This conjunction (*'atf*) is like the conjunction of the clause ﴿And We sent down from the sky﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 18]. In it, too, there is both an argument (*istidlal*) and a favour (*minnah*).

The *'ibrah* (lesson, sign) is the proof, because one passes over (*yu'bar*) from knowing it to another knowledge. The meaning is: in the cattle there is a proof of God Most High's sole creation, the completeness of His power, and the breadth of His knowledge.

*Al-an'am* (the cattle) was previously said to refer, in the general usage of the Arabs, to camels.

The clause ﴿We give you to drink from what is in their bellies﴾ explains the clause ﴿And indeed, in the cattle there is a lesson for you﴾. For this reason it is not conjoined, since it occupies the position of an explicative apposition (*'atf al-bayan*, a conjunction serving as explanation).

The *'ibrah* is achieved from the formation of the milk in their bellies, which is indicated by ﴿We give you to drink﴾. As for ﴿We give you to drink﴾ on its own, it is a favour. A parallel of this verse was discussed in detail in Surah al-Nahl.

The clause ﴿and for you in them are many benefits﴾ and what follows it are conjoined to the clause ﴿We give you to drink from what is in their bellies﴾, since it contains the remainder of the explanation of the lesson, and likewise the clauses after it. These benefits are the wool, the fur, the hair, and the offspring.

As for eating from them, it is also a lesson, since God made them suitable for nourishing mankind with their flesh, which is pleasant in taste, and inspired the methods of roasting, boiling, and cooking it. In this there is a great and manifest favour.

The same applies to the meaning of ﴿and upon them you are carried﴾: in it there is a lesson in God Most High's preparing them for this, and in it there is a manifest favour. The word *haml* (carrying) covers both riding and bearing loads.

[Page 40]

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Bakr, on the authority of 'Asim, read ﴿نَسْقِيكُمْ﴾ with a *fatha* on the *nun*. The rest, except Abu Ja'far, read it with a *damma* on the *nun*. It is said: *saqahu* and *asqahu* have the same meaning. Abu Ja'far read it with a feminine *ta'* (تَسْقِيكُمْ) with a *fatha*, on the basis that the pronoun refers to the cattle.

The conjunction ﴿and upon the ship﴾ is an *idmaj* (interweaving of themes) and a preparation for a smooth transition to the story of Noah.
