Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 23, verses 23–25:

﴿Indeed, We sent Noah to his people, and he said: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. Will you not then be wary of Him?"﴾ ﴿So the chiefs of those among his people who disbelieved said: "This is none but a human being like you, who wants to make himself superior over you. Had Allah willed, He would have sent down angels. We never heard of this among our forefathers of old."﴾ ﴿He is only a man possessed by madness, so wait concerning him for a while.﴾

Since the argument and the favour that preceded were directed at the polytheists who disbelieved in the Prophet ﷺ, and who used as their excuse that they do not believe in the prophethood of a human being like themselves, and asked for the sending down of angels, and branded the Messenger ﷺ with madness, then, because they resembled the people of Noah and those who came after them, it was fitting that the people of Noah be cited to them as an example, as a warning against what befell the people of Noah of punishment. In the course of the argument and the favour, the mention of being carried in the ship occurred, and this was an occasion for the transition, so the good transition (husn al-takhallus) was achieved. Accordingly, the mention of the stories of the Messengers is considered either as a digression (istitrad) within the argument for the Oneness (wahdaniyyah), or as a transition, as will come at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And it is He who produced for you hearing and sight﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 78].

The opening of the sentence with the lam of oath (lam al-qasam) is an emphasis on the threatening content of the story; the meaning is the affirmation of the sending to Noah and what followed it.

The conjunction of Noah's speech to the sending, with the fa' of sequence (fa' al-ta'qib), serves to indicate that he delivered the message of his Lord immediately upon His command, and this is the manner of compliance.

His command to his people to worship Allah implies that they had turned away from the worship of Allah by devoting themselves to the worship of their idols: (Wadd, Suwa', Yaghuth, Ya'uq, and Nasr), until they neglected and forgot the worship of Allah. Likewise, Noah's call to his people is related in most verses in the form of a command to the basic worship of Allah, without the command to restrict their worship to Allah alone, with an indication that they did not deny the existence of Allah. Therefore he followed his words with: ﴿you have no god other than Him﴾.

This is indicated by their saying: ﴿Had Allah willed, He would have sent down angels﴾, for they affirm the existence of Allah. So the clause ﴿you have no god other than Him﴾ is in the position of a reason (ta'lil) for the command to worship Him, and it is a more specific reason than what it explains, and it is more fitting because of its brevity, as it implies the meaning: worship Allah alone. The meaning is: worship Allah, whom you have abandoned in worship, and He is your God, apart from whom there is none; so none other than Him deserves worship, so do not worship your idols along with Him.

"Ghayruhu" (other than Him) is an attribute (na't) of "ilah" (god). The majority read it with the raf' (nominative), considering the position of the modified noun, since the modified noun is governed by a superfluous preposition (harf jarr za'id). Al-Kisa'i read it with the jarr (genitive), considering the word as governed by the superfluous preposition.

Upon the command to single Him out in worship, there follows a interrogative of denunciation regarding their failure to guard against the punishment of Allah, exalted is He. In relating the reply of the chiefs of his people, the customary manner of the Qur'an in relating dialogues has been departed from, namely omitting the conjunction, which is the manner in His saying: ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed I will place upon the earth a khalifah"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30] in Surat al-Baqarah. Here the reply of the chiefs of his people is conjoined with fa' for two reasons:

The first: they did not direct their speech to him, but left him, and turned to their people, refuting for them what Noah had called them to.

The second: to convey that they hastened to deny him and to discredit his call before considering it. The description of the chiefs as "those who disbelieved" is to hint that their disbelief is what caused them to speak this rejection of Noah, and it is an allusion that such a rejection has no substance, but they circulated their disbelief through it, out of fear for the loss of their dominion.

"Min qawmihi" (from among his people) is a second attribute.

The saying of the chiefs of his people: ﴿This is none but a human being like you﴾ was addressed by some of them to others, since the chiefs (mala') are the people of leadership and standing, meaning: the great men of the people said to their common folk.

Their information that he is a human being like them is used figuratively (kinayah) to denounce his claim to messengerhood, by means of a proof drawn from his very nature; they gave them to understand that equality in humanity prevents mediation between Allah and His creation, and this is one of the illusions that misled many nations. The demonstrative "this" refers to Noah, and it implies that the speech of the chiefs took place in the presence of Noah at the time of his call; they shifted from his proper name to the demonstrative because their intent was to belittle his matter and to disparage him in the eyes of the common people, so that they would not accept his words. A parallel of this has already occurred in Surat Hud.

This story is augmented by the citation of their saying: ﴿who wants to make himself superior over you﴾, for the leaders of the people thought that he had come with that call only out of love to be made master over their people, so they feared that their dominion would vanish, and in their ignorance they do not reflect on the states of souls, nor look to the interests of people, but they measure others by the measure of themselves.

Since the aspirations of their own souls were love of leadership and seeking it by standing to serve the idols, they imagined that the one who came to nullify the worship of idols only intended to contest their authority.

Tafaddul (to show favour) means seeking and assuming superiority; fadl originally means excess, then it became common for an increase in nobility and rank, that is, that he should be the most excellent of people, because he had classed them all as being in error.

Their saying: ﴿Had Allah willed, He would have sent down angels﴾ is coordinated (atf) upon the clause ﴿This is none but a human being like you﴾, after they had prepared for it by stating that humanity prevents its bearer from being a messenger of Allah.

The object of the verb of will is omitted, since it is evident from the response of (law), meaning: had Allah willed the sending of a messenger, He would have sent down angels as messengers. The omission of the object of the verb of will is permissible when context indicates it, and that is of the kinds of brevity. It is not restricted to the strange object, as the author of al-Miftah said. Do you not see the saying of al-Ma'arri:

"If you wish, claim that whoever is upon her back is your slave, and call your God to witness, He will witness."
And is there anything stranger than this claim, if strangeness required the mention of the object of will? Since the object of the response of the conditional clause indicates it, its omission from the protasis is good.

The clause ﴿We never heard of this among our forefathers of old﴾ is independent (mustan'afah), by which they intended to deny the call after denying the caller; therefore it was brought as an independent clause, not conjoined, to alert that it is intended in itself and is not a completion of what precedes it, unlike the style of conjoining the clause ﴿Had Allah willed, He would have sent down angels﴾, since its content is part of the purpose of what precedes it.

So the demonstrative "this" refers to the speech that Noah uttered, meaning: we never heard that there is no god for us other than Allah in the time of our forefathers. The intended meaning of the demonstrative is the sense of the speech, not its very words, and this is a common usage. Since the particle of time requires a period of time, its complement must be understood with an elided genitive, meaning: in the period of our forefathers, because "the forefathers" cannot serve as a time-locative.

"The forefathers of old" are the grandfathers.

Since the negated hearing is not hearing with their ears of speech in the time of their fathers, but the intended meaning is: there has not reached us the occurrence of the like of this in the time of our fathers, the verb "heard" has been construed with "bi" to imply the sense of connection (ittisal). They made their lack of knowledge of a thing a proof against the falsehood of that thing, and this is a sophistical argument, since lack of knowledge may result from neglect in acquiring knowledge, and it may result from the absence of a cause requiring the occurrence of its like, namely that people were upon the truth, so there was no reason to address them with such a thing. The people from the time of Adam were upon the natural disposition (fitrah) until polytheism arose among people, and so Allah sent Noah; he is thus the first messenger sent to the people of the earth, as is related in the hadith of the intercession.

﴿He is only a man possessed by madness﴾ is an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), because all that they said stirs in the souls of the hearers the question: if this is the state of his call in falsehood and deceit, then what prompted him to make such claims? It is answered that a defect has befallen his intellect, so he sought what he could not attain, like what all people could not attain, given their classification as being in error. He aspired to what no sensible person would aspire to in its like, so his aspiration indicates that he is mad.

The tanwin in "jinnah" (madness) is for indefiniteness of kind, meaning: he is affected with some degree of madness. This is a moderation on their part regarding his condition, in that they guarded themselves against implicating themselves in describing him with derangement, although what is observed of his condition contradicts that; so they gave their people to understand that he has a slight madness whose effects are not clearly apparent.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 23, verses 23–25:

﴿Indeed, We sent Noah to his people, and he said: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. Will you not then be wary of Him?"﴾ ﴿So the chiefs of those among his people who disbelieved said: "This is none but a human being like you, who wants to make himself superior over you. Had Allah willed, He would have sent down angels. We never heard of this among our forefathers of old."﴾ ﴿He is only a man possessed by madness, so wait concerning him for a while.﴾

Since the argument and the favour that preceded were directed at the polytheists who disbelieved in the Prophet ﷺ, and who used as their excuse that they do not believe in the prophethood of a human being like themselves, and asked for the sending down of angels, and branded the Messenger ﷺ with madness, then, because they resembled the people of Noah and those who came after them, it was fitting that the people of Noah be cited to them as an example, as a warning against what befell the people of Noah of punishment. In the course of the argument and the favour, the mention of being carried in the ship occurred, and this was an occasion for the transition, so the good transition (husn al-takhallus) was achieved. Accordingly, the mention of the stories of the Messengers is considered either as a digression (istitrad) within the argument for the Oneness (wahdaniyyah), or as a transition, as will come at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And it is He who produced for you hearing and sight﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 78].

The opening of the sentence with the lam of oath (lam al-qasam) is an emphasis on the threatening content of the story; the meaning is the affirmation of the sending to Noah and what followed it.

The conjunction of Noah's speech to the sending, with the fa' of sequence (fa' al-ta'qib), serves to indicate that he delivered the message of his Lord immediately upon His command, and this is the manner of compliance.

His command to his people to worship Allah implies that they had turned away from the worship of Allah by devoting themselves to the worship of their idols: (Wadd, Suwa', Yaghuth, Ya'uq, and Nasr), until they neglected and forgot the worship of Allah. Likewise, Noah's call to his people is related in most verses in the form of a command to the basic worship of Allah, without the command to restrict their worship to Allah alone, with an indication that they did not deny the existence of Allah. Therefore he followed his words with: ﴿you have no god other than Him﴾.

This is indicated by their saying: ﴿Had Allah willed, He would have sent down angels﴾, for they affirm the existence of Allah. So the clause ﴿you have no god other than Him﴾ is in the position of a reason (ta'lil) for the command to worship Him, and it is a more specific reason than what it explains, and it is more fitting because of its brevity, as it implies the meaning: worship Allah alone. The meaning is: worship Allah, whom you have abandoned in worship, and He is your God, apart from whom there is none; so none other than Him deserves worship, so do not worship your idols along with Him.

"Ghayruhu" (other than Him) is an attribute (na't) of "ilah" (god). The majority read it with the raf' (nominative), considering the position of the modified noun, since the modified noun is governed by a superfluous preposition (harf jarr za'id). Al-Kisa'i read it with the jarr (genitive), considering the word as governed by the superfluous preposition.

Upon the command to single Him out in worship, there follows a interrogative of denunciation regarding their failure to guard against the punishment of Allah, exalted is He. In relating the reply of the chiefs of his people, the customary manner of the Qur'an in relating dialogues has been departed from, namely omitting the conjunction, which is the manner in His saying: ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed I will place upon the earth a khalifah"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30] in Surat al-Baqarah. Here the reply of the chiefs of his people is conjoined with fa' for two reasons:

The first: they did not direct their speech to him, but left him, and turned to their people, refuting for them what Noah had called them to.

The second: to convey that they hastened to deny him and to discredit his call before considering it. The description of the chiefs as "those who disbelieved" is to hint that their disbelief is what caused them to speak this rejection of Noah, and it is an allusion that such a rejection has no substance, but they circulated their disbelief through it, out of fear for the loss of their dominion.

"Min qawmihi" (from among his people) is a second attribute.

The saying of the chiefs of his people: ﴿This is none but a human being like you﴾ was addressed by some of them to others, since the chiefs (mala') are the people of leadership and standing, meaning: the great men of the people said to their common folk.

Their information that he is a human being like them is used figuratively (kinayah) to denounce his claim to messengerhood, by means of a proof drawn from his very nature; they gave them to understand that equality in humanity prevents mediation between Allah and His creation, and this is one of the illusions that misled many nations. The demonstrative "this" refers to Noah, and it implies that the speech of the chiefs took place in the presence of Noah at the time of his call; they shifted from his proper name to the demonstrative because their intent was to belittle his matter and to disparage him in the eyes of the common people, so that they would not accept his words. A parallel of this has already occurred in Surat Hud.

This story is augmented by the citation of their saying: ﴿who wants to make himself superior over you﴾, for the leaders of the people thought that he had come with that call only out of love to be made master over their people, so they feared that their dominion would vanish, and in their ignorance they do not reflect on the states of souls, nor look to the interests of people, but they measure others by the measure of themselves.

Since the aspirations of their own souls were love of leadership and seeking it by standing to serve the idols, they imagined that the one who came to nullify the worship of idols only intended to contest their authority.

Tafaddul (to show favour) means seeking and assuming superiority; fadl originally means excess, then it became common for an increase in nobility and rank, that is, that he should be the most excellent of people, because he had classed them all as being in error.

Their saying: ﴿Had Allah willed, He would have sent down angels﴾ is coordinated (atf) upon the clause ﴿This is none but a human being like you﴾, after they had prepared for it by stating that humanity prevents its bearer from being a messenger of Allah.

The object of the verb of will is omitted, since it is evident from the response of (law), meaning: had Allah willed the sending of a messenger, He would have sent down angels as messengers. The omission of the object of the verb of will is permissible when context indicates it, and that is of the kinds of brevity. It is not restricted to the strange object, as the author of al-Miftah said. Do you not see the saying of al-Ma'arri:

"If you wish, claim that whoever is upon her back is your slave, and call your God to witness, He will witness."
And is there anything stranger than this claim, if strangeness required the mention of the object of will? Since the object of the response of the conditional clause indicates it, its omission from the protasis is good.

Since the particle of time requires a period of time, its complement must be understood with an elided genitive, meaning: in the period of our forefathers, because "the forefathers" cannot serve as a time-locative.

"The forefathers of old" are the grandfathers.

Since the negated hearing is not hearing with their ears of speech in the time of their fathers, but the intended meaning is: there has not reached us the occurrence of the like of this in the time of our fathers, the verb "heard" has been construed with "bi" to imply the sense of connection (ittisal). He aspired to what no sensible person would aspire to in its like, so his aspiration indicates that he is mad.

Resumptive explanatory clause (istinaf bayani): what was related about their hindering people from believing Noah's call, and the slander they fabricated by accusing him of madness, raises the question of what Noah did when his people denied him. The answer is that he said: ﴿My Lord, help me, because they denied me﴾, and so on.

His supplication for help implies that he regarded their treatment of him as aggression against him in his capacity as a messenger from his Lord.

Naṣr (help) means enabling the one who has been wronged to prevail over the aggressor. Noah asked for help in a general sense, as related here. God informed him that there was no hope in the faith of his people except for those among them who believed, as came in Surat Hud. There was therefore no hope that his help would take the form of their return to obedience, belief in him, and following his religion. At that point Noah asked for a specific help, namely the destruction of those who did not believe, as came in Surat Nuh: ﴿Noah said, "My Lord, leave not upon the earth any dweller from among the disbelievers"﴾ [Nuh: 26] ﴿"For if You leave them, they will mislead Your servants"﴾ [Nuh: 27]. The sequence expressed in God's words here, ﴿Then We revealed to him﴾, is a sequence with omitted intervening sentences, as you know. It is an abridgment in the narration of the story, like His words: ﴿Strike the sea with your staff, and it parted﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 63], and so on in Surat al-Shu'ara.

The bi- in ﴿with what they denied me﴾ is causal (sababiyya) and occupies the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the help derived from the verb of supplication. That is, help that is conditioned by their denial. He set aside his own share in what they had transgressed against and gave priority to the share of the message from God, because aggression against the Messenger is a belittling of the One who sent him.

The clause (﴿an isna' al-fulk﴾, "that you make the ark") is an explanatory clause for "We revealed" (awhayna), because the verb "awhayna" carries the meaning of saying without its letters. A parallel to the clause ﴿And make the ark under Our eyes and Our inspiration﴾ [Hud: 37] has already been discussed in Surat Hud.

Following the command to build the ark, there is a detailed statement of what he is to do when the need to use the ark arises. Its use is timed to the moment of necessity, to deliver the believers and the animals.

The discussion of the meaning of ﴿the oven boiled over﴾ and of ﴿two of each pair, and your family, except those against whom the word has already gone forth﴾ has already been given in Surat Hud.

The zawj (pair) is a name for everything that has another thing attached to it such that it makes it a pair in some state. This was discussed in Surat Hud. There, the expression used was ﴿We said, "Carry in it"﴾ [Hud: 40], and here it is ﴿then thread (usluk) into it﴾. The reason is that the verse of Surat Hud relates what God addressed to him at the occurrence of the Flood, which was a narrow time, so he was commanded to carry aboard the ship those whom God wished to preserve. Thus the carrying was attributed to Noah as a figurative description of the speed in loading into the ship what had been assigned to it, as though his action in bringing them in were that of one who carries something to place it in a location. The verse of this surah relates what God addressed to him before the Flood occurred, informing him of what he would do when the Flood occurred. So he was commanded that at that time he would bring into the ship those whom God had specified, along with the variety of expression in narrating the story.

The meaning of (usluk) is "enter" (adkhil). The verb salaka may be intransitive, meaning "entered," or transitive, meaning "caused to enter." From it is God's words: ﴿What brought you into Saqar?﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 42]. And the line of al-A'sha:

"As he threaded the sakki into the doorway, fayt'q"

The discussion of a phrase like His words ﴿and do not address Me concerning those who did wrong; indeed they will be drowned﴾ has already been given in Surat Hud.

The tanwin on "kullin" is a tanwin of compensation (tanwin 'iwad), which indicates an omitted element to which "kull" is attached. Its estimated sense is: "from every thing that I have commanded you to carry in the ship."

There, the expression used was ﴿We said, "Carry in it"﴾ [Hud: 40], and here it is ﴿then thread (usluk) into it﴾. The reason is that the verse of Surat Hud relates what God addressed to him at the occurrence of the Flood, which was a narrow time, so he was commanded to carry aboard the ship those whom God wished to preserve. Thus the carrying was attributed to Noah as a figurative description of the speed in loading into the ship what had been assigned to it, as though his action in bringing them in were that of one who carries something to place it in a location. The verse of this surah relates what God addressed to him before the Flood occurred, informing him of what he would do when the Flood occurred. So he was commanded that at that time he would bring into the ship those whom God had specified, along with the variety of expression in narrating the story.

The meaning of (usluk) is "enter" (adkhil). The verb salaka may be intransitive, meaning "entered," or transitive, meaning "caused to enter." From it is God's words: ﴿What brought you into Saqar?﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 42]. And the line of al-A'sha:

"As he threaded the sakki into the doorway, fayt'q"

The discussion of a phrase like His words ﴿and do not address Me concerning those who did wrong; indeed they will be drowned﴾ has already been given in Surat Hud.

The majority of readers (al-Jumhur) read ﴿from every pair of two﴾ with "kull" in the construct form (idafa) to "zawjayn." Hafs read "kullin" with tanwin, so that "zawjayn" is the object of "usluk." The tanwin on "kullin" is a tanwin of compensation (tanwin 'iwad), which indicates an omitted element to which "kull" is attached. Its estimated sense is: "from every thing that I have commanded you to carry in the ship."

﴿Then when you and those with you are settled upon the ship, say: "All praise is for Allah, who has delivered us from the wrongdoing people." And say: "My Lord, let me land at a blessed landing place, and You are the best of those who bring to land."﴾

Al-istiwa' (settling, rising to a position) means al-i'tila' (elevation). It has already been discussed at His saying, ﴿Then He established Himself upon the Throne﴾ [al-A'raf: 54], in Surat al-A'raf.

Using al-istiwa' to mean settling inside the ship is a majaz mursal (a figurative usage in which a word is used for something related to its literal meaning) through the relation of the general sense (ʿalaqat al-ita'). Otherwise, the literal meaning of settling in the ship would be entering it. The particle of elevation (ʿala) is used rather than the particle of place (fi), because it is the particle that takes the sense of elevation, indicating firm establishment within the ship. Thus it is a tarshih (a supporting detail that reinforces the figurative sense) for the metaphor.

Al-tanjiya (deliverance) from the wrongdoing people means being delivered from their harm and from being among them, because being among them meant witnessing their disbelief and their abominations, and this is what pains the believer.

The wrongdoing (al-zulm) may be understood as shirk (polytheism), as Allah says: ﴿Indeed, association [with Allah] is a great wrong﴾ [Luqman: 13]. It may also be understood as transgression against what is right, because the disbelievers used to harm Nuh and the believers with various kinds of harm, in falsehood and aggression. Their deliverance was a rescue because they had gathered together as a separate body, so they were safe from mingling with their enemies.

Allah had inspired him through revelation to praise his Lord for the means of salvation He had made easy for him, and to ask Him to cause him to land in a blessed place after that journey. The supplication for this includes a request for safety from the sinking of the ship. This is like the praises which Allah teaches Muhammad (ﷺ) on the Day of Intercession (yawm al-shafa'a), and in that teaching there is an indication that it will be accepted from him.

The clause ﴿and You are the best of those who bring to land﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). It also carries the meaning of giving the reason for his request.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 23, verse 30:

﴿Indeed in that are signs, and indeed We were ever testing.﴾ When he had mentioned this great story, he followed it with a reminder of the point of lesson in it for the Muslims, and so he introduced this resumptive statement for that purpose.

The reference is to what has been mentioned of the story of Nuh with his people and what is in it. The word "ayat" (signs) means proofs, i.e., there are many signs in it: some of them are proofs of the truthfulness of Nuh's prophethood, namely the answering of his supplication, the confirmation of his message, and the destruction of those who denied him; some of them are signs for the likes of the people of Nuh among the nations who denied their messengers; some of them are signs of the great power of Allah the Exalted in bringing about the Flood and in settling those in the Ark in a blessed place; and some of them are signs of the knowledge and wisdom of Allah the Exalted, in that He decreed for the purification of the earth from shirk such a general annihilation of its people, and decreed for the preservation of species such a craft by which He saved from every kind two of a pair so that reproduction might be renewed.

The clause ﴿And indeed We were ever testing﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾, because the content of "﴿And indeed We were ever testing﴾" conveys the meaning: "Indeed in that is a trial," so it is as if it were said: "Indeed in that are signs and a trial, and We are ever testing," i.e., it is Our way to test Our friends. For testing is among the effects of divine wisdom, so that the souls of His friends may be trained by it and show their striving against the satanic impulses, and so that they may attain the good outcomes of trial; and so that the souls of the obstinate may stumble and some of their evil may be curbed for a time.

The meaning: that what preceded the Flood after the sending of Nuh, of the denial of his people, their harm to him and to the believers with him, was only a trial from Allah for His wisdom, the Exalted, so that Allah might distinguish for people the wicked from the good. Had Allah willed, his people would have believed in Nuh; then, had Allah willed, He would have granted him victory over them from the first day; and this is a divine way (sunnah). In this sense is what came in the hadith of Abu Sufyan, that Heraclius said to him: "Thus are the prophets tried, and then the final outcome is theirs." And in the Qur'an: ﴿And the good outcome is for the righteous﴾ [al-A'raf: 128].

Testing (ibtila') has been mentioned in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when Ibrahim was tested by his Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124], and His saying: ﴿And in that was a great trial from your Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 49], in Surat al-Baqarah.

In His saying: ﴿And indeed We were ever testing﴾ there is consolation for the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) regarding what he encounters from the polytheists, and an indirect threat to the polytheists that what they confront the Messenger (ﷺ) with has no permanence, and that it is only a trial which will pass from him and befall them, and each has a share suited to it.

Because this is something that may escape minds, it was treated as a matter about which there is doubt, so it was emphasized with the light (mukhaffafah) "inna" and with the verb "kunna" (we were).

The lam is the one that distinguishes the emphatic light "inna" when its operation is neglected from the negating "inna" (in).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 23, verses 31–32:

﴿Then We produced after them another generation.﴾ ﴿And We sent among them a messenger from themselves, [saying]: "Worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. Will you not then fear Him?"﴾ The sequencing of the story of Noah and his people with the story of another messenger, i.e., another one, and what follows of narratives after it, is intended to show that what befell the people of Noah because of their denial of him was not by chance, but rather it is the sunnah (established way) of Allah regarding those who deny His messengers. For this reason, He did not specify the generation or generations by their names.

The qarn (generation) is the ummah (community). The more evident view is that what is meant here is Thamud, because it is what fits His saying at the end of the story: ﴿So the Cry seized them in truth﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 41], since Thamud were destroyed by the thunderbolt (al-sa'iqah)

Page 50

and because of His saying: ﴿He said, "In a little while they will surely become regretful"﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 40], together with His saying in Surat al-Hijr: ﴿So the Cry seized them at sunrise﴾ [al-Hijr: 83]. Thus their destruction was in the morning. Perhaps their being singled out for mention here, rather than 'Ad, in contrast to what is repeated in other verses, is because the lesson from their condition is more evident, since the traces of their dwellings remain at al-Hijr, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And indeed, you pass by them in the morning﴾ [al-Saffat: 137] ﴿and at night. Will you not then reason?﴾ [al-Saffat: 138].

His saying: ﴿And We sent among them a messenger﴾ means: the messenger was placed among them, and he was from them, i.e., from their tribe. The plural pronoun refers back to (qarn), because it is in the sense of (al-nas, people), as in His saying: ﴿And if two groups among the believers fight﴾ [al-Hujurat: 9].

The verb (arsalna) is transitive with (fi, in) rather than (ila, to) to convey that the messenger was from them and grew up among them; because the generation was not specified by name, so that it might be known whether their messenger was from them or came to them from outside, like Lot to the people of Sodom, Jonah to the people of Nineveh, and Moses to the Copts. The emphasis on the fact that their messenger was from them was intended, to complete the parallel between their situation and the situation of those to whom Muhammad ﷺ was sent.

The speech of their messenger is like the speech of Noah.

And (an) is an explanation of what the verb (arsalna) contains of the meaning of saying.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 23, verse 33–38 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And the chiefs of his people who disbelieved and denied the meeting of the Hereafter, and whom We had given luxury in the worldly life, said: "This is not but a human like you, who eats of what you eat and drinks of what you drink."﴾ ﴿"And if you obey a human like yourselves, then indeed you would be losers."﴾ ﴿"Does he promise you that when you have died and become dust and bones, you will be brought forth?"﴾ ﴿"Far, far is what you are promised!"﴾ ﴿"There is nothing but our worldly life: we die and we live, and we will not be resurrected."﴾ ﴿"He is not but a man who has invented a lie against Allah, and we are not believers in him."﴾

Page 51

The narration of the statement of his people is conjoined (ʿuṭifat) to the narration of his statement, and it was not presented separately, as is the custom in the narration of dialogues, as we have explained more than once in the narration of dialogues introduced by "qāla" (he said) and the like without conjunction. This has been departed from in the preceding verse for the reason we have explained, and it has also been departed from in Surat al-A'raf and Surat Hud, since the response of these people to their messenger was narrated without conjunction.

The reason for this is that the speech of the chiefs narrated here is not their speech narrated in the two surahs, because what is here is their speech addressed to their own people when they said: ﴿This is not but a human like you, who eats of what you eat and drinks of what you drink﴾ to the end of it, out of fear that the call of their messenger would affect the common people. They saw that it was more important to prevent their people's souls from being affected by the call of their messenger than to respond to their messenger, as was explained a little earlier in the story of Noah. By this the aspect of the inimitability (iʿjaz) becomes apparent in the various topics in which the author of al-Kashshaf raised a question without his answer being satisfactory, and his commentators were perplexed and disagreed.

The statement of the chiefs was not conjoined with the particle of consequence (fa') as it occurred in the story of Noah a little earlier, because their statement came later than the time of their messenger's statement, which was the opening of his call; they had answered his speech with rejection and reproach, and when he persisted in his call and repeated it among them, they directed their narrated statement here to their people. For this reason the clause of their response was conjoined, and did not come in the usual style of narrating speeches of dialogues.

Also, because the speech of their messenger was not narrated in the form of "qawl" (saying), but was narrated with the explanatory "an" (that) for what the sense of sending in His saying is implicit: ﴿Then We sent among them a messenger from themselves, [saying] "Worship Allah"﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 32].

Page 52

Allah has narrated in other verses about the people of Hud and the people of Salih that they answered the call of their messenger with rejection and reproach, as the saying of the people of Hud: ﴿They said, "O Hud, you have brought us no clear evidence, and we will not leave our gods on your word, and we are not believers in you"﴾ [Hud: 53] ﴿"We only say that some of our gods have struck you with evil"﴾ [Hud: 54]. And the saying of the people of Salih: ﴿They said, "O Salih, you were among us a man of hope before this. Do you forbid us to worship what our fathers worshipped? Indeed we are, concerning what you call us to, in disquieting doubt"﴾ [Hud: 62].

His saying: ﴿And the chiefs of his people who disbelieved﴾ (﴿who disbelieved﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 24]) is a second description (naʿt) of "al-mala'" (the chiefs), so it is in the same pattern as His saying in the story of Noah: "The chiefs of his people who disbelieved said." The description was delayed here so that the two conjoined descriptions from His saying could be attached to it: ﴿and denied the meeting of the Hereafter, and whom We had given luxury﴾.

Al-liqa' (meeting) is the presence of one person with another. The intended meaning is the meeting of Allah, exalted is He, for the reckoning, as in His saying: ﴿And know that you will meet Him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 223], in Surat al-Baqarah, and at His saying: ﴿O you who believe, when you meet a company, then stand firm﴾ [al-Anfal: 45], in Surat al-Anfal.

The annexation of "liqa'" to "al-Akhirah" is in the sense of "in" (fi), i.e., the meeting in the Hereafter.

And al-itraf is making them people of luxury (taraf). Taraf is abundant blessing. It was mentioned earlier at His saying: ﴿And return to what you were made to enjoy in it﴾ [al-Anbiya': 13], in Surat al-Anbiya'.

In these two descriptions there is an indication that they are the motive for their denial of their messenger: their denial of the meeting of the Hereafter negates for them the expectation of being held accountable after death, and their wealth and blessing incite them to arrogance and haughtiness, since they were accustomed to being lords, not followers. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And leave Me with the deniers, possessors of blessing﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 11]. Therefore they did not accept what their messenger called them to, namely guarding against the punishment of the Day of Resurrection and seeking salvation by following what he commanded them. So some of them said to others: ﴿"And if you obey a human like yourselves, then indeed you would be losers."﴾ ﴿"Does he promise you that when you have died and become dust and bones, you will be brought forth?"﴾

And ﴿This is not but a human like you﴾ is a metonymy (kinaya) for denying his claim to messengership, because they imagined that humanness is incompatible with its possessor being a messenger from Allah. So they mentioned the necessary consequence (malzum) and intended its implication (lazim).

Page 53

The clause ﴿who eats of what you eat and drinks of what you drink﴾ stands in the position of a reason and evidence for humanness, because he eats like them and drinks like them, and does not differ in what he eats or what he drinks.

The object of "tashrabun" (you drink) is omitted, being the returning pronoun of the relative clause, because it is dispensed with by its counterpart in the relative clause mentioned before it.

The lam in "wa la'in ata'tum" (and if you obey) is a preparatory lam for an oath (muwatti'a li-l-qasam), so the clause ﴿indeed you would be losers﴾ is the answer to the oath, and the answer to the condition is omitted, indicated by the answer to the oath. The particle of conditional response (harf al-jaza') was inserted into the answer to the oath because of the resemblance of the answer to the oath to a conditional response, especially when the oath is joined with a conditional particle.

The interrogation in His saying "Does he promise you" (a-ya'iduku) is for astonishment, and it is a shift from denying his claim to messengership to denying what he is sent with.

His saying "that when you have died" to the end is the object of "ya'iduku": i.e., he promises you the bringing forth of those who are brought forth. The meaning: he promises you your bringing forth from the graves after your death and the annihilation of your bodies.

As for His saying "that you will be brought forth," it may be a repetition of the first word "anna-kum" (that you), which required its repetition after explaining it and its predicate. Its repetition yields emphasis on what is asked about, an interrogation of disbelief, to emphasize its improbability. This is the interpretation of al-Jarmi and al-Mubarrad.

It is also possible that "annakum mukhrajun" is a subject (mubtada'), and His saying "when you have died and become dust and bones" is its predicate placed before it, and the clause "idha mittum ... mukhrajun" is the predicate of the first "anna" in "annakum".

They made the cause of the improbability the occurrence of states incompatible with their being resurrected, according to the shortness of their intellects: the state of death, which is incompatible with life, and the state of being dust and bones, which is incompatible with the re-establishment of the human frame afterward.

By "bringing forth" is meant their being brought forth alive with a complete human frame, i.e., brought forth for the Resurrection, by the indication of the context.

Page 54

The clause "Far, far" (hayhat) is an explanation of the clause "he promises you," which is why it was separated and not conjoined.

"Hayhat" is a word built on a fatha at its last letter, and also on a kasra. The majority read it with fatha, and Abu Ja'far read it with kasra. It indicates distance. It is most often used repeated twice, as in this verse, or three times, as in poetry by Humayd al-Arqat and Jarir: ...

There is disagreement about whether it is a verb or a noun. The majority of grammarians held that "hayhat" is a verb-noun (ism fi'l) for the past tense meaning "to be distant," so the meaning of "hayhat kadha" is "far is such-and-such." Then what follows "hayhat" is the subject (fa'il). It was said: it is a noun for distance, i.e., it is an uninflected verbal noun, which is what al-Zajjaj chose in his tafsir. Al-Raghib said: some said al-Zajjaj erred in his explanation and was misled by the lam in His saying: ﴿Far, far is what you are promised!﴾.

It was said: hayhat is an adverb of place that does not inflect, which is the view of al-Mubarrad. Ibn Manzur in Lisan al-'Arab attributed it to Abu 'Ali al-Farisi. He said: Ibn Jinni said: Abu 'Ali used to say about hayhat: "I issue a ruling at one time that it is a noun named as a verb, like sah and mah, and at another time that it is an adverb, according to what comes to mind at the moment."

It has many dialects, the most eloquent of which is that it is with two haa's and an open ta' with a fatha of construction, that its ta' remains in pausal form, and it was said that one pauses on it with a haa', and that it is not nunated with the nunation of indefiniteness.

What follows "hayhat" has been reported in the genitive with lam, as in this verse, and in the nominative, as in the saying of Jarir:

"Far, far is al-'Aqiq and its people, and far is a friend in al-'Aqiq whom we seek."

And it has been reported in the genitive with "min," in the saying of Humayd al-Arqat:

"Hayhat, who is its morning-visitor? Hayhat, hayhat! Hayhat, a stone from Sunaybi'at!"

What is clear in the usage of "hayhat" is that the original form of what follows it is the nominative, on the interpretation of "hayhat" as a past-tense verb meaning "to be distant," as in Jarir's verse.

Page 55

And the more eloquent form is that what follows it is in the genitive with lam, so that it is in dispensing with the subject of the verb-noun, because it is known from what precedes "hayhat" in speech; for it generally does not occur except after a speech. The lam is taken as explanatory (lil-tabyin), meaning clarifying the intended referent of the subject, so that thereby a general statement and then a detail is obtained, which yields strengthening of the report. This lam goes back to the lam of causation. When what follows it is reported in the genitive with "min," then "min" has the sense of "'an" (from), meaning "it is distant from him" or "a distance from him."

However, "hayhat" may be interpreted sometimes as a verb, which is the more common, and sometimes as a verbal noun, so it is a noun of action (ism masdar), built, uninflected, non-derived. The predication with it is like predication with a verbal noun, and this is the approach al-Zajjaj took in explaining this verse, and al-Zamakhshari's statement points to his preference.

Here the verb "tu'adun" (you are promised) comes from "awʿada" (to threaten), while before it came the verb "ya'iduku" from "wa'ada" (to promise), although the promised thing is one thing. Al-Shaykh Ibn 'Arafa said: because the first refers to them in the state of their existence, so it was made a promise, and the second refers to their state after death and annihilation, so the expression by threat was appropriate for it. End.

I say: better than this is that he expressed once by promise and once by threat by way of ihtibak (interlocking), for informing them of the resurrection includes a promise of good if they are truthful and a threat if they deny, so both verbs are mentioned by distribution for brevity.

His saying: ﴿It is nothing but our worldly life﴾ may be an explanation of the improbability in His saying: ﴿Far, far is what you are promised!﴾ and an argument and reason for it; in both cases the clause is separated from the preceding one.

The pronoun "hiya" (it) refers to something not previously mentioned in the speech, but to something mentioned after it, for the purpose of vagueness followed by detail, so that the meaning settles in the hearer's mind. This is one of the places where a pronoun returns to what follows it when what follows is an explanation of it, and for this the noun after the pronoun is made an explanatory appositive (ʿatf bayan).

Page 56

Among this is the poet's verse quoted in al-Kashshaf (first hemistich), and al-Tibi cited it in full:

"It is the soul; what you burden it with, it bears, and for time are days that oppress and do justice."

And Abu al-'Ala's saying:

The discussion of the nominal clause conveying emphasis is the same as the discussion of ﴿And we will not be resurrected﴾.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 23, verses 39–40:**

﴿He said, "My Lord, support me, for they have denied me."﴾ ﴿He said, "In a little while they will surely become regretful."﴾ This is a resumptive clause of explanation (*istinaf bayani*), because what has been related of the chiefs' hindering the people from following him, spreading word about him that he is one who fabricates against God, and their fabricating false arguments for this, is something that prompts a questioner to ask what followed from his situation and theirs after that. So the answer is given: he turned to God, who had sent him, with a supplication that He support him against them. The discussion of a parallel to this has already passed earlier, in the story of Noah.

The reply to the supplication of this Messenger came without a conjunction, because it follows the style of relating dialogues, which we explained in several places, among them His saying: ﴿They said, "Will You place upon it one who causes corruption therein?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30] in Surat al-Baqarah.

In ﴿ʿammā qalīl (in a little while)﴾, the particle ʿan (عَنْ) indicates *mujawazah* (passing beyond), meaning that the thing governed by it, the noun in the genitive that follows it, is passed beyond. It often indicates the passing beyond of the meaning of what it governs, from which the sense of *baʿda* (after) arises, as in His saying: ﴿You will surely ride from stage to stage (ṭabaqan ʿan ṭabaq)﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 19]. Thus it is said that it comes with the meaning of *baʿda*, as the grammarians have mentioned. They followed the apparent sense and the explanation of the meaning, since a particle cannot have the meaning of a noun, for the meanings of particles are incomplete while the meanings of nouns are complete. So the meaning of ﴿ʿammā qalīl (in a little while) they will surely become regretful﴾ is that their becoming regretful in the morning passes beyond a short time, that is, beyond the time of speaking. This passing beyond is figurative, with the particle ʿan, and is borrowed to mean *baʿda* (after) by a subsequent (*tabaʿiyyah*) metaphor.

The word *mā* (ما) is superfluous, for emphasis.

The word *qalīl* (قَلِيلٍ) is an adjective of a deleted noun that the context indicates, or the verb of becoming morning (*al-ʾiṣbāḥ*), which is among the verbs of time. So God promised this Messenger a swift victory.

Their regret will occur at the sight of the beginning of annihilation, and their regret will not benefit them after the punishment has descended.

The word *al-ʾiṣbāḥ* (الإصْباحُ) here is intended to mean the time of morning, not the sense of becoming, as shown by His saying in Surat al-Hijr: ﴿So the blast seized them at sunrise (muṣbiḥīn)﴾ [al-Hijr: 83].

The outcome ﴿So the Cry seized them in truth, and We made them like debris. So away with the wrongdoing people!﴾

[p. 59]
The "fa" (so) requires that the response to their messenger's call be hastened.

The word "seizure" (akhdh) is used figuratively for destruction.

The "Cry" (al-sayha) is the sound of the thunderbolt (al-sa'iqa). This suggests, or specifies, that this people are Thamud. God says: ﴿As for Thamud, they were destroyed by the overwhelming blast﴾ [al-Haqqa 69:5]. And concerning them, in Surat al-Hijr, He says: ﴿The Cry seized them at morning﴾ [al-Hijr 15:83].

Attributing the seizure to the Cry is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli), because the Cry is the cause of the seizure, or accompanies its cause, since it results from the rupture of the sphere of air when the thunderbolt descends.

The "ba" in "in truth" (bi-l-haqq) indicates accompaniment (mulabasa). That is: it seized them in a manner accompanied by truth, meaning there was no injustice done to them, since they deserved it by their wrongdoing. "Debris" (ghuthaʾ) is what the flood carries of dry sticks and leaves. The statement is based on an eloquent simile (tashbih baligh) of condition: it is the comparing of one state to another. That is: We made them like debris in decay and in being piled up in one place, so they perished with a single destruction.

Following the report of their denial is a supplication against them and against their likes, in the manner of a curse and contempt, that they be distanced, as a sign of contempt and abhorrence for them. It is not used in the literal sense of supplication, because these people had already been distanced by destruction. The word "away" (bu'dan) is in the accusative as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) replacing its verb, like "tabban" and "suhqan", meaning: may God ruin him and may He cast him away.

The opposite of this meaning is the saying of the Arabs: "la tab'ad" (with a fatha on the ʿayn), meaning: "may you not be lost." Malik ibn al-Rayb said:

They say, "May you not be lost," while they bury me,
And where is the place of loss except my place?

The intended meaning of "the wrongdoing people" is the disbelievers: ﴿Indeed, associating partners with God is a great wrongdoing﴾ [Luqman 31:13]. This description was chosen here because these people wronged themselves by associating partners with God, and they wronged Hud, because they deliberately lied about God when they said: ﴿He is only a man who has invented a lie against God﴾ [al-Mu'minun 23:38].

The definite article in "the wrongdoers" (al-zalimin) is for comprehensiveness (istighraq), so it includes them, and for this reason the sentence stands in the place of a concluding statement (tadhyil).

[p. 60]
The "lam" in "for the wrongdoing people" (lil-qawm al-zalimin) is for specification (tabyin), and it specifies the intended object of the supplication for the sake of added clarity, as in their saying "suhqan laka" and "tabban lahu." For if it had been said, "so away," it would be known that it was a supplication against him. By adding the "lam," the specification of those against whom the supplication is made is increased. It is connected to an implied element that begins a new clause for the purpose of explanation.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 23, verses 42–43:

﴿Then We produced after them other generations.﴾ ﴿No nation can precede its term, nor can they delay.﴾ Al-qurun (the generations): the nations. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And generations between them, many.﴾ [al-Furqan: 38].

They are the nations to whom no messengers were sent, and who remained upon the following of the sharia (law) of Nuh (Noah), or the sharia of Hud, or the sharia of Salih. Or they were not commanded with a law (shar'), because the restriction to mentioning the nations here, without mentioning the messengers, and then the mention of the messengers immediately after this, indicates that these were either nations to whom no messengers came, for a wisdom that required leaving them in that state, because they were not qualified to receive laws; or because they were following earlier laws.

The clause ﴿No nation can precede its term, nor can they delay﴾ is an interjected clause between the conjoined clauses. It is an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani) for what is implied by His saying: ﴿Then We produced after them generations﴾, from their large number, and not what is implied by describing them as (other, ākharīn) from the ignorance of people about them; and for what is implied by the conjunction of the clause ﴿Then We sent Our messengers in succession﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 44], from the extinction of these generations after the nation whose story was mentioned just before, in His saying: ﴿Then We produced after them other generations﴾, without messengers coming to them. So all of that prompts the question of a questioner about the length of their lifespans and the time of their extinction. It is answered in summary: for each generation among them there is a term that God determined, which it remains until its like, then it becomes extinct and is succeeded by another generation that comes after it, or a generation that was contemporary with it lives on after it; and that what is determined for each generation neither precedes nor follows it, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For every nation there is a term; when their term comes, they cannot delay an hour, nor can they advance it﴾ [Yunus: 49].

Page 61
Al-sabq (precedence) is one traveler passing another and leaving him behind, and its opposite is al-ta'akhkhur (lagging behind). The meaning is clear. The sin and ta' in (yasta'khirun) are added for emphasis, like (istajaba). The pronoun in (yasta'khirun) refers back to (ummah) in terms of its people.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 23, verse 44:

﴿Then We sent Our messengers in succession. Every time a nation's messenger came to them, they denied him, so We made them follow one another [to destruction], and We made them into tales. So away with a people who do not believe.﴾ The messengers who came afterwards, i.e., after these generations, were among them Ibrahim, Lut, Yusuf and Shu'ayb, and whoever was sent before Musa, and messengers whom Allah did not relate to His Messenger.

The purpose is to show the constancy of Allah's sunnah (way/practice) in annihilating those who denied His messengers and obstinately rejected His signs, as indicated by His words: ﴿so We made them follow one another﴾.

As for (tatra), the majority of readers recited it with an alif at its end without tanwin, so it is a masdar (verbal noun) of the form fa'la, like da'wa and salwa, and its alif is the feminine alif, like dhikra, so it is diptote (mamnu' min al-sarf). Its original form is wutra, with a waw at its beginning, derived from al-witr, which means "the single/odd one." The apparent statement of the lexicographers is that it has no verb, meaning "one by one," i.e., one after another, so it is a counterpart to mathna. The waw was changed to a ta' by a non-analogical substitution, just as it was changed in (tijah), meaning "the facing direction," and in (tawlaj), meaning "the wild animal's lair," and (turath), meaning "that which is inherited."

Tatra is only used when there is succession between things with intervals of pause and interruption. From it comes at-tawatur, which is the succession of things with gaps between them. Al-watira is the pause from work. As for succession without a pause, it is al-tadarruk. It is said: "They came in quick succession (mutadarrikin)," i.e., following one another.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Abu Ja'far recited it with tanwin, and this is the dialect of Kinanah. In both readings it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of (rusulana).

Page 62
Know that the word (tatra) was written in all the Mushafs with the form of the original alif at its end, although in the majority's reading it is a feminine alif maqsura, and the rule for the feminine maqsura alif is that it be written in the form of a ya', like taqwa and da'wa. Perhaps the scribes of the Mushafs took both readings into account, so they wrote the alif in its original form, since the reader's pronunciation is suitable for both readings. Yet the original rule for alif is that it be written in its original form, and writing it in the form of a ya' where it is written so indicates its origin or the permissibility of imala (inclination), so this rule was departed from in this word to avoid confusion.

The meaning of the verse: then, after those generations, We sent messengers, i.e., We sent them to other nations, because the sending of a messenger necessarily implies the existence of a nation, and this was stated in His words: ﴿every time a nation's messenger came to them, they denied him﴾. The meaning: most of them denied him, and perhaps all of them did.

In the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas in Muslim, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The nations were displayed before me, and I saw the prophet with a small group, and the prophet with a man or two men, and the prophet with no one with him..." the hadith.

The following of some of them by others means joining them to them in destruction, by the context and by His words: ﴿and We made them into tales﴾, i.e., We made them into things people talk about, as people only talk about a strange and rare thing like it. Al-ahadith here is the plural of uhdusa, which is a name for what people amuse themselves by talking about. The form uf'ula indicates this, as in al-u'juba (marvel) and al-usturah (legend).

This is a metonymy for their annihilation; the meaning is: We made them into tales, perished and unseen.

As for ﴿so away with a people who do not believe﴾, the discussion is like the discussion of ﴿so away with the wrongdoing people﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 41], except that the supplication is attached here to the description that they do not believe, so that from the combination of the two supplications there results an alert to the blameworthiness of disbelief and to the blameworthiness of not believing in the messengers, as an allusion

Page 63
to the polytheists of Quraysh, and it also includes every people who do not believe in Allah's messengers, because the indefinite noun in the context of supplication is general, as in the words of al-Hariri:

O people of this abode, may you be protected from harm.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 23, verses 45–48:

﴿Then We sent Moses and his brother Aaron with Our signs and a manifest authority﴾ ﴿to Pharaoh and his chieftains, but they were arrogant, for they were a haughty people﴾ ﴿and they said: "Shall we believe in two mortals like ourselves, while their people are servants to us?"﴾ ﴿So they denied them, and they became of those who were destroyed﴾

Al-ayat (الآياتُ): the miracles. Their attribution to the Divine Name (ḍamīr al-jalala) serves to highlight them and to magnify them. Al-sultan al-mubin (السُّلْطانُ المُبِينُ): the clear proof which Allah inspired in Moses, and which prevailed over Pharaoh and his chieftains. The bāʾ (الباءُ) here indicates accompaniment (lil-mulabasa), meaning: We sent him accompanied by the miracles and the proof.

Mala' Fir'awn (مَلَأُ فِرْعَوْنَ): the people of his assembly, the scholars of his religion, and they were the sorcerers. The mission was directed to them rather than to the rest of the Egyptian (Qibt) nation because the call of Moses and his brother was addressed to Pharaoh and the people of his state, who held in their hands the management of the nation's affairs, for the liberation of the Children of Israel from their enslavement of them. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So go to him and say: Indeed we are two messengers of your Lord; so send with us the Children of Israel and do not torment them﴾ [Ta-Ha: 47]. They were not sent with a sharia to the Qibt. As for the call to monotheism (tawhid), it was a prelude to establishing the prophethood for them.

The conjunction of (fa-istakbarū) (فاسْتَكْبَرُوا) with the fa of sequence (fa al-ta'qib) indicates that they did not reflect upon the call, the signs and the proof, but rather they went to excess in pride. The sin and ta' (السِّينُ والتّاءُ) are for emphasis, meaning: they became exceedingly proud, to the extent that they paid no attention to the signs of Moses or his proof.

The clause ﴿wa kanū qawman ʿālīn﴾ (وكانُوا قَوْمًا عالِينَ), "and they were a haughty people," is a parenthetical clause (mu'taridha) between the verb (istakbarū) and what follows from it, His saying (fa-qālū), and it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) regarding Pharaoh and his chieftains. The meaning: they were arrogant in that they turned away from responding to the call of Moses and Aaron, and their characteristic was pride and haughtiness, i.e., arrogance was their nature and disposition. We have explained at His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿la-āyātin li-qawmin yaʿqilūn﴾ [al-Baqara: 164] in Surat al-Baqara that the use of a description upon the word (qawm) or the report with the word (qawm) followed by an active participle is intended to indicate the firm establishment of that attribute in the described (the people) or its firm establishment in those people. So the meaning here is: their arrogance in refusing to receive the call of Moses, his signs and his proof arose from their innate disposition of pride and their habituation to it. Thus al-ʿuluww (العُلُوُّ) means arrogance and tyranny. Its explanation will come at His saying: ﴿Indeed Pharaoh exalted himself in the land﴾ [al-Qasas: 4] in Surat al-Qasas. This is elaborated by the consequent clause in His saying: ﴿So they said: "Shall we believe in two mortals like ourselves, while their people are servants to us?"﴾, which is subordinate to His saying (fa-istakbarū), meaning: Pharaoh and his chieftains were arrogant against following Moses and Aaron, and they made clear the cause of their arrogance by their saying: ﴿Shall we believe in two mortals like ourselves, while their people are servants to us?﴾. This is not the speech of Pharaoh, but the speech of some of the chieftains to others, and since they had all agreed upon it, it was attributed to them all. As for Pharaoh, he was listening to their opinion and counsel, and he had another statement, related in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Pharaoh said: "O chiefs, I do not know of any god for you other than me"﴾ [al-Qasas: 38], for Pharaoh was counted among the rank of gods, because although he was a human in form, he acquired divinity by being the son of the gods.

The interrogative in (anu'minu) (أنُؤْمِنُ) is one of denial (inkari), meaning: it is not for us to believe in them while they are like us in humanity, and they are not fit to be sons of the gods, because they came with the denial of the divinity of the gods. So the chieftains of Pharaoh, in their misguidance, sought, as a condition for the validity of a message from Allah, that the messenger be distinct from those to whom he is sent. Therefore they used to imagine their gods as strange kinds: such as a human body with the head of a cow, or the head of a bird, or the head of a jackal, or the body of a lion with a human head. They attached no weight to the differences in the ranks of souls and intellects, though these are most fit for manifesting disparity, since they are the seat of humanity. This doubt is the cause of the misguidance of most nations who denied their messengers.

The lam (اللّامُ) in His saying (libasharayn) (لِبَشَرَيْنِ) serves to transitive the verb (nu'minu) (نُؤْمِنُ). It is said of one who believes the informant in what he reports: āmana lahu (آمَنَ لَهُ), so the verb (āmana) is transitive with the lam on the basis that he accepted the report for the sake of the reporter, i.e., for the sake of his trustworthiness in himself. The original meaning of this lam is the lam of cause and purpose. From it is His saying: ﴿So Lot believed in him﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 26], and His saying: ﴿And if you do not believe me, then leave me alone﴾ [al-Dukhan: 21]. As for the transitivity of the verb of belief by the bāʾ (بِ), it is used when what is attached to it indicates a report; you say: āmantu bi-anna Allaha wahid (آمنتُ بِأنَّ اللَّهَ واحِدٌ), "I believed that God is one." By this the difference becomes clear between your saying: āmantu bi-Muhammad (آمنتُ بِمُحَمَّدٍ) and your saying: āmantu li-Muhammad (آمنتُ لِمُحَمَّدٍ). The meaning of the first: you affirmed something (concerning him, i.e., his message). Therefore it is not said: āmantu lillah; rather one says: āmantu billah. And one says: āmantu bi-Muhammad and āmantu li-Muhammad. The meaning of the first relates to his essence, namely the prophethood, and the meaning of the second is that you affirmed him in what he brought.

(Mithlana) (مِثْلِنا) is an adjective of (basharayn) and it is of the kind where its singular and masculine form may be consistently used without regard to the disagreement with the form of the thing described, as here. It may also agree with its described noun, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed those whom you call upon besides Allah are servants like you﴾ [al-A'raf: 194].

This is a disparagement of their prophethood from the aspect of their personal condition; then they followed it with a disparagement from the aspect of their origin and lineage, saying: ﴿while their people are servants to us﴾, meaning: and they are from a group who are servants to us and lower than us, so how could they rule over us?

His saying (ʿabidun) (عابِدُونَ) is the plural of ʿabid, meaning: obedient, submissive. The Children of Israel had been servants and menials to the Copts, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And this is a favor with which you remind me, that you enslaved the Children of Israel﴾ [al-Shuʿara': 22].

Upon their saying was built the determination to deny them, related in His saying: "So they denied them", meaning: their affair was settled upon denying them. Then upon their denial was built that they became of those destroyed, for Allah destroyed them by drowning, meaning: they were grouped into the line of the peoples who were destroyed. This is more forceful than saying "so they were destroyed," as has passed us more than once.

The sequence (taʿqib) here is customary sequence (taʿqib ʿurfi), because since the drowning arose from the denial, the denial continued until the time of destruction.

In this there is an allusion (taʿrid) warning Quraysh for their denial of their messenger ﷺ, because in His saying ﴿of those destroyed﴾ there is an indication that destruction is the sunna of Allah concerning those who deny His messengers.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So go to him and say: Indeed we are two messengers of your Lord; so send with us the Children of Israel and do not torment them﴾ [Ta-Ha: 47]. They were not sent with a sharia to the Qibt. As for the call to monotheism (tawhid), it was a prelude to establishing the prophethood for them.

The conjunction of (fa-istakbarū) (فاسْتَكْبَرُوا) with the fa of sequence (fa al-ta'qib) indicates that they did not reflect upon the call, the signs and the proof, but rather they went to excess in pride. The sin and ta' (السِّينُ والتّاءُ) are for emphasis, meaning: they became exceedingly proud, to the extent that they paid no attention to the signs of Moses or his proof.

The clause ﴿wa kanū qawman ʿālīn﴾ (وكانُوا قَوْمًا عالِينَ), "and they were a haughty people," is a parenthetical clause (mu'taridha) between the verb (istakbarū) and what follows from it, His saying (fa-qālū), and it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) regarding Pharaoh and his chieftains. The meaning: they were arrogant in that they turned away from responding to the call of Moses and Aaron, and their characteristic was pride and haughtiness, i.e., arrogance was their nature and disposition. We have explained at His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿la-āyātin li-qawmin yaʿqilūn﴾ [al-Baqara: 164] in Surat al-Baqara that the use of a description upon the word (qawm) or the report with the word (qawm) followed by an active participle is intended to indicate the firm establishment of that attribute in the described (the people) or its firm establishment in those people. So the meaning here is: their arrogance in refusing to receive the call of Moses, his signs and his proof arose from their innate disposition of pride and their habituation to it. Thus al-ʿuluww (العُلُوُّ) means arrogance and tyranny. Its explanation will come at His saying: ﴿Indeed Pharaoh exalted himself in the land﴾ [al-Qasas: 4] in Surat al-Qasas. This is elaborated by the consequent clause in His saying: ﴿So they said: "Shall we believe in two mortals like ourselves, while their people are servants to us?"﴾, which is subordinate to His saying (fa-istakbarū), meaning: Pharaoh and his chieftains were arrogant against following Moses and Aaron, and they made clear the cause of their arrogance by their saying: ﴿Shall we believe in two mortals like ourselves, while their people are servants to us?﴾. This is not the speech of Pharaoh, but the speech of some of the chieftains to others, and since they had all agreed upon it, it was attributed to them all. As for Pharaoh, he was listening to their opinion and counsel, and he had another statement, related in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Pharaoh said: "O chiefs, I do not know of any god for you other than me"﴾ [al-Qasas: 38], for Pharaoh was counted among the rank of gods, because although he was a human in form, he acquired divinity by being the son of the gods.

The interrogative in (anu'minu) (أنُؤْمِنُ) is one of denial (inkari), meaning: it is not for us to believe in them while they are like us in humanity, and they are not fit to be sons of the gods, because they came with the denial of the divinity of the gods. So the chieftains of Pharaoh, in their misguidance, sought, as a condition for the validity of a message from Allah, that the messenger be distinct from those to whom he is sent. Therefore they used to imagine their gods as strange kinds: such as a human body with the head of a cow, or the head of a bird, or the head of a jackal, or the body of a lion with a human head. They attached no weight to the differences in the ranks of souls and intellects, though these are most fit for manifesting disparity, since they are the seat of humanity. This doubt is the cause of the misguidance of most nations who denied their messengers.

The lam (اللّامُ) in His saying (libasharayn) (لِبَشَرَيْنِ) serves to transitive the verb (nu'minu) (نُؤْمِنُ). It is said of one who believes the informant in what he reports: āmana lahu (آمَنَ لَهُ), so the verb (āmana) is transitive with the lam on the basis that he accepted the report for the sake of the reporter, i.e., for the sake of his trustworthiness in himself. The original meaning of this lam is the lam of cause and purpose. From it is His saying: ﴿So Lot believed in him﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 26], and His saying: ﴿And if you do not believe me, then leave me alone﴾ [al-Dukhan: 21]. As for the transitivity of the verb of belief by the bāʾ (بِ), it is used when what is attached to it indicates a report; you say: āmantu bi-anna Allaha wahid (آمنتُ بِأنَّ اللَّهَ واحِدٌ), "I believed that God is one." By this the difference becomes clear between your saying: āmantu bi-Muhammad (آمنتُ بِمُحَمَّدٍ) and your saying: āmantu li-Muhammad (آمنتُ لِمُحَمَّدٍ). The meaning of the first: you affirmed something (concerning him, i.e., his message). Therefore it is not said: āmantu lillah; rather one says: āmantu billah. And one says: āmantu bi-Muhammad and āmantu li-Muhammad. The meaning of the first relates to his essence, namely the prophethood, and the meaning of the second is that you affirmed him in what he brought.

(Mithlana) (مِثْلِنا) is an adjective of (basharayn) and it is of the kind where its singular and masculine form may be consistently used without regard to the disagreement with the form of the thing described, as here. It may also agree with its described noun, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed those whom you call upon besides Allah are servants like you﴾ [al-A'raf: 194].

This is a disparagement of their prophethood from the aspect of their personal condition; then they followed it with a disparagement from the aspect of their origin and lineage, saying: ﴿while their people are servants to us﴾, meaning: and they are from a group who are servants to us and lower than us, so how could they rule over us?

His saying (ʿabidun) (عابِدُونَ) is the plural of ʿabid, meaning: obedient, submissive. The Children of Israel had been servants and menials to the Copts, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And this is a favor with which you remind me, that you enslaved the Children of Israel﴾ [al-Shuʿara': 22].

Upon their saying was built the determination to deny them, related in His saying: "So they denied them", meaning: their affair was settled upon denying them. Then upon their denial was built that they became of those destroyed, for Allah destroyed them by drowning, meaning: they were grouped into the line of the peoples who were destroyed. This is more forceful than saying "so they were destroyed," as has passed us more than once.

The sequence (taʿqib) here is customary sequence (taʿqib ʿurfi), because since the drowning arose from the denial, the denial continued until the time of destruction.

In this there is an allusion (taʿrid) warning Quraysh for their denial of their messenger ﷺ, because in His saying ﴿of those destroyed﴾ there is an indication that destruction is the sunna of Allah concerning those who deny His messengers.
