Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 23, verse 49:

Page 66
﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book, so that they might be guided.﴾ When the call of Moses and Aaron to Pharaoh and his chiefs was mentioned, and what followed from their denial, which was their destruction, the account of Moses' mission was completed with its important parts that continue, and with the missions of those messengers mentioned earlier, namely the giving of the Book to Moses for the guidance of the Children of Israel, so that their being guided would be achieved. This is to be followed by the lesson of their opposition to their messengers, in His saying after that: ﴿so they divided their affair among themselves into sects﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 53], for the admonition of those who denied their messenger through that is more fitting. Here the turning away from Aaron occurred, because his mission had ended, since he was limited to conveying the call to Pharaoh and his chiefs, as that station was one of disputation and argument. So Moses asked his Lord to associate his brother Aaron with him in conveying it, because he was more eloquent than him in tongue in explaining the proof and the clear authority.

The definite article in (al-Kitab) is for prior reference (al-'ahd), and it is the Torah. For this reason the pronoun in ﴿so that they might be guided﴾ clearly refers not to something mentioned in the speech but to something known from the context, namely the people addressed by the Torah, who are the Children of Israel. Thus the coherence of the pronouns is evident within the context without need to interpret His saying ﴿We gave Moses﴾ as meaning "We gave the people of Moses," as the Kashshaf adopted.

And (la'alla) expresses hope, because it is of the nature of that Book that the people's being guided by it is awaited from its being given.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 23, verse 50:

﴿And We made the son of Mary and his mother a sign, and We sheltered them on a high ground, a place of settlement and of flowing water.﴾

Since the greatest sign of ʿIsa (Jesus) lay in his very self, in the manner of his creation, the concern here was to mention that, and his prophethood is not mentioned, because the miracle of his creation is itself indicative of the truthfulness of his prophethood. As for His saying, ﴿and his mother﴾, it is an inclusion (idmaj) that serves to expose the foolishness of the Jews regarding what they slandered Mary, peace be upon her, with. For what God made a sign for her and her son, they made into a point of criticism and an object of mockery against both of them.

Page 67

The indefiniteness of ﴿ayah﴾ (sign) is for magnification, because it is a sign that contains within it many signs. And since their collective whole indicates the truthfulness of ʿIsa in his prophethood, their whole was made a great sign of his truthfulness, as you have learned.

As for His saying, ﴿and We sheltered them on a high ground﴾, it is an honouring of the two of them, since God made them the object of His care and the manifestation of His power and kindness.

Al-iwa' (sheltering) is making another a dweller (aawi), i.e., one who resides. It was discussed earlier at His saying, ﴿or I would take refuge in a mighty pillar﴾ [Hud: 80] in Surat Hud, and at His saying, ﴿I will betake myself to a mountain that will protect me from the water﴾ [Hud: 43] in Surat Hud.

Al-rubwa, with a dammah on the ra', is the elevated part of the earth; the ra' may also take the three vowels. It was discussed earlier at His saying, ﴿like a garden on a height﴾ [al-Baqarah: 265] in al-Baqarah. The intended meaning of this sheltering is God's revelation to Mary that she should go off alone to a high ground when the pangs of childbirth drew near, so that she might give birth to ʿIsa in a place secluded from people, to protect ʿIsa from their harm.

Al-qarar is remaining in a place, i.e., it is suitable to be a place of settlement. The high ground was thus described by the meaning that occurs in it through the slightest association, namely by what it contained of fruit-bearing palm trees, so that she would be in their shade and would not need to seek her own sustenance.

Al-maʿin is apparent water flowing over the surface of the earth. It is a description applied to a omitted noun, i.e., ماءٌ مَعِينٌ (flowing water), the description indicating it, like His saying, ﴿We carried you in the flowing vessel﴾ [al-Haqqah: 11]. This is in the sense of His saying in Surat Maryam: ﴿Your Lord has made beneath you a stream﴾ [Maryam: 24], ﴿and shake towards you the trunk of the palm tree; it will drop upon you ripe dates﴾ [Maryam: 25], ﴿so eat and drink and be comforted﴾ [Maryam: 26].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 23, verse 51:

﴿O messengers, eat of the good things and act righteously. Indeed, I am Knowing of what you do.﴾

Page 68
It is necessary to posit an omitted verb of speech, since the spoken words stand in its place, and this is a fresh, independent statement (isti'naf ibtida'i). The meaning is: "We said: ﴿O messengers, eat﴾." The reported speech here is related according to its sense, because the address mentioned here was not directed to the messengers at one time, given the difference in their eras. Thus the meaning is: "We said to every messenger of those whose mention has passed: Eat of the good things and act righteously. Indeed, I am Knowing of what you do."

This is in the manner of distribution (al-tawzi') of the meaning of the discourse, a usage common in addressing groups. From it comes the phrase: "The people rode their animals" (rakiba al-qawmu dawabbahum).

The purpose of this is to show the honour of the messengers before God and their purity in their bodily and spiritual affairs. Eating of the good things is bodily purity, and righteous action is purity of the soul.

The connection of this fresh statement is the words: ﴿And We gave them refuge on a high ground, a place of settlement and of running water﴾ (al-Mu'minun: 50). And it serves to refute the belief of the peoples who gave as a reason for rejecting their messengers that they eat food, as God said in the preceding verse: ﴿This is only a human like you; he eats of what you eat and drinks of what you drink﴾ (al-Mu'minun: 33), and He said: ﴿And they said: "What is this messenger that he eats food and walks in the markets?"﴾ (al-Furqan: 7). It also serves to nullify what the Christians invented of monasticism (al-rahbaniyyah). These are benefits of argument and instruction which had a great effect in this place.

The imperative in His words "eat" (kulu) is for permission (al-ibahah). Although eating is a natural matter for humans, what is meant here is its necessary implication, namely informing the deniers that eating does not contradict messengerhood, and that He who sent the messengers permitted them to eat.

The attachment of "of the good things" (min al-tayyibat) to the permission derived from the imperative indicates a condition: that what is permitted be of the good things, i.e., that the food be good. It adds to the refutation of the deniers that messengers avoid only the foul things and do not avoid what God has made lawful for them of the good things. The good things are what is neither forbidden nor disliked.

Page 69
The righteous action is joined to the command to eat the good things as an allusion that the aspiration of the messengers is directed only toward righteous deeds. This is like His words: ﴿There is no blame upon those who believed and did righteous deeds for what they have eaten, when they fear God, believe, and do righteous deeds﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 93), and what is meant there is what they consumed of wine before its prohibition. His words "Indeed, I am Knowing of what you do" are an exhortation to increase in righteous deeds, since that implies a promise of reward for them and that nothing of them is lost; so the statement is used in the sense of exhortation.

[Page 69 continues]

﴿And indeed, this, your community, is one community, and I am your Lord, so fear Me.﴾ The conjunction *wa* may link to the sentence ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things﴾ (23:51) and what follows it, so that this is part of what was said to the messengers. The sense would be: "And We said to them: Indeed, this, your community, is one community…" to the end of the verse. It may also be a conjunction linking to the narratives of the sendings (*qasas al-irsal*), which begin with His words: ﴿And We certainly sent Noah to his people﴾ (23:23). Those narratives were related to them so that they would be guided by them to the fact that the matter of the messengers, from the beginning of their mission, was the call to affirm God's unity in divinity (*tawhid*). On this reading, the context of this verse is like the context of the verse in Surat al-Anbiya': ﴿Indeed, this, your community, is one community﴾ (21:92), and so on.

This verse differs from the verse in Surat al-Anbiya' in having three recitations (*qira'at*, the canonical variant readings). The readers agreed on the recitation of that verse with a kasra on the hamza of *inna*. As for this verse, the majority (*al-Jumhur*) read *wa-anna* with a fatha on the hamza and a shadda on the nun. It may be addressed to the messengers, or to those who are addressed by the warning, on both interpretations. The fatha on the hamza is explained by assuming a *lam* of purpose (*lam kay*) governing the words ﴿so fear Me﴾, according to those who do not consider the presence of the *fa'* (of consequence) in it to prevent the fronting of its *ma'mul* (the element it governs). Or it is governed by an omitted element indicated by ﴿so fear Me﴾, according to those who forbid fronting the *ma'mul* over the *'amil* (governing element) when that is linked with *fa'*, as was mentioned in His words, exalted is He: ﴿So fear Me alone﴾ (16:51) in Surat al-Baqarah.

[Page 70]
The meaning on this reading is: "And because your religion is one religion, in which the object of worship is not multiplied; and because I am your Lord, so fear Me and do not associate anything with Me." This is addressed to the messengers, with their communities intended, or it is addressed to those whom the Qur'an addresses.

'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read with a kasra on the hamza of *inna* and a shadda on the nun. The kasra on the hamza of *inna* is either because it occurs within the reported speech on the first interpretation, or because it begins a new sentence on the second interpretation. The meaning is as previously mentioned for the majority reading.

Ibn 'Amir read with a fatha on the hamza and a light nun (*takhfif*), taking it as the light form of the fathah *anna*. Its noun is an omitted pronoun of the matter (*damir sha'n*), and its predicate is the sentence following it. Its meaning is the same as the majority reading.

The demonstrative (*ism al-ishara*) "this" refers to the sacred law (*shari'a*) of each of the prophets, or to the sacred law of Islam, on both interpretations regarding who is addressed by this verse.

Emphasizing the statement with the particle *inna* in all the recitations serves to refute the polytheists among the communities of the messengers, or the polytheists addressed by the Qur'an.

The explanation of its parallel in Surat al-Anbiya' has already been given. However, here the phrase is ﴿so fear Me﴾, while there it is ﴿so worship Me﴾. It may be that God commanded them both to worship and to be mindful of Him, but in each surah He related one of the two commands. It may also be that both commands occurred in a single address, of which part was mentioned in Surat al-Anbiya' and most of it in Surat al-Mu'minun, according to what the context of narration required in each of the two surahs. It is also possible that each of the two commands, the command to worship and the command to be mindful, occurred in a separate address, one resembling the other, with one exceeding the other according to what the context of the address required, either with the intention of conveying it to the communities, as in Surat al-Anbiya', or with the intention of specifying the messengers, as in Surat al-Mu'minun. This is supported by the fact that Surat al-Mu'minun explicitly mentions the address to the messengers.

Whichever of the two possibilities is correct, the reasoning is this: in Surat al-Anbiya', the messages of the messengers to their peoples concerning monotheism are not mentioned, except the message of Abraham in His words: ﴿And We had certainly given Abraham his sound judgment﴾ (21:51). Then the mention of other messengers and prophets came, with praise of them, and the distance between that and the story of Abraham was long. So the command to worship God, that is, to single Him out in worship, which is the meaning in which the religions are united, was more fitting there, because the intent of that command is that it should reach their peoples. So mentioning the command to worship was more fitting to the context in that surah, because it is the portion of the communities that is greater. The prophets and messengers were never otherwise, so the command is not directed at the prophets with it, since that would become obtaining what is already obtained, unless it is intended as a command to persist. As for the verse of this surah, it came after the mention of what the messengers were sent with to their peoples, namely monotheism and the nullification of association, so the portion of the messengers in that was greater, as the opening of the address with ﴿O messengers﴾ (23:51) indicates. Therefore the mention of the command to be mindful of God was more suitable to the context here, because mindfulness (*taqwa*) has no limit, and the messengers are commanded to it and to increase in it, as He, exalted is He, said concerning His Prophet: ﴿O you wrapped in garments﴾ (73:1), ﴿Stand [in prayer] through the night, except a little﴾ (73:2), ﴿half of it, or reduce from it a little﴾ (73:3), ﴿or add to it﴾ (73:4). Then He said concerning the community: ﴿So recite what is easy of the Qur'an﴾ (73:20), and so on. Some indication of this has already passed in the commentary on Surat al-Anbiya', but what we have mentioned here is more extensive, so include it with that and rely upon it.

It was missed in Surat al-Anbiya' to explain the grammar (*'arabiyya*) of His words: ﴿Indeed, this, your community, is one community﴾ (21:92), so it is necessary to elaborate on it here. The demonstrative "this" refers to a matter present in the mind, made clear by the predicate and the situation, and for that reason the demonstrative is feminine, that is: "This sacred law which We revealed to you is your sacred law." The meaning of this statement is that you adhere to it, you do not diminish from it, and you do not change anything in it. For this purpose, the predicate was made into what should properly be an explanation of the demonstrative, because it was not intended to explain the demonstrative, but rather to predicate something of the demonstrative in order to convey the identity between the referent of the demonstrative and its predicate, so it conveys that it is itself, unchanged from its state.

Al-Zajjaj said: "Such a construction is among the subtle and obscure points of grammar, for it is only permitted where the predicate is already known. In your saying 'This is Zayd standing,' it is only said to someone who knows him, and his standing conveys something new. If it were not so, it would follow that he would not be Zayd when he was not standing, and that is not correct."

From this it is known that the purpose of predicating something of the demonstrative is not its literal meaning. Rather, the predicate is used figuratively to mean exhortation and constant attachment, and this resembles what is implied by the benefit (*lazim al-fa'ida*), even if it does not occur in their examples. Among such examples is His words: ﴿And this is my husband, an old man﴾ (11:72). Sarah knew that the angels recognized Abraham as her husband, since they had given her good news of Isaac. The meaning is: "This one you see is my husband, from whom the promised offspring is expected," that is, his condition contradicts the glad tidings, and for that reason such a construction is followed by a circumstantial clause (*hal*) that clarifies the intended meaning of the predicate, as in this verse. A subtle point concerning that verse has already been mentioned.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 23, verse 53:

﴿So they broke their affair into sects among themselves, each faction rejoicing in what it had.﴾

The particle of sequence (fa' al-ta'qib) is used here to indicate that the nations did not delay after the messengers conveyed to them ﴿And indeed this, your community, is one community, and I am your Lord, so fear Me﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 52], but rather broke their affair among themselves: they took many gods, and their religion became divided into fragments, for every group there was an idol and a worship specific to it. The pronoun in (taqatta'u) refers to the nations, which is understood from the context, and they are the intended meaning of His saying: ﴿And indeed this, your community, is one community, and I am your Lord, so fear Me﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 52]. The plural pronoun refers to the nations of the messengers, as indicated by the context.

Thus the discourse is framed as a censure. For this reason, the fa' together with sequence may also convey the sense of consequence (al-tafri') — meaning: as a consequence of what We had commanded them of monotheism, they did the opposite of what was required of them. The discourse thus conveys, beyond censure, a sense of wonder at their condition. What further intensifies the sense of censure is its concluding clause: ﴿each faction rejoicing in what it had﴾, meaning: while they are not in the state of those who rejoice.

The root of (taqatta'a) is the intransitive form (mutawi') of qatta'a. It is used as a transitive verb with the meaning of qatta'a, aiming to express intensity in the occurrence of the action. Its parallel is takhawwafahu al-sayr (the journey diminished him), i.e., reduced him; tajahhamahu al-layl (the night frowned upon him) and ta'arrafahu al-zaman (time made him known). The meaning is: they broke their affair among themselves into many pieces, i.e., they dispersed into many sects (nihal), so that each group made for itself a religion. It is also permissible to take (taqatta'u) as intransitive, with the breaking attributed to them in an indefinite manner, and then specified by His saying (amrahum), as if it were said: "they broke into an affair." Many of the Kufan grammarians permit the specifier (tamyiz) to be definite. We have expounded on the meaning of ﴿So they broke their affair into sects among themselves﴾ in the surah of al-Anbiya'.

The word (amr) here means matter, condition, and its referent is the affairs of their religion.

Al-zubur, with a damma on the zay and a damma on the ba' as recited by the majority, is the plural of zabur, which means book. The name of the book has been borrowed for religion, because it is the nature of religion to have a book for its adherents. It thus appears to be a mocking metaphor (isti'arah tahakkumiyyah), since each group did not have a book, but they adopted for themselves creeds and beliefs which, had they been recorded, would have been books.

Abu 'Amr recited it, according to one transmission from him, as (zubaran), with a damma on the zay and a fatha on the ba', which is the plural of zubrah, meaning a piece.

The clause ﴿each faction rejoicing in what it had﴾ is a concluding appendage (tadhyil) to what precedes it, because fragmentation necessitates partisanship, so it was concluded with the statement that each group among them rejoices in its religion. In the discourse there is an omitted qualifier for (hizb), i.e., each faction of them, by the indication of the context. Al-farah is intense gladness, i.e., they are content and exultant that they have adopted their own way in religion. The meaning is: they rejoice in their religion without evidence or insight, but merely from adhering to what is customary. This is alluded to by (ladayhim), which implies that it was firmly established among them from before, i.e., by the religion that is in their possession. Thus they do not accept those who oppose them and they hostilely oppose them, and this leads to division and disunity within the one community, which is contrary to the intent of God. For this reason His saying ﴿And indeed this, your community, is one community﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 52] was appended to it. Anciently, partisanship was a cause of the collapse of religions and nations, and it is part of the call of Satan, by which he clothes falsehood in the form of truth.

Al-hizb: the group gathered upon a matter, whether of belief or action, or those agreed upon it.

﴿So leave them in their confusion for a time.﴾

This is a shift in the discourse to address the Prophet ﷺ. The pronoun of plurality refers to something known from the context, namely the idolaters of Quraysh, for they are among the factions who "divided their affair among themselves into sects" (see 23:53), or they are precisely those. Among them are those who took al-'Uzza as their god, among them those who took Manat, and among them those who took Dhu al-Khalasa, and so on.

The apparent meaning of the statement is abandonment, but its intended meaning is granting them respite and warning them of the evil outcome that awaits them at some point. For this reason the word "ḥīn" (a time) is left indefinite when it is made the limit of their being given respite, meaning an unspecified time, as in His saying: ﴿It will not come upon you except suddenly﴾ (7:187).

The word "ghamra" (ghamrah, a deep confusion or heedlessness) literally means water that covers a person's height so as to drown him. It was mentioned in His saying: ﴿But if you could see the wrongdoers in the agonies of death﴾ (6:93), in Surat al-An'am. Its being attributed to their pronoun ("ghamratihim," their confusion) is because it clings to them so closely that it has become known by them. This is an image of their state of being occupied with the prosperity and luxurious living they enjoy, away from reflecting on what the Messenger calls them to, which would save them from punishment. It is likened to a people whom water has overwhelmed, so that they are about to drown while thinking that they are swimming.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 23, verses 55–56:

﴿Do they think that what We extend to them of wealth and children,﴾ ﴿We are hastening to them in good things? Rather, they do not perceive.﴾

It is most likely that this sentence is a badal ishtimal (inclusive apposition) of the sentence ﴿So leave them in their confusion until a time.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 54], on the basis that the sentence "fa-dharhum" (so leave them) includes the meaning of not caring about the circumstances they are in, which have distracted them from considering the call of Islam and deceived them into thinking that they are in a place of honour with Allah because of the might and luxury He has bestowed upon them. It also includes the threat that this has an end to which they will come, and that Allah has given them what they have during a time of blessing as a gradual lead-on (istidraj) for them. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And leave Me with the deniers, the possessors of luxury, and give them respite a little.﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 11]

Page 75
And His saying: ﴿Let not the movement of those who disbelieve through the lands deceive you.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 196] ﴿A little enjoyment.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 197]

The interrogative in "a-yahsabuna" (do they think) is one of denunciation and reproach for this assumption, whether this assumption is held by all the polytheists or is not held by some of them, because their state is the state of one who is likely to hold this assumption, so this assumption is denounced for him, either to remove it from his own self or to prevent it from arising within himself.

And "anna-ma" here consists of two words: "anna" (that), the emphasizing particle, and "ma" (what), the relative pronoun. They were written joined in the Mushaf, just as "innama" (indeed only), the restrictive particle, is written, because the old orthography was not fully regulated; its proper form is to be written separately.

And al-imdad (extending) means giving a madad (supply), which is a gift. And "min mal wa banin" (of wealth and children) is an explanation of the relative "ma".

And al-musara'ah (hastening) means hurrying, and here it is used metaphorically for seeking what is desired and being eager to attain it. In the hadith of 'A'isha, that she said to the Prophet ﷺ: "I see that your Lord only hastens to fulfil your desire," meaning: He gives you what you love, because one who is keen to please a person hastens to grant him what he desires; and it is said: "So-and-so runs in your shares (of fortune)." The object of "nusari'u" (We hasten) is omitted, its estimated form being: "nusari'u lahum bihi" (We hasten to them with it), i.e., with what We extend to them of wealth and children. It is omitted because "numiddu-hum bihi" (We extend to them with it) indicates it.

The "fi" (in) here is figurative in its sense of location: "al-khayrat" (good things) is treated as a path in which the hastening takes place by walking, so "fi" is a implicit metaphorical indicator (qarina makniyya). This was discussed previously at His saying: ﴿O Messenger, let not those who hasten into disbelief grieve you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 41] and His saying: ﴿You see those in whose hearts is a disease hastening toward them﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 52], both in Surat al-'Uqud, and at His saying: ﴿Indeed they used to hasten to good deeds﴾ [al-Anbiya': 90] in Surat al-Anbiya'.

"Al-khayrat" is the plural of khayr with the suffix -at, and it is among the rare plurals, like "suradiqat."

Page 76
It was discussed previously at His saying: ﴿And those—for them are the good things﴾ [al-Tawbah: 88] in Surat Bara'ah, and was discussed in Surat al-Anbiya'.

And "bal" (rather) is a turning away from the assumed (opinion), not a turning away from the assumption itself, as is clear from the context; i.e., "We are not hastening to them with good things as they assumed; rather, they do not perceive the wisdom of that extension and that it is for their istidraj and their disgrace by establishing the proof against them."

[Page 77]

This statement corresponds to what the "heedlessness" (al-ghamrah) contains in His saying: ﴿So leave them in their confusion﴾ (Al-Mu'minun: 54). That heedlessness includes turning away from the worship of God and from believing in His signs, associating partners with God, stinginess toward the weak and spending their wealth on pleasures, and denying the Resurrection. All of this is included in the heedlessness, so in opposition to it the passage mentions the conditions of the believers in praise of them. Do you not see His saying after this: ﴿Rather, their hearts are in confusion about this﴾ (Al-Mu'minun: 63)?

This sentence therefore serves as a detailed explanation of the general heedlessness, while also conveying the contrast with the conditions of the believers. The detail was chosen to be stated through the opposite, because these qualities are good and their opposites are ugly. This avoids mentioning their vices, and thereby achieves a wonderful concision (ijaz) and an antithesis (tibaq, contrast), one of the finest forms of rhetorical embellishment (badi'), and preserves eloquence from the repugnance of an ugly description.

The sentence opens with ﴿Indeed﴾ (inna) to emphasise the news. The use of the relative pronouns indicates the basis on which the statement is built, namely that they hasten to good deeds and race toward them. The repetition of the relative pronouns emphasises each of their attributes, so none is mentioned merely as a follower by conjunction. The intended meaning is the group who are characterised by one of these attributes. The ﴿min﴾ (from) in ﴿from the fear of their Lord﴾ indicates cause (ta'lil, the stating of a reason).

Ishfaq (apprehension) is the anticipation of something disliked, and it was discussed earlier at His saying: ﴿and they, from fear of Him, are apprehensive﴾ (Al-Anbiya: 28) in Surah al-Anbiya. The object of the anticipation has been omitted, since it is evident that it is the one whose wrath caused the apprehension. That is, they anticipate His anger and His punishment.

By "signs" (ayat) is meant the proofs contained in the Qur'an, among them the inimitability of the Qur'an. The meaning is that out of fear of their Lord they dread His punishment, and the complement of "apprehensive" has been omitted because the context indicates it.

The fronting of the three prepositional phrases before their governing verbs is for the sake of the fawasil (verse-endings, the rhyming pauses), together with attention to their content.

The meaning of ﴿they give what they give﴾ is that they give wealth as charity, gifts and expenditures in the way of God. God says: ﴿And gives wealth, in spite of love for it, to relatives﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 177), and He says: ﴿And woe to the polytheists, who do not give zakah﴾ (Fussilat: 6–7). The use of "giving" (ita') for giving wealth is common in the Qur'an, and it is clearly what is meant here.

The phrase "what they give" was expressed instead of "charities" or "wealth" so that it would include every kind of giving that is prescribed by the Law, and both little and much. Perhaps some believers have no wealth on which zakah is due, yet they give from what they earn.

The clause ﴿and their hearts are fearful﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). ﴿And We do not burden any soul beyond its capacity. With Us is a Book that speaks with the truth, and they will not be wronged﴾ is a *tadhyil* (a concluding statement that closes and confirms what precedes it) for what came before about the states of those who are "fearful of their Lord" (﴿Those who are fearful of their Lord﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 57]). Since the previous passage mentioned what necessitated the disbelievers' opposition to what they were commanded regarding the monotheism of the religion, and then mentioned what indicated the piety of the believers through their fear, the soundness of their faith, their giving, and their hastening to good deeds, this was concluded by stating that Allah demanded from those who had divided their affair (among themselves) only an obligation that does not burden them, and that Allah excused those believers who could not reach the level of those who surpass them in deeds, with an excuse that requires that their reward be credited for what they missed, when they have exerted the utmost of their capacity. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿There is no blame upon the weak, nor upon the sick, nor upon those who find nothing to spend, when they are sincere to Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Tawbah: 91].

So His saying ﴿And We do not burden any soul beyond its capacity﴾ is a statement whose intended meaning is its necessary implication, which is the recording of shortcoming against those who had divided their affair among themselves, the cutting off of their excuse, and the facilitation of the excuse for ﴿those who are fearful of their Lord﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 57]. This is like His saying the Exalted: ﴿Allah intends ease for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185], together with what this contains of consoling the broken hearts of the believers who could not catch up with others due to incapacity or poverty.

Because this meaning is observed, His saying ﴿And with Us is a Book that speaks with the truth﴾ is conjoined to it, and it means the comprehensiveness of His knowledge of their states and intentions. The "Book" here is the matter in which the deeds are recorded, good and bad, and the term "Book" is applied to it because of its comprehensiveness. In His saying "with Us" there is an indication that this is preserved, such that no one can alter it by addition or subtraction. "Speaking" is used figuratively for indicating, and it is permissible that the speaking of the Book be literal, such that the written letters have sounds, and the power of Allah is not limited.

As for His saying ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾, the fitting interpretation is that it is directed at the censure of the negligent and the averse, so the pronoun refers back to what the pronoun in ﴿so they divided their affair﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 53] and similar pronouns refer to, relying on the contextual indication, and His saying ﴿Rather, their hearts are in confusion about this﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 63] and what follows of pronouns.

[Page 80]

Injustice on this interpretation is taken in its literal sense, which is the deprivation of what is right and transgression.

It is also permissible that the pronoun refers to the generality of souls in His saying ﴿We do not burden any soul beyond its capacity﴾, so that His saying ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾ is part of the concluding statement, and injustice on this interpretation is used to mean diminishing from what is due, like His saying the Exalted: ﴿Both gardens brought forth their produce and did not fall short of it in anything﴾ [al-Kahf: 33]. Thus it is a threat to one group and a promise to another group.

And this is the more fitting of the two interpretations with respect to the inimitability of the Qur'an (i'jaz).

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 23, verse 63:**

﴿Nay, but their hearts are in confusion about this, and they have deeds other than that, which they are doing.﴾

This is an *idrab intiqal* (a turning away to a new subject, a transition) to something more striking than what preceded it. It describes another state of heedlessness (*ghamra*) into which the polytheists have plunged. They are in a confusion that has overwhelmed their hearts and kept them far from acquiring the character of those who are "fearful of their Lord" (﴿who are apprehensive of their Lord﴾). How could their deeds, which are opposed to the deeds of the believers, be fitting for anything but their disbelief? For "each acts according to his own manner" (*shakila*).

The preposition *min* in His saying ﴿min hadha﴾ ("about this") gives the impression of substitution (*badaliyya*), meaning: they are in a confusion that has made them distant from this.

The demonstrative *hadha* ("this") refers to what was mentioned just before of the attributes of the believers, from His saying ﴿Indeed, those who are apprehensive of their Lord﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 57] up to His saying ﴿and they are foremost in them﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 61].

The word *dun* ("other than") indicates opposition to the states of the believers, meaning: they are not fit to adorn themselves with such noble qualities.

His saying ﴿and they have deeds other than that, which they are doing﴾ explains *hadha*, meaning: their deeds, which they perform, are other than that.

This reminds me of the words of Muhammad ibn Bashir al-Kharijī in praise of 'Urwa ibn Zayd al-Khayl:

O you who wish to be a youth like Ibn Zayd, he has indeed cleared the paths for you.

Count the virtues of character that were counted for him; did he ever revile anyone, or was he reviled, or was he miserly?

If you spend wealth or exert yourself in its pursuits, he will have compassion for you, and you will do less than what he did.

The *lam* in ﴿lahum a'mal﴾ ("they have deeds") is for *ikhtisas* (exclusivity). Placing the prepositional phrase with it before the subject ("mubtada'") restricts the predicate to the subject (*qasr al-musnad ilayh 'ala al-musnad*), meaning: they have deeds which they do not perform other than the works of faith and good deeds.

The description of ﴿a'mal﴾ ("deeds") by the clause ﴿hum laha 'amilun﴾ ("they are doing them") indicates that they persist in them and do not desist from them, because they have been harmed by them through their deep immersion in them.

The nominal sentence is used to convey the continuity of those deeds and their steadfastness in them.

It is also permissible that the placement of *laha* ("them") before *'amilun* ("doing") serves to express exclusivity by *qasr al-qalb* (restriction by reversal), meaning: they do not perform any other righteous deeds to which they were called. It is also permissible that it is for the sake of observing the *fasila* (verse-ending rhyme), since the restriction has already been conveyed by placing the subject first.

[Page 82]

*Ḥattā* here is *ibtidā'iyya* (introducing a new statement, "until" in an initiatory sense). It was already discussed in Surat al-Anbiya' at His saying: ﴿Until, when Gog and Magog are let loose﴾ [al-Anbiya' 96].

With *ḥattā al-ibtidā'iyya*, what follows it is the beginning of a new statement. The word that marks the limit is not a single particle, as it is with the prepositional *ḥattā* (*ḥattā al-jārra*) and the conjunctive *ḥattā* (*ḥattā al-'ātifa*). Rather, the limit is understood from the context. Most often it has the sense of a logical consequence (*tafrī'*).

With this limit, the speech becomes a threat to them of a punishment that will befall them, from which they will cry out with no refuge from it. The apparent reading is that it is a punishment in this world, as indicated by His saying: ﴿And if We had shown them mercy and removed the harm that is upon them, they would persist in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾ [al-Mu'minun 75].

[Page 83]

The first *idhā* is temporal, containing the sense of a condition (*shart*). For this reason, its original and usual use is to indicate a future time. The second *idhā* is sudden (*fujā'iyya*), entering upon the response (*jawāb*) of the conditional *idhā*.

*Al-mutrafūn* are those given over to *taraf*, which is luxury (*rafāhiyya*), meaning those who are pampered, as in His saying: ﴿And leave Me with the deniers, the people of plenty﴾ [al-Muzzammil 11]. So the *mutrafūn* among them are their leaders and their elders. The pronoun attached to them refers to all the polytheists, the people of confusion (*ghamra*).

The seizing is attributed to the *mutrafīn* among them because they are the ones who misled most of their people. Had their word not held sway over their people, the common folk would have followed the truth, because the common people are closer to fairness when they understand the truth, since they are spared most of the causes of stubbornness, such as fear of losing dominance and the end of comfort. Likewise, it is right that the leaders of nations be held accountable for the consequences that fall upon the common people as a result of their errors and reckless conduct, whether through misguidance or poor judgment. They should also be asked about the loss they caused when they led those who followed them into the pit of danger, as He said: ﴿And they will say, "Our Lord, we obeyed our leaders and our elders, and they led us astray from the way."﴾ [al-Ahzab 67] ﴿"Our Lord, give them double punishment and curse them with a great curse."﴾ [al-Ahzab 68] And He said: ﴿That they may bear their burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection, and some of the burdens of those whom they mislead without knowledge. Unquestionably, evil is what they bear﴾ [al-Nahl 25].

Singling out the affluent for punishment, although the nature of divine punishment, if it is worldly, is to encompass all people, hints that the affluent are the cause of the punishment descending upon the common folk. Also, the affluent feel the punishment most intensely, since they are not accustomed to hardship and pain. It is nonetheless known that the punishment encompasses all of them, from His saying: ﴿Then, when they cry out﴾, for the two pronouns in *idhā hum* and *yajārūn* refer to what the pronoun in *mutrafīhim* refers to, as indicated by His saying: ﴿My verses were recited to you﴾ through His saying: ﴿...you turned back on your heels, being arrogant, speaking nonsense at night﴾, for that was the action of all of them.

It is also possible that *al-mutrafīn* means all the polytheists, in which case the construction (*iḍāfa*) is explanatory (*bayāniyya*). The mention of *al-mutrafīn* then serves as a frightening element in the threat, reminding them that the punishment will remove their luxury. The people of Makkah were in luxury and ease, since they were safe from the raids of other peoples, because they were the people of the secure Sanctuary (*ḥaram*). The fruits of everything were brought to them, and they were honored among all the tribes. Al-Akhtal said:

*"As for the people, except Quraysh, we are the best of them in deeds."*

Their provision also came to them from every place. He said: ﴿Who fed them against hunger and secured them against fear﴾ [Quraysh 4]. The meaning, then, is: "until when We seize them while they are in their luxury," as in His saying: ﴿And leave Me with the deniers, the people of plenty, and give them respite a little﴾ [al-Muzzammil 11].

It is also possible that what is meant is the punishment descending specifically upon the affluent, that is, their chiefs and nobles. This is the punishment of the sword on the day of Badr, for on that day the leaders of Quraysh were killed, and they were the people of the well (*qalīb*). Shaddad ibn al-Aswad said:

*"What is it with the well of Badr, the well,*
*of wooden bowls adorned with hump-meat?"*

*"And what is it with the well of Badr, the well,*
*of singing girls and noble drinking companions?"*

He means those whom the well contained, men whose disposition was feeding, merriment and pleasures.

The pronoun in ﴿then, when they cry out﴾, on this interpretation, refers to others than the affluent, since the affluent have perished. The rest cry out from grief over what befell their people and from fear that the killing would continue among the remainder. They cry out each time one of their leaders is struck down. Also, the people of Makkah were astonished at that calamity, and they mourned their dead with elegies and lamentations.

[Page 84]

Furthermore, the apparent meaning of this punishment is a punishment that will befall them in the future, after the revelation of this verse, which is Meccan. It follows that this punishment was preceded by another punishment that befell them before it, as indicated by His saying: ﴿And We had already seized them with punishment﴾ [al-Mu'minun 76], and so on. Therefore, the punishment mentioned here is one they were threatened with. It is either the second hunger that befell the people of Makkah through the supplication of the Prophet (ﷺ) after his migration. That was because when Thumamah ibn Uthal al-Hanafi embraced Islam, following the expedition of Khalid ibn al-Walid against Banu Kalb in which he had taken Thumamah captive and he had become Muslim, he prevented grain from leaving the land of his people in al-Yamamah for the people of Makkah. Al-Yamamah had been the source of their food, to the extent that it was called the countryside of the people of Makkah. So hunger befell them, to the point that they ate *al-'ilhiz* (a kind of plant-paste) and carrion for seven years. Or it is the punishment of the sword that befell them on the day of Badr.

It was also said that this punishment is one that occurred before the revelation of the verse, and it is determined that it was the punishment of hunger that befell them during the days the Prophet (ﷺ) stayed in Makkah. Then God removed it from them through the blessing of His Prophet and the safety of the believers. This is what is mentioned in Surat al-Dukhan: ﴿Our Lord, remove the punishment from us; indeed, we are believers﴾ [al-Dukhan 12].

It was also said that the punishment is the punishment of the Hereafter. What weakens this view is that the punishment of the Hereafter will be mentioned in His saying: ﴿Until, when death comes to one of them, he says, "My Lord, send me back"﴾ [al-Mu'minun 99], and the verses following, through His saying: ﴿"You remained not but a little, if you had only known"﴾ [al-Mu'minun 114], as you will see.

Several of the earlier possibilities also arise from this, and their explanation is not hidden.

The meaning of *yajārūn* is "they cry out." Its verbal noun is *al-ja'r*. The noun is *al-ju'ār*, with a *ḍamma* on the *jīm*, and it is a metaphor for the intensity of the pain of the punishment, to the point that they cannot endure it, so there comes from them the cry of moaning, woe and destruction. The clause ﴿Do not cry out today﴾ is parenthetical between what precedes it and what follows from it, His saying: ﴿Have they not contemplated the word?﴾ [al-Mu'minun 68]. It is the object of an implied saying, meaning: "It is said to them: Do not cry out today."

This saying is an inner speech (*kalām nafsī*), which God informed them of in order to frighten them about a punishment whose descent will not be relieved by their crying out, since no one answers their crying and no one brings them relief from it. It is a punishment beyond human capacity, and no one hopes to take on its removal. This is a despairing of them from deliverance from the punishment with which they were threatened.

[Page 85]

If the punishment means the punishment of the Hereafter, then the saying is verbal, and its purpose is to cut off their hope of deliverance.

The prohibition against crying out is used with the sense of equalization (*taswiya*). The occurrence of a prohibition in the sense of equalization is analogous to the occurrence of a command in the sense of equalization. I have found their combination in His saying: ﴿Be patient or be not patient; it is the same for you﴾ [al-Tur 16].

The clause ﴿Indeed, you are from Us, not helped﴾ is a reason (*ta'līl*) for the prohibition used in the sense of equalization. That is: "Do not cry out, for your crying is of no use, since no protector can protect you from Our punishment." So the position of *inna* conveys causation, for it does the work of the *fā'* of consequence.

*Tunṣarūn* is construed with the sense of deliverance, so the verb takes *min* ("from"). That is: "You will not be delivered from Our punishment." There is therefore an omitted *muḍāf* after *min*, and the omission of the *muḍāf* in such a context is common in usage. The fronting of the prepositional phrase serves to emphasize the side of God, Exalted, and to preserve the rhyme (*fāṣila*).

His saying ﴿My verses were recited to you﴾ is a resumption (*isti'nāf*). The predicate is used with the sense of rebuke and reproach. The clause was not conjoined to ﴿Indeed, you are from Us, not helped﴾ because it intends to convey a meaning other than causation, since there is little benefit in combining two causes.

The "verses" here are the verses of the Qur'an, as indicated by *tutlā* (is recited), since *tilāwa* means recitation (*qirā'a*).

*Al-nukūṣ* is returning from the way one came, which is fleeing. *Al-a'qāb* are the hindmost parts of the feet. *Al-nukūṣ* here is a figure of speech for turning away, and mention of the heels is a supporting image (*tarshīḥ*) for the figure. It was already mentioned in His saying: ﴿When the two hosts sighted each other, he turned back on his heels﴾ [al-Anfal 48] in Surat al-Anfal.

The verb *kuntum* is mentioned to indicate that this was their habit. The present tense is mentioned to indicate repetition, so this is a disposition from them that is continually repeated.

The pronoun in *bihi* may refer to the verses, since they stand for the Qur'an. Then *mustakbirīn* means "turning away out of arrogance," and the *bā'* means *'an* ("from"). Or *mustakbirīn* is construed with the sense of "scoffing," and so it takes *bā'*, indicating that it is construed in that sense.

[Page 86]

It is also possible that the pronoun refers to the House or the Sacred Mosque, even though no mention of it has preceded it, because it is present in minds. A pronoun that has no antecedent mentioned is never heard without its being understood, by the aid of the context, to be the intended referent, especially since the recitation of the verses to them has been mentioned. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite the verses of the Qur'an to them in the Sacred Mosque, because it was their gathering place. Then the *bā'* is locative (*ẓarfiyya*). In this there is a rebuke for their arrogance, and that their arrogance was in that place which God commanded to be a locus of humility and noble character. Thus arrogance in the place where the one standing is expected to be devoutly obedient to God, a *ḥanīf*, is the most reprehensible arrogance.

It is also related from Mundhir ibn Sa'id al-Ballūṭī al-Andalusī, judge of Cordova, that the pronoun in *bihi* refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the *bā'* is then transitive (*ta'diya*), with *mustakbirīn* construed with the sense of "deniers," because their arrogance is the cause of their denial.

*Sāmiran* is a second circumstantial accusative (*ḥāl*) from the pronoun of the addressees, meaning: "while you are conversing at night." *Al-sāmir* is a collective noun for those who converse at *samar*, that is, during the night, which is its darkness, or the light of its moon. *Al-samar* has been applied to talk at night, so *al-sāmir* is like *al-ḥājj* ("pilgrim") and *al-ḥāḍir* ("present") and *al-jāmil* ("camel-driver") in the sense of "pilgrims," "those present," and "a group of camel-drivers." In my view, it is also permissible that *sāmiran* means the gathering for night conversation, where they meet to talk at night, and its accusative form is by removal of the preposition, meaning: "in your nighttime gathering," as He said: ﴿And you commit in your gatherings the evil﴾ [al-'Ankabut 29].

*Tahjurūn* with a *ḍamma* on the *tā'*, a *sukūn* on the *hā'* and a *kasra* on the *jīm* is, in the recitation of Nāfi', the present tense of *ahjara*, when one utters *al-hujr*, with a *ḍamma* on the *hā'* and a *sukūn* on the *jīm*, which means idle speech, abuse and bad talk. The remaining ten (readers) recited it with a *fatḥa* on the *tā'*, from *hajara*, when one talks idly. The clause is in the position of a qualifier for *sāmiran*, meaning: "while you are conversing with idle talk." The leaders of Quraysh used to converse around the Ka'bah, speaking slanderously about the religion and denying the Messenger (ﷺ).

[Page 82]

[Page 83]

So the *mutrafūn* among them are their leaders and their elders. The pronoun attached to them refers to all the polytheists, the people of confusion (*ghamra*).

The seizing is attributed to the *mutrafīn* among them because they are the ones who misled most of their people. Had their word not held sway over their people, the common folk would have followed the truth, because the common people are closer to fairness when they understand the truth, since they are spared most of the causes of stubbornness, such as fear of losing dominance and the end of comfort. Likewise, it is right that the leaders of nations be held accountable for the consequences that fall upon the common people as a result of their errors and reckless conduct, whether through misguidance or poor judgment. They should also be asked about the loss they caused when they led those who followed them into the pit of danger, as He said: ﴿And they will say, "Our Lord, we obeyed our leaders and our elders, and they led us astray from the way."﴾ [al-Ahzab 67] ﴿"Our Lord, give them double punishment and curse them with a great curse."﴾ [al-Ahzab 68] And He said: ﴿That they may bear their burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection, and some of the burdens of those whom they mislead without knowledge. Singling out the affluent for punishment, although the nature of divine punishment, if it is worldly, is to encompass all people, hints that the affluent are the cause of the punishment descending upon the common folk. Also, the affluent feel the punishment most intensely, since they are not accustomed to hardship and pain. It is nonetheless known that the punishment encompasses all of them, from His saying: ﴿Then, when they cry out﴾, for the two pronouns in *idhā hum* and *yajārūn* refer to what the pronoun in *mutrafīhim* refers to, as indicated by His saying: ﴿My verses were recited to you﴾ through His saying: ﴿...you turned back on your heels, being arrogant, speaking nonsense at night﴾, for that was the action of all of them.

It is also possible that *al-mutrafīn* means all the polytheists, in which case the construction (*iḍāfa*) is explanatory (*bayāniyya*). The mention of *al-mutrafīn* then serves as a frightening element in the threat, reminding them that the punishment will remove their luxury. The people of Makkah were in luxury and ease, since they were safe from the raids of other peoples, because they were the people of the secure Sanctuary (*ḥaram*). The fruits of everything were brought to them, and they were honored among all the tribes. Al-Akhtal said:

*"As for the people, except Quraysh, we are the best of them in deeds."*

Their provision also came to them from every place. He said: ﴿Who fed them against hunger and secured them against fear﴾ [Quraysh 4]. The meaning, then, is: "until when We seize them while they are in their luxury," as in His saying: ﴿And leave Me with the deniers, the people of plenty, and give them respite a little﴾ [al-Muzzammil 11].

It is also possible that what is meant is the punishment descending specifically upon the affluent, that is, their chiefs and nobles. This is the punishment of the sword on the day of Badr, for on that day the leaders of Quraysh were killed, and they were the people of the well (*qalīb*). Shaddad ibn al-Aswad said:

*"What is it with the well of Badr, the well,*
*of wooden bowls adorned with hump-meat?"*

*"And what is it with the well of Badr, the well,*
*of singing girls and noble drinking companions?"*

He means those whom the well contained, men whose disposition was feeding, merriment and pleasures.

The pronoun in ﴿then, when they cry out﴾, on this interpretation, refers to others than the affluent, since the affluent have perished. The rest cry out from grief over what befell their people and from fear that the killing would continue among the remainder. They cry out each time one of their leaders is struck down. Also, the people of Makkah were astonished at that calamity, and they mourned their dead with elegies and lamentations.

[Page 84]

Furthermore, the apparent meaning of this punishment is a punishment that will befall them in the future, after the revelation of this verse, which is Meccan. Therefore, the punishment mentioned here is one they were threatened with. It is either the second hunger that befell the people of Makkah through the supplication of the Prophet (ﷺ) after his migration. That was because when Thumamah ibn Uthal al-Hanafi embraced Islam, following the expedition of Khalid ibn al-Walid against Banu Kalb in which he had taken Thumamah captive and he had become Muslim, he prevented grain from leaving the land of his people in al-Yamamah for the people of Makkah. Al-Yamamah had been the source of their food, to the extent that it was called the countryside of the people of Makkah. So hunger befell them, to the point that they ate *al-'ilhiz* (a kind of plant-paste) and carrion for seven years. Or it is the punishment of the sword that befell them on the day of Badr.

It was also said that this punishment is one that occurred before the revelation of the verse, and it is determined that it was the punishment of hunger that befell them during the days the Prophet (ﷺ) stayed in Makkah. Then God removed it from them through the blessing of His Prophet and the safety of the believers. This is what is mentioned in Surat al-Dukhan: ﴿Our Lord, remove the punishment from us; indeed, we are believers﴾ [al-Dukhan 12].

Several of the earlier possibilities also arise from this, and their explanation is not hidden.

It is a punishment beyond human capacity, and no one hopes to take on its removal. This is a despairing of them from deliverance from the punishment with which they were threatened.

*Tahjurūn* with a *ḍamma* on the *tā'*, a *sukūn* on the *hā'* and a *kasra* on the *jīm* is, in the recitation of Nāfi', the present tense of *ahjara*, when one utters *al-hujr*, with a *ḍamma* on the *hā'* and a *sukūn* on the *jīm*, which means idle speech, abuse and bad talk. The remaining ten (readers) recited it with a *fatḥa* on the *tā'*, from *hajara*, when one talks idly. The clause is in the position of a qualifier for *sāmiran*, meaning: "while you are conversing with idle talk." The leaders of Quraysh used to converse around the Ka'bah, speaking slanderously about the religion and denying the Messenger (ﷺ).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 23, verses 68–70:

[p. 87]
﴿Have they not then pondered the Word, or has there come to them what had not come to their forefathers of old? Or have they not recognized their Messenger, so that they deny him? Or do they say, "There is madness in him"? Nay, he has brought them the truth, but most of them are averse to the truth.﴾

The fa' (فاء) here serves to make the discourse follow on from the preceding discourse, which is His saying: ﴿Nay, their hearts are in confusion about this﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 63] up to His saying: ﴿talking nonsense about it by night, abandoning it﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 67]. This sequence (tafri') is interposed between the sentence ﴿Nay, their hearts are in confusion about this﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 63] and the sentence ﴿Even if We had mercy upon them and removed what afflicts them of harm, they would persist in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 75].

What follows (al-mufarra') is a series of interrogations about the cause of their aversion and the continuance of their hearts in confusion until the punishment promised to them descends upon them.

These interrogations are used for rebuke by way of metonymy (al-majaz al-mursal), because the clarity of an error necessarily implies doubt as to whether it could have issued from rational people, and that doubt calls for the question of whether such an error could have occurred among rational people.

The upshot of the meanings of these interrogations is an enumeration of the sources of their misguidance and error; for this reason they were singled out for mention with matters of this kind. Likewise they serve as an argument against them, a cutting off of their excuse, and an awakening for them, showing that all the attributes of the Messenger are indicative of his truthfulness.

The first interrogation concerns their failure to ponder what is recited to them of the Qur'an, which is what is meant by "the Word" (al-qawl), that is, the speech. God the Exalted said: ﴿Do they not then ponder the Qur'an?﴾ [al-Nisa': 82]. Tadabbur (contemplation, "pondering") is the exercise of the intellectual faculty upon the indications of signs for that to which they were set up. Its root is that it derives from looking at the back (dubur) of a matter, i.e., at what does not appear to the contemplator at first glance. It has already been discussed at His saying: ﴿Do they not then ponder the Qur'an? Had it been from other than God, they would have found in it much discrepancy﴾ [al-Nisa': 82], in Surat al-Nisa'.

[p. 88]
The meaning is that if they had pondered the word of the Qur'an, they would have known that it is the truth, by the evidence of its inimitability (i'jaz) and the soundness of its aims. Their persistence in obstinacy was only because they did not ponder the Word. This is one of the causes by which they were submerged in disbelief.

The second interrogation is the one implied after (am) and His saying: ﴿Or have they not recognized their Messenger﴾. Here (am) is a particle of transitional disjunction from one interrogation to another, namely the disconnected (munqati'ah) (am), meaning (bal), and it necessarily requires an interrogative to be understood after it. So His saying ﴿or has there come to them what had not come to their forefathers﴾ is to be understood as: "Nay, has there come to them...?" Coming (al-maji') is used figuratively for informing and conveying, and likewise coming (al-ityan).

The relative (ma) refers to a religion. The meaning is: "Has there come to them a religion that had not come to their forefathers of old?", namely the religion calling to the Oneness of God and affirming the Resurrection. For this reason they used to say: (﴿Indeed, we found our fathers upon a community, and indeed we are following in their footsteps, guided﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 22]). For this reason God the Exalted said: ﴿And so We did not send before you any warner into a town but its affluent ones said, "Indeed, we found our fathers upon a community, and indeed we are following in their footprints."﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 23] ﴿He said, "Even if I brought you better guidance than that upon which you found your fathers?" They said, "Indeed, we are disbelievers in that with which you have been sent."﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 24].

Furthermore, if what is intended is the apparent meaning of the relative clause, namely ﴿that had not come to their forefathers of old﴾, in the sense that the religion which has come to them has no precedent among them, then it is necessary that there be a note of mockery in the speech, since they denied a religion that had come to them and whose coming had not preceded their forefathers. The point of the mockery is that it is the nature of every messenger who brings a religion that his religion should be new; and if the people already had its like, its coming would be an achieving of what is already achieved.

If, however, what is intended by the relative clause is that it opposes what their forefathers were upon, since that is part of the meaning of (﴿had not come to their forefathers﴾), then the speech is merely a confusing of the issue, i.e., there is no direction for their disbelief in it, since it opposes what their forefathers were upon, for a religion can only be opposed to error. This is in the sense of His saying: ﴿Or have We given them a Book before this, so that they hold fast to it?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 21] ﴿Nay, they say, "Indeed, we found our fathers upon a community, and indeed we are following in their footsteps, guided."﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 22].

[p. 89]
As for the third interrogation, which is implied after the second (am) in His saying ﴿or have they not recognized their Messenger﴾, it is an interrogation about their not recognizing the Messenger, on the basis that non-recognition of him is one of two possibilities regarding their state, since they cannot be free of one of the two. As for their recognizing him, that is what is presumed of them, so the more fitting subject of interrogation is their non-recognition of him; it is supposed in the way that the less likely thing is supposed, because it is the locus of astonishment which necessarily entails rebuke. For their hurling at the Messenger the charges of lying, sorcery and poetry suits the supposition that they did not know him before, since one who truly knows a man does not describe him with what is far from him. Accordingly, their denial of him is made a consequence of their non-recognition of him, i.e., their denial of his perfect attributes.

Thus the attaching of the pronoun referring to the person of the Messenger to (munkirun, deniers) is of the type of ascribing a judgment to the essence while the intended meaning is its attributes, like His saying: ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers﴾ [al-Nisa': 23]. These attributes are truthfulness, freedom from sorcery, and that he is not among the ranks of poets.

How well Abu Talib said:

They have certainly known that our son is not one accused of lying among us, nor is he attributed to the speech of falsehoods.

And God the Exalted said, regarding what He commanded His Messenger: ﴿Indeed I have dwelt among you a lifetime before it﴾ [Yunus: 16], i.e., the Qur'an. ﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 80].

Since man may be struck by something that removes his faculties, namely the derangement of his intellect, the words ﴿or do they say, "There is madness in him"﴾ are conjoined to ﴿or have they not recognized their Messenger﴾. This is the fourth interrogation, i.e., perhaps they claimed that their Messenger, whom they know, has been afflicted with madness, so that his truthfulness has turned into lying.

Jinnah (جِنَّة) is madness, which is the mental derangement that afflicts a person; they used to believe it came from the touch of the jinn. Jinnah is also applied to the jinn, who are created beings hidden from our sight, as in His saying: ﴿from among the jinn and mankind﴾ [al-Nas: 6]. Jinnah is also applied to the ailment resulting from being struck by the jinn, and its bearer is majnun (mad); this is the intended meaning here, by the evidence of the preposition bi (ب) of association. It was discussed earlier at His saying:

[p. 90]
﴿Have they not reflected? There is no madness in their companion﴾ [al-A'raf: 184], in Surat al-A'raf. They did not in fact suppose him to be mad, but they used to say it with their tongues as slander. The utterance by their tongues is not the target of the interrogation. Then what was founded upon what they had fabricated is annulled, so the particle of disjunction (bal), which carries the sense of istidrak (correction), is placed in the statement.

The truth (al-haqq) is that which is established in reality and in the actual state of affairs; it applies to essences and their attributes, to kinds, to meanings, and to reports. It is the opposite of falsehood, the opposite of sorcery, and the opposite of poetry. Thus whatever the Prophet ﷺ brought them of reports, commands and prohibitions is wholly associated with the truth. By this, what they said about the Qur'an and about the Messenger, peace be upon him, is refuted: the saying of those who did not ponder the Qur'an, and of those who regarded only conformity with what their first forefathers were upon, and of those who did not know the condition of their Messenger who is from among themselves, and the saying of one who casts slander, by which they attributed the truthful one to deception and confusion.

The truth that the Prophet brought them comprises first the affirmation of the Oneness of God the Exalted and the affirmation of the Resurrection, and what follows from that of the laws revealed at Mecca, such as the commanding of prayer and zakat, the maintaining of kinship ties, acknowledging the merit of the meritorious, restraining the wicked from their wickedness, the brotherhood of Muslims toward one another, equality among them in right, the prohibition of abominations such as fornication and the killing of souls, the burying of daughters alive, aggression, the consuming of wealth falsely, the humiliation of the orphan and the needy, and the like, along with the abolition of what was the state of the Age of Ignorance of aggression, and the system of kinship in which they were raised from an ancient time. Thus everything the Messenger brought on that day is that which accords with the requirement of the order of civilization upon which God created the world, and so it is the truth, as He said: ﴿We did not create them except with truth﴾ [al-Dukhan: 39]. Since the speech of the liar and the speech of the madman, which is peculiar to this and which neither the rational nor the truthful share, do not accord with this truth, establishing that what the messengers brought is the truth is a refutation of their denial of its truthfulness. And as for their saying "he is mad", what follows "Nay" is a refutation of their saying.

The consistency of the pronouns indicates that the pronoun in (aktharuhum, most of them) refers back to the people spoken of in His saying: ﴿So leave them in their confusion﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 54]. The meaning is: most of the polytheists of Quraysh are averse to the truth.

[p. 91]
This is a recording against them that their natures recoil from the truth which opposes their desires, because of what they had acquired of polytheism, the committing of abominations, injustice, arrogance, usurpation, and all manner of corruption, let alone what they were upon of corrupt belief in associating partners with God and the deeds that follow from it, as He the Exalted said: ﴿And they have deeds other than that which they are doing﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 63]. Therefore, without doubt, they were by this averse to the truth, because the very kind of truth is incompatible with these natures. Among these was Abu Jahl. God the Exalted said: ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening﴾ [al-An'am: 52], up to His saying: ﴿so that they say, "Are these the ones upon whom God has bestowed favour from among us?"﴾ [al-An'am: 53].

The aversion to the truth is ascribed to most of them rather than all of them out of fairness toward those among them who possessed sound judgment, who knew the falsity of polytheism and inclined toward the truth, but who used to side with their tyrants out of appeasement and out of preserving their own dignity, knowing that if they openly proclaimed the truth they would meet harm and belittlement from their tyrants. Among these were Abu Talib, al-Abbas and al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. Disbelief encompassed them all.

Since the operator governing it was weakened by being postponed, the object is joined with the reinforcing lam (لام التقوية).
