Here (am) is a particle of transitional disjunction from one interrogation to another, namely the disconnected (munqati'ah) (am), meaning (bal), and it necessarily requires an interrogative to be understood after it. So His saying ﴿or has there come to them what had not come to their forefathers﴾ is to be understood as: "Nay, has there come to them...?" Coming (al-maji') is used figuratively for informing and conveying, and likewise coming (al-ityan).

The relative (ma) refers to a religion. The meaning is: "Has there come to them a religion that had not come to their forefathers of old?", namely the religion calling to the Oneness of God and affirming the Resurrection. For this reason they used to say: (﴿Indeed, we found our fathers upon a community, and indeed we are following in their footsteps, guided﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 22]). For this reason God the Exalted said: ﴿And so We did not send before you any warner into a town but its affluent ones said, "Indeed, we found our fathers upon a community, and indeed we are following in their footprints."﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 23] ﴿He said, "Even if I brought you better guidance than that upon which you found your fathers?" They said, "Indeed, we are disbelievers in that with which you have been sent."﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 24].

Furthermore, if what is intended is the apparent meaning of the relative clause, namely ﴿that had not come to their forefathers of old﴾, in the sense that the religion which has come to them has no precedent among them, then it is necessary that there be a note of mockery in the speech, since they denied a religion that had come to them and whose coming had not preceded their forefathers. The point of the mockery is that it is the nature of every messenger who brings a religion that his religion should be new; and if the people already had its like, its coming would be an achieving of what is already achieved.

If, however, what is intended by the relative clause is that it opposes what their forefathers were upon, since that is part of the meaning of (﴿had not come to their forefathers﴾), then the speech is merely a confusing of the issue, i.e., there is no direction for their disbelief in it, since it opposes what their forefathers were upon, for a religion can only be opposed to error. This is in the sense of His saying: ﴿Or have We given them a Book before this, so that they hold fast to it?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 21] ﴿Nay, they say, "Indeed, we found our fathers upon a community, and indeed we are following in their footsteps, guided."﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 22].

[p. 89]
As for the third interrogation, which is implied after the second (am) in His saying ﴿or have they not recognized their Messenger﴾, it is an interrogation about their not recognizing the Messenger, on the basis that non-recognition of him is one of two possibilities regarding their state, since they cannot be free of one of the two. As for their recognizing him, that is what is presumed of them, so the more fitting subject of interrogation is their non-recognition of him; it is supposed in the way that the less likely thing is supposed, because it is the locus of astonishment which necessarily entails rebuke. For their hurling at the Messenger the charges of lying, sorcery and poetry suits the supposition that they did not know him before, since one who truly knows a man does not describe him with what is far from him. Accordingly, their denial of him is made a consequence of their non-recognition of him, i.e., their denial of his perfect attributes.

Thus the attaching of the pronoun referring to the person of the Messenger to (munkirun, deniers) is of the type of ascribing a judgment to the essence while the intended meaning is its attributes, like His saying: ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers﴾ [al-Nisa': 23]. These attributes are truthfulness, freedom from sorcery, and that he is not among the ranks of poets.

How well Abu Talib said:

They have certainly known that our son is not one accused of lying among us, nor is he attributed to the speech of falsehoods.

And God the Exalted said, regarding what He commanded His Messenger: ﴿Indeed I have dwelt among you a lifetime before it﴾ [Yunus: 16], i.e., the Qur'an. ﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 80].

Since man may be struck by something that removes his faculties, namely the derangement of his intellect, the words ﴿or do they say, "There is madness in him"﴾ are conjoined to ﴿or have they not recognized their Messenger﴾. This is the fourth interrogation, i.e., perhaps they claimed that their Messenger, whom they know, has been afflicted with madness, so that his truthfulness has turned into lying.

Jinnah (جِنَّة) is madness, which is the mental derangement that afflicts a person; they used to believe it came from the touch of the jinn. Jinnah is also applied to the jinn, who are created beings hidden from our sight, as in His saying: ﴿from among the jinn and mankind﴾ [al-Nas: 6]. Jinnah is also applied to the ailment resulting from being struck by the jinn, and its bearer is majnun (mad); this is the intended meaning here, by the evidence of the preposition bi (ب) of association. It was discussed earlier at His saying:

[p. 90]
﴿Have they not reflected? There is no madness in their companion﴾ [al-A'raf: 184], in Surat al-A'raf. They did not in fact suppose him to be mad, but they used to say it with their tongues as slander. The utterance by their tongues is not the target of the interrogation. Then what was founded upon what they had fabricated is annulled, so the particle of disjunction (bal), which carries the sense of istidrak (correction), is placed in the statement.

The truth (al-haqq) is that which is established in reality and in the actual state of affairs; it applies to essences and their attributes, to kinds, to meanings, and to reports. It is the opposite of falsehood, the opposite of sorcery, and the opposite of poetry. Thus whatever the Prophet ﷺ brought them of reports, commands and prohibitions is wholly associated with the truth. By this, what they said about the Qur'an and about the Messenger, peace be upon him, is refuted: the saying of those who did not ponder the Qur'an, and of those who regarded only conformity with what their first forefathers were upon, and of those who did not know the condition of their Messenger who is from among themselves, and the saying of one who casts slander, by which they attributed the truthful one to deception and confusion.

The truth that the Prophet brought them comprises first the affirmation of the Oneness of God the Exalted and the affirmation of the Resurrection, and what follows from that of the laws revealed at Mecca, such as the commanding of prayer and zakat, the maintaining of kinship ties, acknowledging the merit of the meritorious, restraining the wicked from their wickedness, the brotherhood of Muslims toward one another, equality among them in right, the prohibition of abominations such as fornication and the killing of souls, the burying of daughters alive, aggression, the consuming of wealth falsely, the humiliation of the orphan and the needy, and the like, along with the abolition of what was the state of the Age of Ignorance of aggression, and the system of kinship in which they were raised from an ancient time. Thus everything the Messenger brought on that day is that which accords with the requirement of the order of civilization upon which God created the world, and so it is the truth, as He said: ﴿We did not create them except with truth﴾ [al-Dukhan: 39]. Since the speech of the liar and the speech of the madman, which is peculiar to this and which neither the rational nor the truthful share, do not accord with this truth, establishing that what the messengers brought is the truth is a refutation of their denial of its truthfulness. And as for their saying "he is mad", what follows "Nay" is a refutation of their saying.

The consistency of the pronouns indicates that the pronoun in (aktharuhum, most of them) refers back to the people spoken of in His saying: ﴿So leave them in their confusion﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 54]. The meaning is: most of the polytheists of Quraysh are averse to the truth.

[p. 91]
This is a recording against them that their natures recoil from the truth which opposes their desires, because of what they had acquired of polytheism, the committing of abominations, injustice, arrogance, usurpation, and all manner of corruption, let alone what they were upon of corrupt belief in associating partners with God and the deeds that follow from it, as He the Exalted said: ﴿And they have deeds other than that which they are doing﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 63]. Therefore, without doubt, they were by this averse to the truth, because the very kind of truth is incompatible with these natures. Among these was Abu Jahl. God the Exalted said: ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening﴾ [al-An'am: 52], up to His saying: ﴿so that they say, "Are these the ones upon whom God has bestowed favour from among us?"﴾ [al-An'am: 53].

The aversion to the truth is ascribed to most of them rather than all of them out of fairness toward those among them who possessed sound judgment, who knew the falsity of polytheism and inclined toward the truth, but who used to side with their tyrants out of appeasement and out of preserving their own dignity, knowing that if they openly proclaimed the truth they would meet harm and belittlement from their tyrants. Among these were Abu Talib, al-Abbas and al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. The meaning, then, is: "Nay, he has brought them the truth, and they all disbelieved in it: as for most of them, out of aversion to the truth; and as for a few of them, out of appeasement toward the rest." Disbelief encompassed them all.

The fronting of the object in His saying ﴿averse to the truth (lil-haqq kari'un)﴾ serves to give emphasis to mention of the truth, so that the listener is held in attention for what follows, and the goodness of hearing it strikes his soul with wonder at those who hate it. Since the operator governing it was weakened by being postponed, the object is joined with the reinforcing lam (لام التقوية).

[Page 92]

This conditional clause of impossibility, *"Had the truth followed their desires, the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them would have been corrupted"* (23:71), is joined to the preceding statement, *"and most of them are averse to the truth"* (al-Mu'minun: 70), to add further condemnation of their desires, since these desires lead to the corruption of the world and of those in it. That is enough to show its heinousness and abomination.

The truth here is the truth mentioned earlier in His words, *"Rather, He has brought them the truth, but most of them are averse to the truth"* (al-Mu'minun: 70). It is that which conforms to actual existence and to the realities of things. From His words, *"Had the truth followed their desires,"* it is understood that the aversion of most of them to the truth arises from the truth being contrary to their desires, so it is recorded against them that they are people of desire. *Hawa* (desire) is craving and love for what suits the aim of its possessor, and it is a verbal noun used in the sense of the object. Desire applies specifically to the cravings of the soul's impulses, meaning cravings for actions that the natural disposition (*jibillah*) does not require. Thus the craving for food, drink and the like, which the natural disposition calls for, is not desire. Desire is rather the craving for what the innate nature (*fitrah*) does not require, such as the craving for oppression and humiliating people, or the craving for what the natural disposition does require but which is desired in a manner or state that the natural disposition does not require, because of the corruption and harm that follow from that state, such as the craving for food that has been seized unlawfully and the craving for fornication. Thus the meaning of desire returns to the object desired, which the natural disposition does not require.

*Ittiba'* (following) is a commonly used figurative expression (*majaz*) for agreement, i.e., *"Had the truth agreed with what they crave."* The meaning of the truth agreeing with desires is that the quiddity (*mahiyyah*) of the truth would be in harmony with the desires of the souls. The realities of things have a fixed existence outside the mind, whether they agree with what people crave or not. Among them are the existential realities, which are the foundation; they are established in actual fact, such as the oneness of God, His not begetting, and the reality of resurrection for recompense. Their being true is identical with their being established outside the mind.

Among them are also the notional realities that exist in consideration (*i'tibar*), which are established in considerations. Their being true is their being in accordance with what the order of the world requires, such as the burying of daughters being oppression, the killing of people being aggression, and gambling being taking someone's wealth without right for the one who takes it. Were it supposed that the truth lay in the opposites of these things, the heavens and the earth would be corrupted, and whoever is in them would be corrupted, i.e., the people who are in the heavens and the earth.

The necessary connection between the corruption of the heavens and the earth and the corruption of people, and between the truth following the desires of the polytheists regarding realities, is that their desires are diverse. Among them some agree, but most of them differ, and the greatest agreement of their desires is achieved through polytheism. So if the truth established in reality agreed with their claims, the foundations of the order of the worlds would be disrupted.

The principle of realities is the reality of the Creator, exalted is He. Were the reality to be the plurality of gods, the worlds would be corrupted by His words, exalted is He, *"Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would have been corrupted"* (al-Anbiya': 22), and its detailed explanation has already passed in the surah of al-Anbiya'. That is the essence of the truth and its foundation, and its breakdown is a breakdown of the order of the heavens and the earth, as already mentioned. Allah, exalted is He, has said in this surah, *"Allah has not taken any son, nor was there with Him any god"* (al-Mu'minun: 91), and so on. Among their false desires is that they made it part of Allah's perfection that He should have a son.

Then we move the discussion to the rest of the realities of what the Messenger (ﷺ) brought of the truth. Were it supposed that the established fact were the opposite of that, corruption would seep into the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them. If it were supposed that there is no resurrection for recompense, the established fact would be that there is no recompense for deeds. Then no one would do good, since there is no hope of reward, and no one would abandon evil, since there is no fear of punishment. Evil would overwhelm good and falsehood would overwhelm truth, and that is corruption for those in the heavens and the earth. He, exalted is He, said, *"Did you think that We created you in vain and that you would not be returned to Us?"* (al-Mu'minun: 115). Likewise, if the truth were the goodness of transgression and the falsehood the ugliness of justice, people would hurl themselves at one another with destruction to the utmost of their ability, and the livestock and the crops would perish. He, exalted is He, said, *"When he turns away, he strives in the land to cause corruption therein and destroy crops and livestock; and Allah does not like corruption"* (al-Baqarah: 205). So it is with their diverse desires. Their affair becomes even more corrupt when the truth follows, at every moment, a desire contrary to the desire it had followed before, so no order and no law becomes stable.

This meaning relates to His words, exalted is He: *"We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play. We did not create them except with truth, but most of them do not know"* (al-Dukhan: 38).

Apparently the *man* (who/whoever) in His words *"and whoever is in them"* is applied to the rational beings among humans and angels. The corruption of humans, on the assumption that the truth follows the desires of the polytheists, is clear from what we have established.

As for the corruption of the angels, it is because among the desires of the polytheists is their claim that the angels are the daughters of Allah. If the reality were that the true nature of the angels is being children of Allah, that would lead to their being gods, because that which is begotten of a kind must be similar to that from which it is begotten, since the offspring is a copy of its father. Thus what follows from the belief in a plurality of gods would follow from it. Furthermore, if it were not part of the essential nature of the angels that they are subjugated to the obedience of Allah and the execution of His commands, their realities would be corrupted, so they would corrupt what Allah commands them to set right, and vice versa, and thus the benefits would be disrupted.

It is also permissible that *man* applies to all created beings by way of predominance (*taghlib*) in the usage of *man*. The necessary connection is established primarily together with the necessary connection between the plurality of gods and the corruption of the heavens and the earth. Then it extends to the diversity of the quiddities of existent things, so they become unfit for what they were created for, and the world is corrupted. Some later philosophers proposed an inquiry into the possibility of the annihilation of the world and proposed causes which, if any one of them existed in this world, would bring that about. Among these they counted that atmospheric events would occur which corrupt the minds of all humans, so they would combine to destroy the world. Thus, if Allah were to arrange the order according to the dictates of desires, by opposing the truth to what it is in reality, as they wish, that would return corruption upon the whole world, and they would be included in that corruption, because they are among what is in the heavens and the earth. Consider, then, how feeble are the opinions that do not distinguish between harm and benefit even for themselves. That is enough of an abomination, for they hate the truth, and it refutes their claim that what the Messenger brought are the actions of a madman.

\* \* \*

*"Rather, We have brought them their reminder, but they, from their reminder, are turning away"* (al-Mu'minun: 71, continued).

This is a refutation of what the supposition in His words, *"Had the truth followed their desires,"* implied. That is: rather, the truth did not follow their desires, so We conveyed the truth to them in its proper form through the Qur'an, which is a reminder for them that awakens their minds from their slumber. It is as though it reminds their minds of the truth that they had forgotten because of the passage of time over the misguidance of their forefathers, which they had instituted for them. It became their desires, which they grew accustomed to, so they would not accept departing from it, and they turned away from the truth because it opposed it. Thus the conveying of the truth to them by the proofs is made equivalent to reminding a forgetful person of something whose time has long passed for him. As 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said in his letter to Abu Musa al-Ash'ari: "for the truth is ancient." Allah, exalted is He, said, *"And Allah establishes the truth by His words, though the criminals dislike it"* (Yunus: 82).

The verb *atayna-hum* (We have brought them) is transitive with the particle *bi* (with), because it is used figuratively to mean sending and directing.

The word *dhikr* (reminder) may be a verbal noun meaning reminding. It may also be a noun for speech that reminds its hearers of what they have neglected, and this is the characteristic of the divine books. The annexation of *dhikr* to their pronoun is a verbal (lafzi) annexation, of the type where the annexed noun is the object of the verbal noun.

The *fa'* (then) is for making their turning away a consequence of bringing the reminder to them. That is: consequently, upon sending the reminder to them, their turning away from it resulted. The meaning is: We sent the Qur'an to them so that it would remind them.

It has also been said: the annexation of *dhikr* to their pronoun is a semantic (ma'nawi) annexation, meaning the reminder they asked for when they used to say: *"Had we had with us a reminder from the earlier peoples, we would have been sincere servants of Allah"* (al-Saffat: 168). In this case *dhikr* is a verbal noun in the sense of the agent, i.e., that by which they would be reminded. The *fa'* in this case is an eloquent *fa'* (*fa' fasihah*), meaning: "Behold, We have given them a Book, but they turned away from their reminder, which they had asked for." This is like His words, exalted is He, *"Had we had with us a reminder from the earlier peoples"* (al-Saffat: 168), i.e., from messengers before Muhammad (ﷺ), *"we would surely have been sincere servants of Allah. But they disbelieved in it"* (al-Saffat: 169). It is also like the verse of 'Abbas ibn al-Ahnaf:

They said: "Khurasan is the farthest that is aimed at with us, then the return."
Indeed we have come to Khurasan.

And His words, exalted is He: *"lest you say, 'No bringer of good tidings or warner came to us.' But there has come to you a bringer of good tidings and a warner"* (al-Ma'idah: 19).

The expression of their turning away by a nominal sentence serves to indicate the permanence of their turning away and its firm hold upon them. The fronting of the prepositional phrase over its governing verb is for emphasis on mentioning them, so that their turning away from it becomes a matter of wonder.

[Page 96]

﴿Or do you ask them for a payment? But the payment of your Lord is better, and He is the best of providers.﴾

(Am) is conjunctive, coordinating with ﴿Or do they say, "He has a jinn"?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 70]. It marks a shift to another interrogation, concerning the motives for their turning away from the Messenger and the persistence of their hearts in heedlessness.

The implied interrogation here is one of denial, meaning: "You do not ask them for a payment, so that they could excuse their aversion to you on account of it, being miserly with their wealth." This is similar in meaning to God's words: ﴿Say: "Whatever payment I have asked of you, it is yours. My reward is only from God"﴾ [Saba': 47], by way of supposition. The sense is: "If I had asked you for a payment, I would have returned it to you; so what prevents you from following me?" Also His words: ﴿Or do you ask them for a payment, so that they are burdened with debt?﴾ [al-Tur: 40]. All of this is in the sense of mockery. More explicit than both is His words: ﴿Say: "I do not ask you any payment for it, except affection for my near kin"﴾ [al-Shura: 23].

This shift was made to negate that the cause of their turning away from the call of the Messenger lay in something coming from him or caused by him. The three preceding interrogations concerned causes of aversion originating from them. Thus the interrogation in ﴿Do you ask them for a payment?﴾ is one of denial, since it is not permissible that the Messenger would do anything that obliges those addressed to turn away from his call. Accordingly, the responsibility for the aversion rests entirely with them.

Al-kharj (الخَرْج) is a fixed gift levied on persons or on lands, like a tribute (al-ita'a). As for al-kharaj (الخَراج), it is said to be a synonym of al-kharj, which is the apparent position of the majority of the lexicographers. Ibn al-A'rabi, however, distinguished between them: al-kharj is a tribute levied on persons, and al-kharaj is a tribute levied on lands.

It is also said: al-kharj is what the giver offers voluntarily, while al-kharaj is what he is bound to pay. In al-Kashshaf: "The correct view is that al-kharj is more specific than al-kharaj," meaning that al-kharj is more general, as corrected by the author of al-Fara'id in quoting al-Tibi, as in your saying: kharaj al-qarya (the land-tax of the village) and kharj al-kurda (the payment for the ...), an increase in wording for an increase in meaning. For this reason, the reading of whoever read (﴿kharjan fa-kharaju rabbika khayr﴾) is good. That is, "Or do you ask them for a little of the gifts of creatures in return for your guidance to them? The abundant gifts of the Creator are better." End of quotation.

This is what should be relied upon, because the原 basic principle in the language is the absence of synonymy.

Now, the majority read ﴿Or do you ask them for kharjan? Then the kharaj of your Lord is better.﴾ Ibn 'Amir read (kharjan fa-kharju rabbika). Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read (﴿Or do you ask them for kharajan? Then the kharaj of your Lord is better.﴾). As for the reading of the majority, its justification on the basis that the two words are synonyms is that they follow the variation of expression, avoiding repetition of the same word in a context that does not require repeating both words, given the closeness of the two words. This differs from His words: ﴿Say: "Whatever payment I have asked of you, it is yours. My reward is only from God"﴾ [Saba': 47], where the word ajr (payment) is repeated after three other words.

As for the basis of the distinction chosen by al-Zamakhshari, the justification of the majority's reading lies in its containing variation of expression and an embellishment of intensification.

As for the readings of Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf, their justification on the path of synonymy is that both forms came according to the speaker's choice in usage, together with the good harmony of matching the two words. They cannot be justified on the path of al-Zamakhshari.

The author of al-Kashshaf said: God established the argument against them in these verses (i.e., His words: ﴿Do they not ponder the Word?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 68] up to here), and cut off their excuses and pretexts, by [showing] that the one sent to them is a man whose matter and condition are well known, whose secret and public life are known, worthy that someone like him be chosen for the message from among them; that he had not been encountered so that he would claim such a great claim falsely; that he did not make it a ladder to gain their worldly goods and to seek their wealth; and that he called them only to the religion of Islam, which is the straight path, while exposing what was hidden of their diseases, which is their failure to reflect and contemplate, their frivolity regarding the religion of their misguided forefathers without proof, their pretext that he is a madman after the truth has become manifest and the confirmation from God through miracles and clear signs has been established, and their aversion to the truth and their turning away from what holds their share of the Reminder. End of quotation.

[Page 97]

The clause ﴿and He is the best of providers﴾ is parenthetical, completing the purpose by praising God and describing the breadth of His bounty. It also serves to emphasize the meaning of ﴿the payment of your Lord is better﴾.

[Page 98]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 23, verses 73–74:

﴿And indeed, you invite them to a straight path.﴾ ﴿And indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter are deviating from the path.﴾

The affirmation of the Messenger's innocence from what they fabricated against him is followed by the affirmation of Islam's innocence from the falsehoods they attributed to it. Such affirmation of innocence is accomplished by asserting its opposite, namely that it is a straight path (ṣirāṭ mustaqīm), meaning a road without crookedness or obstacles. The statement is thus an allusion (taʿrīḍ) to those who believed the opposite of this. The application of the description "straight path" to Islam is because it leads to what every intelligent person seeks: salvation and the attainment of good. Just as the traveler toward his goal cannot reach it except by a road, and his arrival is not assured or easy unless the road is straight, so when the Prophet ﷺ invited them to Islam, he invited them to walk a path that leads to the goal without hardship.

The emphasis with (inna) and the lām is in view of the fact that it is brought as an allusion to the deniers regarding what the Prophet ﷺ invited them to.

Likewise the emphasis in His saying: ﴿And indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter are deviating from the path.﴾ The expression here employs the relative pronoun, and its clause is a manifest noun in place of the pronoun, for he departed from saying: "And indeed they are deviating from the path." The purpose of it is what the clause indicates regarding the cause of their deviation from the straight path: that its cause is their not believing in the Hereafter.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿This is a straight path upon Me﴾ [al-Hijr: 41] has already occurred in Surat al-Hijr.

Page 99
The definiteness in (al-ṣirāṭ), meaning: they are deviating from the path as such, since they have not sought a path of salvation. Thus they deviate from the road, let alone the straight road. For this reason, the definiteness in His saying ﴿from the path﴾ is not for prior reference to the path mentioned, because the definiteness of the genus (taʿrīf al-jins) is more complete in attributing them to error, by the indication that they do not believe in the Hereafter, which is the goal of the doer from his action. So they are, then, deviating from every path that leads to it, since they have no aspiration to reach it.

Al-nākib: one who turns away from something, who avoids it. Its verb is like naṣara and faraḥa. It seems to be derived from al-mankab, which is the side of the shoulder, because the one who turns away from something turns his face away from it with his side.

The definiteness in (al-ṣirāṭ), meaning: they are deviating from the path as such, since they have not sought a path of salvation. Thus they deviate from the road, let alone the straight road. For this reason, the definiteness in His saying ﴿from the path﴾ is not for prior reference to the path mentioned, because the definiteness of the genus (taʿrīf al-jins) is more complete in attributing them to error, by the indication that they do not believe in the Hereafter, which is the goal of the doer from his action. So they are, then, deviating from every path that leads to it, since they have no aspiration to reach it.

Al-nākib: one who turns away from something, who avoids it. Its verb is like naṣara and faraḥa. It seems to be derived from al-mankab, which is the side of the shoulder, because the one who turns away from something turns his face away from it with his side.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 23, verse 75:

﴿And even if We had mercy upon them and removed the affliction that is upon them, they would persist in their transgression, wandering blindly.﴾ It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon the clause ﴿Until when We seize their affluent ones with punishment, behold, they cry out for help﴾ [al-Muʾminun: 64], and what lies between them are interjections (iʿtirāḍāt) that argue against them, censure them, and cut off their excuses. That is: they are not such that, if Allah were to answer their supplication when the punishment descends upon them and remove the punishment from them, they would return to what they were in of heedlessness (al-ghamrah) and evil deeds, because these had become their innate disposition (sajiyyah) that never leaves them.

This has the same meaning as His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿Indeed, We will remove the punishment a little; indeed, you will return [to disbelief]﴾ [al-Dukhan: 15].

Here, (law) (if/even if) is followed by a past-tense verb that is intended to refer to the future, by the indication of the context, since the context is one of warning and of despairing them of relief when the promised punishment descends, and it is not a context of excusing Allah for not answering them or for withholding His mercy from them, since it is evident that this does not suit the context of threat and intimidation. As for this verb coming in the past form, that is out of consideration for what was common in speech of pairing (law) with the present form; for its original function is to indicate impossibility in the past, and therefore the original rule is that the verb following it is not put in the jussive.

Al-lajaj (with a fatha on the lam): persistence in contention and not desisting from it. It is said: lajja yaljju and yalajju (with kasra and fatha on the lam in the present tense, according to the variation of the vowel of the ʿayn in the past tense).

Al-ṭughyan: the most intense form of arrogance. Al-ʿamah: hesitation (tarammud) in error. (Fi ṭughyanihim) is connected to (yaʿmahun); it was placed before it for the sake of emphasis on mentioning it, and for observing the rhyme (fawasil). (Fi) here is of figurative location (al-ẓarfiyyah al-majaziyyah), the meaning intended from it being causation (al-sababiyyah). His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And He extends them in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾ [al-Baqarah: 15] has already preceded in Surat al-Baqarah.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 23, verses 76–77:**

﴿Indeed, We seized them with punishment, but they did not humble themselves before their Lord, nor did they supplicate.﴾ ﴿Until, when We opened upon them a door of severe punishment, at once they were in despair therein.﴾

This is an argument for the meaning of His saying: ﴿And if We had mercy upon them and removed what afflicted them of adversity, they would persist in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 75], based on their earlier persistence in polytheism, their turning away from seeking refuge in God, and their failure to take warning from the fact that the punishment which befell them was the recompense for their polytheism.

The preceding sentence is an address to the Prophet ﷺ, who knows his own truthfulness, so he had no need of corroboration. However, since it concerned the polytheists, and was of a kind that would reach their ears while they did not believe that it was the speech of one whose truthfulness is beyond doubt, the context required that they be argued against by the evidence of their own past conditions. Therefore, before it came ﴿So leave them in their confusion for a time﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 54], and after it came ﴿Say: To whom belong the earth and whoever is in it, if you should know?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 84].

The definite article in His saying (bil-'adhab, "with the punishment") is for prior reference (al-'ahd, "reference to something already known"), meaning: with the punishment mentioned just before, in His saying: ﴿Until, when We seize their affluent ones with punishment﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 64], etc. The object of the circumstantial clause (al-hal) is what is conjoined to its clause, namely His saying: ﴿they did not humble themselves before their Lord﴾. So do not suppose that the repetition of the word "punishment" here indicates that it is a different punishment from the one mentioned just before, on the basis that repeating the first would be pointless. This verse has the same meaning as His saying in Surah al-Dukhan: ﴿How will they have the reminder, when there had already come to them a clear messenger, then they turned away from him﴾ [al-Dukhan: 13], up to His saying: ﴿Indeed, We will remove the punishment a little; indeed, you will return [to disbelief]﴾ [al-Dukhan: 15]. The meaning is: when We seized them with punishment, their portion was nothing but wailing and crying out, rather than repentance and seeking forgiveness.

It has also been said: this is a different punishment, preceding the punishment mentioned just before. On this view, it fits with the earlier explanations that it is either the first famine or the second famine, in relation to the punishment of the Day of Badr.

Al-istikana (humbling oneself) is a verbal noun meaning submission, derived from al-sukun (stillness), because one who submits ceases movement before the one he submits to. It is an ifti'al form from al-sukun, to indicate the firmness and strength of stillness. Its alif is the alif of the iftial form, like al-idtirab (agitation), and the ta' is an augmentation, as in its augmentation in isti'adha (seeking refuge).

It has also been said: the alif is for ishba' (lengthening of a vowel), meaning that it was added in the derivation and became fixed in the word. But this is not the kind of ishba' that users employ irregularly, as in the verse of Tarafa:

*yanba'u min dhifrayi ghadubin jasratin*

meaning: yanbu'u (it flows). In al-Kashshaf (by al-Zamakhshari), he pointed, for the citation of ishba' in such forms, to the verse of Ibn Hirma:

*Wa anta min al-ghawa'ili hina turma* ∗∗∗ *wa min dhammi al-rijali bi-muntaziah*

He intended: bi-muntazah, so he lengthened the fatha.

It is unlikely that (istakanu) is an istif'al form from al-kawn (being), for two reasons: from the standpoint of its root, since the meaning of "being" in it is not sound, and from the standpoint of its form, since interpreting the sin and ta' in it as conveying the meaning of seeking (talab) is not clear.

The use of the present tense in (yatadarra'una, "they supplicate") indicates the continual negation of their supplication. Al-tadarru' is supplication with humility; it was mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿so that they might humble themselves﴾ [al-An'am: 42] in Surah al-An'am.

[Page 102]

The discussion of the clause ﴿Until, when We opened upon them a door﴾ is like the discussion of ﴿Until, when We seized their affluent ones with punishment﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 64].

The (idha, "when") in His saying ﴿Until, when We opened upon them a door﴾ is like the (idha) that preceded in His saying ﴿Until, when We seized their affluent ones with punishment﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 64], etc.

Opening a door is a figurative depiction of their being suddenly struck by the punishment after it had been withheld from them, in accordance with His saying: ﴿And Allah would not punish them while you are among them﴾ [al-Anfal: 33]. Close to this figure is His saying: ﴿And if it had been entered upon them from its sides﴾ [al-Ahzab: 14].

The state of their being struck by the punishment, after they had been in safety and well-being, is likened to the state of people in a closed house, whose door is opened upon them by a hateful enemy. Or it may be said: the state of the punishment being imposed upon them is likened to the state of a door being opened behind which the punishment had been stored, so that when the door was opened, the punishment poured down upon them. This is like the figure in His saying: "and the oven boiled over" (Wa fara al-tannur), and the saying: "the cup overflowed with the deeds of so-and-so" (tafahat al-ka'su bi-a'mal fulan), and His saying: ﴿Indeed, for those who wronged there is a portion like the portion of their companions﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 59], and the verse of 'Alqama:

*fa-haqqa li-Shasin min nadaka dhanubu*

From this is the saying of the scribes: "the door of such-and-such was opened wide" (futiha bab kadha 'ala misra'ayhi), as a figure for the abundance of that thing, and "he bestowed upon him a scroll of kindness" (afada 'alayhi sijjilan min al-ihsan). And the verse of Abu Tammam:

*min sha'irin waqafa al-kalamu bi-babihi* ∗∗∗ *wa-iktanna fi kanafayi dhurahu al-mantiqu*

[It is said of] a poet at whose door speech has stood, and within whose two wings of protection eloquence has been enclosed.

He described (bab, "door") by its being (﴿dha 'adhabin shadid﴾, "possessing severe punishment"), rather than adding "door" to "punishment" and saying "a door of punishment," as He said: ﴿So your Lord poured upon them a whip of punishment﴾ [al-Fajr: 13]. This is because (dha 'adhab, "possessing punishment") conveys, through the strength of the punishment's attachment to the door, what the idafa (construct) "door of punishment" does not convey, and so that "punishment" could be described as "severe" (shadid). This is unlike His saying ﴿a whip of punishment﴾ [al-Fajr: 13], where the description "severe" is dispensed with, because it is the object of the verb (sabba, "poured"), which indicates abundance.

By "the severe punishment" is meant a future punishment. The stronger view is that what is meant is the punishment of the sword on the Day of Badr. From Mujahid: it is the punishment of hunger.

It has also been said: it is the punishment of the Hereafter. On this view, the door may be literal, and it is one of the gates of Hell, as in His saying: ﴿until, when they reach it, its gates will be opened﴾ [al-Zumar: 71].

Al-iblas is intense despair of deliverance. It is said: abalasa, when one is humbled and despairs of escape. It is always used with the hamza, and they did not mention a bare verb for it. The apparent view is that it is derived from al-balas, like sahab (cloud), which means a coarse cloth (al-misḥ), and that the original sense of abalasa is "to become one who wears al-balas." It was the emblem of those who renounced worldly comfort. It is said: labisa al-musuh (he wore the coarse woolen garments), when one becomes ascetic.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 23, verse 78:

﴿It is He who brought into being for you hearing, sight, and hearts; little is it that you give thanks.﴾

This is a return to the purpose of the argument (gharad al-istidlal) concerning God's exclusive possession of the attributes of divinity, and a reminder of the blessings He has bestowed upon people, so that they may give thanks by devoting worship to Him alone. This passage had moved away from that purpose at His saying: ﴿And upon them and upon the ship you are carried﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 22], and it shifted to drawing a lesson from the ship of Noah, peace be upon him. It was then followed by drawing lessons from the stories of the peoples of the messengers, after His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And upon them and upon the ship you are carried﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 22]. So this sentence is either conjoined (ma'tufah) to the sentence ﴿And indeed, in the livestock there is a lesson for you﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 21], and the purpose is one, with what lies between them being transitions; or it is a new sentence (mustanfa'ah), a return to the purpose of argument and blessing, and the indication of this has already been mentioned at His saying: ﴿And We certainly sent Noah to his people﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 23].

In this shift from one style to another, then the return to the purpose, there is a renewal of the mind's vigour and a stirring of attentiveness to the speech, and it is one of the methods of Arab speech in their sermons and long discourses. Al-Sakkaki named it "qira al-arwah" (the hospitality of souls), and considered it one of the effects of the generosity of the Arabs.

His saying: ﴿It is He who brought into being for you hearing﴾ is a reminder of the oneness of God, exalted is He.

It is more apparent that the pronoun of majesty (damir al-jalala) is the predicate (musnad) and the relative noun (ism al-mawsul) is the subject (musnad ilayh); because they knew that a creator had brought into being for them hearing and sight, so the one who is the subject of the relative clause (sahib al-silah) is more deserving of being considered the subject. And since they worshipped other than Him, they were treated as one who did not know that He is the One who brought into being for them hearing; so the speech comes to them as a statement conveying restriction of the predicate to the subject (qasr al-qalb) or restriction of the subject (al-ifrad), i.e., "God is the One who brought that into being, not your idols." The address is to the polytheists by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person), or to all people, or to the Muslims, and the purpose of it is an allusion (ta'ridh) to the polytheists.

Al-insha' (bringing into being) means innovation (al-ihdath), i.e., creation (al-ijad).

He made al-absar and al-af'idah plural in consideration of the multiplicity of their possessors. As for the singular of al-sam'a (hearing), it follows the original form of the verbal noun in the singular; for the origin of al-sam'a is that it is a verbal noun (masdar). It has been said: the plural is in consideration of the objects of perception: since sight relates to many kinds of existing things, and the intellects perceive genera and species, the two were made plural on this basis; and hearing was made singular because it relates only to one kind, which is sounds.

(Qalilan) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of the pronoun in (lakum). (Ma) is a verbal (masdariyyah) particle. The implied meaning is: "while your giving thanks is little." If the address is to the polytheists, then thanks means monotheism (al-tawhid), i.e., the thanks that comes from you is little in comparison with your association of another with Him in worship. If the address is to all people, then thanks is general to every thanks for a blessing, and it is little in comparison with the small number of those who give thanks, because most people are polytheists, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And you will not find most of them grateful﴾ [al-A'raf: 17]. If the address is to the Muslims and the purpose is an allusion to the polytheists, then thanks is general, and making it little is an incitement to increase in it and to renounce polytheism.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 23, verse 79:

﴿And it is He who created you (dhara'akum) on the earth, and to Him you will be gathered.﴾

Page 105
It is in the manner of His saying: ﴿And it is He who produced for you hearing and sight﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 78].

Al-dhar' (dhar'): dispersal (al-bath). It has been mentioned earlier in Surat al-An'am. This is a reminder of the blessing of bringing into existence and life, facilitating settlement on the earth, and multiplying the kind; for dhar' necessarily entails all of that. This is another argument for God Most High's sole claim to divinity (al-infiradu bil-ilahiyyah), since they already know that He has no partner in creation, so how could they associate with Him in divinity other kinds (asnaf) which they know do not create anything? It is also an argument for resurrection (al-ba'th), since the One who brought people into existence from non-existence is able to restore their life after their bones have decayed (taqatta'a awsaluhum).

The dhar' is contrasted with its opposite, which is al-hashr (gathering) and al-jam' (assembling), for al-hashr gathers everyone who was on the earth of mankind. In it there is the rhetorical device of antithesis (tibaq).

The purpose of this contrast is a refutation of those who deny resurrection. Therefore, placing the prepositional phrase first in ﴿ilayhi tuhsharun﴾ implies a veiled threat (ta'rid bil-tahdid) that they are being gathered to God, and He will requite them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 23, verses 80–81:

﴿And He it is who gives life and causes death, and to Him belongs the alternation of the night and the day. Will you not then reason?﴾

This is from the same style as ﴿And He it is who produced for you hearing﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 78]. The mention of the Gathering (al-hashr) is followed by the mention of giving life, because resurrection (al-ba'th) is a form of giving life, by way of incorporation (idmaj), so that the proof for the possibility of resurrection is included within the proof for the comprehensive control (al-tasarruf) over the world.

As for the mention of causing death, it is for the sake of the relation of opposition (al-tadadd), and because it indicates the immensity of power and dominion (al-qahr). Since giving life includes the creation of wakefulness, and causing death includes the creation of sleep, as God the Exalted said: ﴿God takes the souls at the time of their death﴾ [al-Zumar: 42], and so on, the alternation of night and day is joined to this, that it is by His power, for that same relation; and because in the directing (tasrif) of night and day there is an indication of immense power, and knowledge is an indication of the singling out of the attributes of divinity, and of the occurrence of resurrection, as God the Exalted said: ﴿As He originated you, you will return﴾ [al-A'raf: 29].

The lam in ﴿to Him belongs the alternation of the night and the day﴾ [Yunus: 6] denotes possession (al-milk), meaning: by His power is the directing of night and day. The day corresponds to life, and for this reason the stirring of the day is called resurrection (ba'th); and the night corresponds to death, and for this reason God called sleep a taking (wafat) in His saying: ﴿It is He who takes you in the night, and knows what you have committed by day, then raises you up therein﴾ [al-An'am: 60].

The fronting of the prepositional phrase ("to Him") serves to restrict (qasr), meaning: the alternation of night and day belongs to Him and not to another; so other than He does not merit divinity.

Since these proofs convey to whoever reflects upon them knowledge that God is One and that resurrection is certain, and since those addressed had associated others with Him and had not been guided by these proofs, they were placed in the rank of those without intellect. Thus their lack of reason was rebuked by the rhetorical interrogation (al-istifham al-inkari), grounded (mufarra'), by the fa' on the four proofs, in His saying: "Will you not then reason?"

This is a concluding phrase (tadhyil) referring back to His saying: ﴿and to Him you will be gathered﴾ and what follows it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 23, verses 80–81:

﴿And He it is who gives life and causes death, and to Him belongs the alternation of the night and the day. Will you not then reason?﴾

This is from the same style as ﴿And He it is who produced for you hearing﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 78]. The mention of the Gathering (al-hashr) is followed by the mention of giving life, because resurrection (al-ba'th) is a form of giving life, by way of incorporation (idmaj), so that the proof for the possibility of resurrection is included within the proof for the comprehensive control (al-tasarruf) over the world.

As for the mention of causing death, it is for the sake of the relation of opposition (al-tadadd), and because it indicates the immensity of power and dominion (al-qahr). Since giving life includes the creation of wakefulness, and causing death includes the creation of sleep, as God the Exalted said: ﴿God takes the souls at the time of their death﴾ [al-Zumar: 42], and so on, the alternation of night and day is joined to this, that it is by His power, for that same relation; and because in the directing (tasrif) of night and day there is an indication of immense power, and knowledge is an indication of the singling out of the attributes of divinity, and of the occurrence of resurrection, as God the Exalted said: ﴿As He originated you, you will return﴾ [al-A'raf: 29].

The lam in ﴿to Him belongs the alternation of the night and the day﴾ [Yunus: 6] denotes possession (al-milk), meaning: by His power is the directing of night and day. The day corresponds to life, and for this reason the stirring of the day is called resurrection (ba'th); and the night corresponds to death, and for this reason God called sleep a taking (wafat) in His saying: ﴿It is He who takes you in the night, and knows what you have committed by day, then raises you up therein﴾ [al-An'am: 60].

The fronting of the prepositional phrase ("to Him") serves to restrict (qasr), meaning: the alternation of night and day belongs to Him and not to another; so other than He does not merit divinity.

Since these proofs convey to whoever reflects upon them knowledge that God is One and that resurrection is certain, and since those addressed had associated others with Him and had not been guided by these proofs, they were placed in the rank of those without intellect. Thus their lack of reason was rebuked by the rhetorical interrogation (al-istifham al-inkari), grounded (mufarra'), by the fa' on the four proofs, in His saying: "Will you not then reason?"

This is a concluding phrase (tadhyil) referring back to His saying: ﴿and to Him you will be gathered﴾ and what follows it.

**[p. 107]**

This is an *idmaj* (the incorporation of one topic into another, here introducing another root of polytheism, which is the denial of resurrection after death). The particle (بَلْ) (*bal*, "rather") is used for *al-idrab al-ibtali* (a rejecting turn, in which what precedes is dismissed), dismissing their claim that they reason, and affirming their denial of resurrection together with an explanation of what led them to deny it, namely *taqlid* (blind imitation). The meaning is that they do not reason about the proofs, but follow the sayings of their fathers.

The discourse shifts from the second person to the third person, an *iltifat* (a shift in grammatical person). The reason is that the speech has moved from rebuke and threat to describing their error, and this change suits the third person, since the third person carries a sense of distance. The pronoun refers to the addressees.

**[p. 108]**

The word "saying" (القَوْلُ) here means what agrees with belief, because the basic principle in speech is that it corresponds to the belief of its speaker. So the meaning is: "Rather, they assumed what the former ones assumed."

"The former ones" (الأوَّلُونَ) are their ancestors by lineage, or their ancestors in religion from the polytheist nations.

The clause ﴿They said: "When we have died and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be raised?"﴾ and so on is a *badal mutabiq* (a corresponding substitution, an apposition that matches the original in meaning) for the clause ﴿They said what the former ones said﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 81]. It details the general similarity. The pronoun attached to the second (قالُوا) refers to what the pronoun of the first (قالُوا) referred to, and does not refer to (الأوَّلُونَ). It is permissible to treat the second (قالُوا) as a *istinaf bayani* (an explanatory resumption), explaining (ما قالَ الأوَّلُونَ) ("what the former ones said"), in which case the pronoun refers to (الأوَّلُونَ). The meaning is the same under both readings. Under both views, the repetition of the verb (قالُوا) is of the kind where the verb governing the substituted element is repeated in the element substituted. Its purpose here is to express wonder at this saying.

The majority of readers recite ﴿أإذا مِتْنا﴾ with two hamzas, as an interrogative about the conditional. Ibn 'Amir recites it with one hamza, in the form of a statement, with the interrogative implied in the clause (إنّا لَمَبْعُوثُونَ).

The majority recite ﴿أإنّا لَمَبْعُوثُونَ﴾ [al-Isra': 49] with two hamzas, to emphasize the first interrogative hamza by introducing a similar one before the answer of the conditional. Nafi' and Abu Ja'far recite it without an interrogative hamza. The presence of the interrogative hamza before the conditional is sufficient to convey the interrogative about its answer.

The interrogative is one of denial, and (إذا) (*idha*, "when") is an adverb of time modifying the word (لَمَبْعُوثُونَ) ("shall be raised").

Combining the mention of death with becoming dust and bones serves to strengthen the denial, by making the Qur'an's report of the occurrence of resurrection appear monstrous. That is, revival after that complete dissolution.

Relating the emphasis of the one making the claim increases the monstrousness of the claim in their minds.

The clause ﴿Indeed we and our fathers were promised this before﴾ and so on is a justification for the denial and a reinforcement of it. They made the basis of their rejection of resurrection that it had been promised repeatedly over many periods, yet it did not happen, and none of their fathers was raised.

**[p. 109]**

The reason for mentioning the fathers is to counter what someone might say to them: "You will be raised before you become dust and bones." So they prepared the answer that the promise of resurrection was not limited to them, such that they would fall into doubt by the possibility of its occurring to them after their death and before their bodies perished. Rather, this is an ancient promise that was made to their earliest fathers, and long periods have passed, their remains have been seen in their graves, and none of them has been raised.

The clause ﴿This is nothing but the fables of the former ones﴾ belongs to the first saying. It is a *istinaf bayani* answering a question raised by their saying ﴿Indeed we and our fathers were promised this before﴾. The question would be: How did a number of callers, in different ages, agree on this claim while knowing it would not occur? Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 23, verses 84–85:

﴿Say, "To whom belongs the earth and whoever is in it, if you know?"﴾ ﴿They will say, "To Allah." Say, "Then will you not remember?"﴾

Page 109

This is a resumption of argument against them concerning the affirmation of Allah's oneness (tawhid). The discourse returns, connected to His saying: ﴿It is He who gives life and causes death, and His is the alternation of the night and the day. Then will you not reason?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 80].

The interrogative here is taqriri (confirmatory), meaning: answer this, and they can only answer that it belongs to Allah. The purpose is to establish the necessary consequence of their answer, which is that He, exalted is He, is singular in oneness.

The clause ﴿if you know﴾ is a conditional whose answer has been omitted because the interrogation indicates it; its estimated meaning is: then answer me concerning the question. In this condition there is a directing of their minds to reflect, so that it becomes clear to them that the earth belongs to Allah and that whoever is in it belongs to Allah. The fact that all of that belongs to Allah may be hidden, because people are accustomed to attributing effects to their proximate causes and actions to those who directly perform them. So they were alerted, by His saying ﴿if you know﴾, to reflection, that is: if you know with certainty. For this reason it is followed by His saying ﴿They will say, "To Allah,"﴾ that is: they answer immediately upon reflection, with a prompt answer. See what preceded in the explanation of His exalted saying ﴿Say, "To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth?" Say, "To Allah."﴾ [al-An'am: 12] in Surat al-An'am.

The sentence ﴿Say, "Then will you not remember?"﴾ comes as a response to their acknowledgment and admission that it belongs to Allah. The interrogative is denunciatory (inkari), a denunciation of their failure to take heed of this, that is: their minds should perceive the indication of that to His singularity in divinity. He was specified with remembrance because in some of it the indication is hidden and requires reflection.

[p. 110]

Commanding them to "say" is repeated, even though what is said differs, and the sentence ﴿Who is the Lord of the heavens?﴾ is not joined by a conjunction, because it falls within a series of enumerations. So it was fitting that the command to speak be repeated without dispensing with a conjunctive particle. The purpose is that these questions follow one another in succession, as a rebuttal by proof. For this reason, the sentence ﴿If you know﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 88] was not repeated in the second and third questions, being content with its opening at the first.

Al-Jumhur (the majority of readers) recited ﴿They will say, "To Allah"﴾ with the preposition lam attached to the Name of Majesty (Allah), as a report of their expected answer in meaning, not in wording. This is because, when they were asked with "man" (who), which is used to ask for the identification of the essence of the one asked about, the customary usage required that the answer name the essence of the one asked about. Instead, the answer turned away from that to what concerns the seven heavens and the Throne being owned by Allah. This is a turn toward the meaning rather than the wording, in consideration of the fact that the one asked about was regarded through the attribute of lordship (rububiyyah), and lordship entails dominion (mulk). A parallel to this usage is the verse recited by al-Qurtubi and the author of al-Mat'la' (Sahib al-Mat'la'):

"When it is said: Who is the Lord of the towns and the villages, and the Lord of the noble steeds? I say: Khalid."

I have not found anyone who preceded these two in mentioning this verse, and perhaps they took it from the tafsir (exegesis) of al-Zajjaj, who did not attribute it to a speaker. Perhaps its speaker followed the pattern of the usage of the verse.

I say: The more fitting course is to explain the reason for shaping the verse in this style. I see that this is for the purpose of an allusion (ta'rid) that they avoid saying, "The Lord of the seven heavens is Allah," because they had affirmed partners with Allah in the heavens, when they worshipped the angels. Thus they deviated from what would negate lordship from their objects of worship, and confined themselves to acknowledging that the heavens are Allah's possession, because that does not nullify the illusions of their polytheism from their root. Do you not see that they say in the talbiyah (the pilgrim's call) during Hajj: "At Your service, You have no partner, except a partner who is Yours, You own him and what he owns" (labbayka la sharika laka, illa sharikan huwa laka, tamlikuhu wa ma malak). So in reporting their answer in this wording there is a censure (tawarruk) against them. For this reason, the report of their answer was followed by a rebuke for them, denying them the fear of Allah, the Exalted.

[p. 111]

Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub recited ﴿They will say, "Allah"﴾ without the preposition lam, and it is thus in the Mushaf of Basra. In that case, the Name of Majesty is in the nominative, as the predicate (khabar) of "man" in the words ﴿Who is the Lord of the heavens?﴾. The meaning is the same. With this interrogation, the conditional clause ﴿If you know﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 84] and the like was not used, as it was in the previous one, because the solitary lordship of Allah, the Exalted, over the heavens and the Throne is not doubted by the polytheists, since they did not claim divinity for their idols in the heavens and the higher worlds.

Their admonition was singled out, following their answer, with urging toward the fear of Allah (taqwa), because it had become clear from the preceding verse that they could do nothing but acknowledge that Allah owns the earth and whoever is in it. That verse was followed by urging them to remember, so that it would become clear to them that they are the servants of Allah, not the servants of idols. It also became clear from this verse that He is the Lord of the heavens, which are greater than the earth, and that they could do nothing but acknowledge this. This fits urging them to fear Him, because He alone deserves obedience, and that they obey His Messenger, for the fear of Allah includes obedience to what the Messenger (ﷺ) brought.

The object of ﴿you fear﴾ (tattaqun) is omitted, by treating the verb as if it were intransitive, because it signifies a specific meaning, namely the fear of Allah that encompasses carrying out what is commanded and avoiding what is forbidden.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 23, verses 88–89:**

﴿Say: "In whose hand is the dominion (malakut) of everything, who gives protection while none can be protected against Him, if you know?"﴾ ﴿They will say, "To Allah." Say, "Then how are you deluded?"﴾

You have already come to know the point behind the repetition of the statement (al-qawl).

Al-malakut is an intensive form of al-mulk (dominion), with the letter mim vowelled with a damma. Al-malakut is dominion accompanied by control over the various kinds and realms, and for this reason it is followed by (kulli shay'in), "everything."

Al-yad (the hand) means power (al-qudra). The meaning of (yujir) is that He gives relief and protects whomever He wills from harm. Its verbal noun is al-ijara (protection), which conveys the sense of dominance. When it is followed by the preposition of elevation (ʿala), it indicates that the one over whom it is used is overpowered in the sense that the one protected cannot be harmed. Thus the meaning of (﴿la yujaru ʿalayhi﴾), "none can be protected against Him," is that no one can prevent anyone from His punishment, and this conveys complete might.

The verb in (﴿yujaru ʿalayhi﴾) is in the passive voice, intending the negation of the action from every agent, so it conveys generality together with brevity.

Since this control of Allah is hidden and requires the intellect to reflect in order to perceive it, the question is followed by His words, ﴿if you know﴾ (Al-Mu'minun: 84), just as the first question was followed by a similar phrase, urging them to know Him and to be guided to Him.

Then it is followed by what indicates that if they reflect, they will know, so it is said: ﴿They will say, "To Allah"﴾ (Al-Mu'minun: 85).

Al-Jumhur (the majority of reciters) read ﴿They will say, "To Allah"﴾ (Al-Mu'minun: 85) with the preposition lam attached to the divine name, like its predecessor. Abu ʿAmr and Yaʿqub read it without the lam, and you have already learned this in its earlier parallel.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 23, verse 90:

﴿Nay, We have brought them the truth, and indeed they are liars.﴾

This is an idrab (a transition, "nay") to negate the supposition that they are bewitched; that is, "Rather, the matter is not as it appeared to them. What We have brought them is the truth, meaning the Qur'an." The ba' (in bi-l-haqq) is for transitivity, as one says "dhahaba bihi," meaning "he took it away" (adhhabahu). This is like His saying earlier: ﴿Nay, We have brought them their reminder﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 71].

The shift from address (khitab), from His saying ﴿Then how are you deluded?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 89], to the third person (ghaybah) is an iltifat (shift of grammatical person), because they are the ones to whom the speech is addressed in this sentence. Here al-haqq (the truth) means sincerity and truthfulness; therefore it is contrasted with ascribing to them falsehood regarding what they hurled at the Qur'an, in their saying: ﴿This is nothing but the fables of the ancients﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 83].

The contrast between al-haqq and (kadhibun, liars) is a muhassin al-tibaq (an embellishment of antithesis).

صفحة ١١٣
The emphasis of ascribing to them falsehood with (inna, indeed) and the lam serves to affirm the report.

In arranging these proofs, the method of progression (al-taraqqi) has been followed: it begins with asking about the Owner of the earth and whoever is in it, because these are the realms closest to the comprehension of the addressees. Then it ascends to reasoning from the lordship of the heavens and the Throne, and then ascends further to what is more general and comprehensive, namely His absolute disposal over all things. For this reason the particle of generality, (kull, all), is brought in it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 23, verses 91–92:

﴿Allah has not taken any son, and there is not with Him any god; otherwise, each god would have taken away what he created, and some of them would have overcome others. Exalted is Allah above what they describe.﴾ ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, and high is He above what they associate with Him.﴾

The argument for the affirmation of God's oneness was followed by the argument for the negation of partners to Him in divinity. The conclusion was placed before the syllogism so that it would itself become the thing sought (al-matlub), for the conclusion (al-natijah) and the thing sought (al-matlub) are one in meaning but differ in consideration. By consideration of its occurring right after the syllogism, it is called a conclusion (natijah); by consideration of it being a claim (da'wa) for which the proof, namely the syllogism, is established, it is called the thing sought (matlub), as in the science of logic (mantiq). There is a point in placing it first: this sought-after matter is clearly evident and needs no proof except to increase tranquility. So His words, ﴿Allah has not taken any son, and there is not with Him any god﴾, are the thing sought, and His words, ﴿otherwise, each god would have taken away what he created﴾ to the end of the verse, are the proof. Placing this sought-after matter before the proof made it unnecessary to state the conclusion explicitly right after the proof. The negation of a son was mentioned for thorough refutation of the various beliefs of the idolaters among the Arabs, for some of them imagined that they had risen above worshipping idols, so they worshipped the angels and said: they are the daughters of Allah.

The negation of a son was placed before the negation of a partner, although most idolaters were worshippers of idols rather than worshippers of angels, because the doubt of those who worship angels is stronger than the doubt of those who worship idols; for the angels are not observed, so the signs of createdness are not manifest on them as they are on idols, and because those who claimed them to be daughters of Allah are closer to deception than those who claimed stones to be partners of Allah. We have already pointed to this a little earlier at His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: Who is the Lord of the seven heavens?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 86], the verse.

And ( إذن ) (idhan) is a particle of response and consequence for a preceding statement, either spoken or implied. The statement being answered here is what is contained in His words, ﴿and there is not with Him any god﴾; so the answer is the opposite of that negation. Since this opposite is an impossible occurrence, it was necessary to posit a condition for it by way of supposition and assumption, and the particle prepared for such a condition is (law) of impossibility, so the estimate is: "And if there were with Him a god, each god would have taken away what he created."

The retention of the lam at the beginning of the statement that follows (idhan) is evidence that the implied element is the condition of (law), because the lam must accompany the response of (law), and because most occurrences of (idhan) are a response to (law). Therefore it was permissible to omit the condition here, since its estimate is evident.

This explanation was already given at His words, ﴿Indeed, you would then be like them﴾ [al-Nisa': 140] in Surat al-Nisa'.

So His words, ﴿otherwise, each god would have taken away what he created﴾, are an argument for the impossibility of there being gods with Allah.

The reason the argument was not made for the impossibility of Allah taking a son is that the argument for what follows makes it unnecessary; for what follows is more general than it, and the negation of the more general entails the negation of the more specific. For if Allah had a son, the sons would be gods, because the offspring of every existent comes into being only in the likeness of the essence of its origin, as indicated by His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: If the Most Merciful had a son, I would be the first of the worshippers﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 81], meaning: for Him.

The word "taking away" in His words, ﴿each god would have taken away﴾, is a metaphor for independence in what is taken away and the absence of another's sharing in it. The explanation of how this argument is coherent: if there were gods with Allah, this would necessitate that the gods be equal in the attributes of divinity, and those attributes are perfections in their entirety. Thus each god would be a creator of created things, since the existence of contingent beings is established and they are created. It is impossible for the gods to converge on one created thing, for that would be either through incapacity to be independent in creating some of the created things, and this does not contradict divinity, or it would be obtaining what is already obtained, which is impossible. So it is necessary that each god be independent with a portion of created things. Let us suppose that the created things of each god are equal to the created things of another, on the basis that wisdom requires a definite quantity of created things known to the God who created them; then it is necessary that the god who did not create a portion of created things have no lordship over what he did not create, and this leads to deficiency in each of the gods, and this entails the impossible, for divinity requires perfection, not deficiency. Undoubtedly, those created things, after their creation, will be exposed to increase and decrease, strength and weakness, according to the accidents of existence that surround them, which created things do not escape, as is observed in the created things of the one God, Exalted is He. There is no escape from this, for the Creator of created things placed in them properties inseparable from them, as His wisdom required; so those created things are necessarily manifestations of their properties. Therefore this necessarily entails that the created things of some gods surpass the created things of others through accidents of activities and concomitants inseparable from that. Undoubtedly all of this entails two false consequences. The first is that each god would be specialized with his created things, so no other god could act upon them, nor could he act upon the created things of others; this requires that each god be incapable of acting upon the created things of others. This entails the impossible, for incapacity is a deficiency, and deficiency contradicts the true nature of divinity. This is a demonstrative proof of oneness, for it leads to the impossibility of its opposite. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿each god would have taken away what he created﴾.

The second of the two consequences is that the created things of some gods become more abundant or stronger than the created things of another god, through accidents that require this, such as the effects of psychological acts and the effects of regions and events, as is observed in the differing conditions of the created things of the one God, Exalted is He. Undoubtedly this leads to the dominance of the god whose created things surpass those of the god whose created things decline, and this requires that some of those gods become stronger than others, which contradicts equality in divinity. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿and some of them would have overcome others﴾.

This second consequence is based on what is customary among thinkers as necessary implications of divinity; otherwise it would be permissible for the gods to agree not to create created things capable of variation, by creating only stones or iron, for example; but this contradicts the reality of created things.

It is also permissible for the gods to agree that none of them should dominate another, because the dominion of each is not greater than the dominion of the other, on the basis that they share the same wisdom, which preserves them from doing what would lead to disruption of divine glory; yet this meaning is not free from mere accommodation, and that indicates weakness of power. Thus the argument in this verse is demonstrative, and it is like the argument in His words: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would have been corrupted﴾ [al-Anbiya': 22]. However, that argument is based on the necessity of deficiency in the essence of the gods, which those who deny it do not allow, while the other is based on the necessity of disruption of the conditions of celestial and terrestrial created things, which observation refutes.

As for the purely demonstrative proof of the impossibility of multiplicity of gods in essence, it has other premises, which the scholars of kalam have fully set out in a manner that leaves no currency for the belief in association. The scholar 'Umar al-Qazwini has pointed to one way of it in this place of his gloss on the Kashshaf, but he stood alone in a claim derived from the verse, and it is not as he claimed. al-Shihab al-Alusi has cited it, so if you wish, reflect upon it.

Since this proof required the invalidity of their claim, the proof was followed by the glorification of Allah above the statements of the idolaters with His words: ﴿Exalted is Allah above what they describe﴾, and this stands in the position of the conclusion of the proof. What they describe Him with is what they specifically attributed to Him of partners in divinity, and of the impossibility of resurrection for Him, and the like; and this is what the purpose of the speech concerns.

Having followed the argument for the negation of a partner with His words, ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾, the intended meaning is the generality of knowledge and its encompassing of everything, as the definite article in (﴿the unseen and the witnessed﴾) indicates through true comprehensiveness: that is, He knows every hidden thing and every manifest thing. This is to remove the suspicion that one might say: each god's independence in what he created may not lead to some gods rising above others, since it is possible that none of the gods knows the extent of the difference between his dominion and the dominion of another, so no god rises above another because each is occupied with his own dominion. The answer to this is that if a god may be non-creator of a portion of created things that others created, lest powers overlap over one set of objects, he cannot be ignorant of what others created, because attributes of knowledge do not overlap; so when one of the gods knows the extent of his partners' dominion, the one who knows the greater extent of his own dominion rises above whoever is lesser in dominion. Thus it is clear that His words, ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾, complete the argument for the negation of partners, and for this reason His words, ﴿so high is He above what they associate with Him﴾, are introduced after it with (fa).

Nafi', Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr from 'Asim, Abu Ja'far and Khalaf read (Knower of the unseen) with the nominative ('alimu), as the predicate of an omitted subject, which is a common ellipsis in usage when one wishes to predicate something of a thing after predicates or attributes have been applied to it.

Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr, Hafs from 'Asim and Ya'qub read it with the genitive ('alimi), as an attribute of the divine name in His words, ﴿Exalted is Allah above what they describe﴾.

(ma) is verbal-masdar. The meaning: "so high is He above their associating," that is, He is too great to be described as sharing in His mighty attribute; that is, He is exalted above that.
