The preceding verses have made clear the utmost extent of the polytheists' misguidance, the absence of any excuse for them regarding their religion toward God, and God's anger against them for that. They are equal in this with the nations for whom God hastened punishment in this world and stored up another punishment for the Hereafter. This was a warning to them of the like of it and a threat of what they would be told. It was also a cause of concern for the Prophet ﷺ, that punishment might descend upon his people during his lifetime, and of fear of its terror. So God taught His Prophet to ask for deliverance from that punishment. In this instruction there is an allusion that God will save them from the punishment by His wisdom, and an indication that God will show His Prophet the descent of punishment upon those who deny him, as is the case with instruction in supplication, as in His words: ﴿Our Lord, do not impose blame upon us if we forget or make a mistake﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286], and so on.

This sentence is thus an explanatory resumptive clause (isti'naf bayani, a new clause answering what is stirring in the soul), answering what was stirring in the heart of the Messenger of God, upon him be prayers and peace. This was indeed fulfilled in what befell the polytheists on the day of Badr and the day of Hunayn. Accordingly, the threat mentioned here is a threat of punishment in this world, as His words require: ﴿so do not place me among the wrongdoing people﴾.

The word "Rabb" (Lord) is mentioned repeatedly in this supplication as a preface to the answer, because the attribute of lordship (rububiyyah) requires compassion toward the one who is nurtured. The added "ma" (what), which is redundant and used for emphasis, was introduced after the conditional particle "in" (if), so the conditional verb is joined with the energetic nun (nun al-tawkid) to increase the certainty of linking the consequent to the condition. A parallel to the repetition of emphatic particles between the condition and its response is the verse of al-A'sha:

"If you see us barefoot, having no sandals for ourselves — indeed, thus are we: we go barefoot at times and wear sandals at others."

That is: know for certain that we sometimes go barefoot and at other times wear sandals, for that reason, i.e., for the sake of concealing the steps, not because of finding a sandal at one time and lacking it at another, as is the condition of the destitute.

This construction has already occurred in His words: ﴿And if an incitement from Satan incites you﴾ [al-A'raf: 200], at the end of al-A'raf. The meaning is: since what they are promised is present in my lifetime, I call upon you not to place me among them at that time.

The use of the locative particle "fi" (among) in His words: ﴿among the wrongdoing people﴾ indicates that he was commanded to ask for a state of being in a place other than the place of the polytheists. This was fulfilled by the migration to Madinah, so the locative sense here is literal, i.e., "among them."

The statement in His words: ﴿And indeed, We are able to show you what We promise them﴾ is used to produce hope that the threat against the deniers will be realized during the lifetime of the Messenger ﷺ; otherwise there would be no need to inform the Messenger of God's power over that.

In His words: ﴿to show you﴾ there is an allusion that he is safe from what they are promised reaching him, and that he will see it with his own eyes without being present in it. It may appear that this is a strange promise, because it is customary for punishment to be from heaven; when God saves some of His messengers from it, such as Lot, He removes them from the place of punishment. But the punishment of these people was not from heaven, so it was realized in the slaying of their chieftains on the day of Badr, in the sight of the Messenger of God ﷺ. The Messenger of God stood over the well of Badr, called them by their names one by one, and said to them: "We have found what our Lord promised us to be true, so have you found what your Lord promised to be true?" By this purpose the position of the two emphatic particles, "inna" (indeed) and the lam, becomes evident as hitting the target of the miraculous nature (i'jaz) of the Qur'an.

They are equal in this with the nations for whom God hastened punishment in this world and stored up another punishment for the Hereafter. This was a warning to them of the like of it and a threat of what they would be told. It was also a cause of concern for the Prophet ﷺ, that punishment might descend upon his people during his lifetime, and of fear of its terror. So God taught His Prophet to ask for deliverance from that punishment. In this instruction there is an allusion that God will save them from the punishment by His wisdom, and an indication that God will show His Prophet the descent of punishment upon those who deny him, as is the case with instruction in supplication, as in His words: ﴿Our Lord, do not impose blame upon us if we forget or make a mistake﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286], and so on.

This sentence is thus an explanatory resumptive clause (isti'naf bayani, a new clause answering what is stirring in the soul), answering what was stirring in the heart of the Messenger of God, upon him be prayers and peace. This was indeed fulfilled in what befell the polytheists on the day of Badr and the day of Hunayn. Accordingly, the threat mentioned here is a threat of punishment in this world, as His words require: ﴿so do not place me among the wrongdoing people﴾.

The word "Rabb" (Lord) is mentioned repeatedly in this supplication as a preface to the answer, because the attribute of lordship (rububiyyah) requires compassion toward the one who is nurtured. The added "ma" (what), which is redundant and used for emphasis, was introduced after the conditional particle "in" (if), so the conditional verb is joined with the energetic nun (nun al-tawkid) to increase the certainty of linking the consequent to the condition. A parallel to the repetition of emphatic particles between the condition and its response is the verse of al-A'sha:

"If you see us barefoot, having no sandals for ourselves — indeed, thus are we: we go barefoot at times and wear sandals at others."

That is: know for certain that we sometimes go barefoot and at other times wear sandals, for that reason, i.e., for the sake of concealing the steps, not because of finding a sandal at one time and lacking it at another, as is the condition of the destitute.

It may appear that this is a strange promise, because it is customary for punishment to be from heaven; when God saves some of His messengers from it, such as Lot, He removes them from the place of punishment. By this purpose the position of the two emphatic particles, "inna" (indeed) and the lam, becomes evident as hitting the target of the miraculous nature (i'jaz) of the Qur'an.

﴿Repel evil with that which is better; We are best aware of what they describe.﴾

When God informed His Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, by hinting to him that He would carry out the threat against those among his deniers who had rejected him, and the Messenger and the Muslims knew that God had guaranteed them victory, He followed this by commanding him to repel his deniers with that which is better, and not to let their denial constrict his breast. Therefore he repelled evil with good, as is the manner of Islamic adab (good conduct). Its explanation will come in Surah Fussilat, at His saying: ﴿Repel with that which is better﴾ [41:34].

As for His saying: ﴿We are best aware of what they describe﴾, it is a statement used as kinaya (metonymy), meaning that God deals with those who harmed His Messenger with the punishment they deserve, because the One who knows the circumstances best acts in accordance with what fits those circumstances, with justice. In this there is reassurance for the soul of the Messenger ﷺ.

[Page 120]

The object of (yasifun, "they describe") has been omitted, and its implied form is: "what they describe you with," i.e., what constricts your breast. This is a pledge that He will repay them for what He knows of them. For many a person who shows evil may conceal in his heart some good, as there were among them those who felt compassion toward the Prophet in their hearts. And many a person is the opposite, as God said: ﴿And among people is one whose speech about the worldly life impresses you, and he calls God to witness what is in his heart, yet he is the most stubborn of opponents﴾ [2:204].

The phrase (allati hiya ahsan, "that which is better") is intended to mean the complete good deed. The superlative form is used for emphasis, as in His saying: ﴿The prison is more beloved to me﴾ [12:33].

The cultivation of character (takhalluq) through this verse is that the perfect believer should entrust the matter of those who transgress against him to God. God then takes up the victory for one who relies upon Him. And if he meets evil with good, God's victory is more healing to his heart and more firmly established in its support. What is the power of a creature compared with the power of the Creator, who defeated the confederates without armies or troops?

Such was the character of the Prophet ﷺ. He never took revenge for himself, and he would supplicate to his Lord. It is mentioned in al-Madarik (Kitab al-Madarik, a biographical dictionary), in the biography of ʿAbd Allah ibn Ghanim, that a man called Ibn Zurʿa had standing and high position, and Ibn Ghanim had ruled against him in a matter of genuine right which had consequences for him. Ibn Zurʿa met Ibn Ghanim in a deserted place and insulted him, and Ibn Ghanim turned away from him. Afterwards, when Ibn Zurʿa met him on the road, he greeted Ibn Ghanim, who returned the greeting, welcomed him, went on with him to his home, and prepared food for him. When he wished to part from him, Ibn Zurʿa said to Ibn Ghanim: "O Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman, forgive me, and consider me absolved of what I said to you." Ibn Ghanim said to him: "As for this, I will not do it until I stand you before God, the Exalted. And as for whether any harm or punishment from me should reach you in this world, that will not happen."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 23, verses 97–98:

﴿And say: "My Lord, I seek refuge in You from the whisperings of the devils."﴾ ﴿And I seek refuge in You, my Lord, lest they be present with me.﴾

Page 121

The apparent reading is that the conjoined clause follows directly on what it is conjoined to, so that his saying ﴿And say: "My Lord, I seek refuge in You from the whisperings of the devils"﴾ is connected to His saying ﴿Repel evil with that which is better﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 96]. When God commanded His Messenger ﷺ to entrust their recompense to his Lord, He commanded him to seek refuge from the devils hindering him from repelling with that which is better; that is, to seek refuge from the devil stirring up the impulse of anger and vengeance in the soul of the Prophet ﷺ. In this case, (al-shayatin, "the devils") is used in its literal sense. The meaning of the "whisperings of the devils" is their activity in stirring the faculties found in the human soul (that is, in matters other than those of conveying the message), such as stirring the faculty of anger, as al-Ghazali interpreted the saying of the Prophet ﷺ in the hadith: "But God helped me against him, so he submitted." God's command to His Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, to seek refuge from the whisperings of the devils entails God's guarantee of a response, as in His saying: ﴿Our Lord, do not burden us as You burdened those before us﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286]. Or his command to seek refuge from the whisperings of the devils may be intended to mean: persistence in safety from them. In al-Shifa, it is said: "The community is in agreement (that is, mujamma'ah) on the Prophet's ﷺ being protected from the devil, not in his body with kinds of harm, nor in his thoughts with whisperings."

It is also possible that the sentence ﴿And say: "My Lord, I seek refuge in You from the whisperings of the devils"﴾ is a conjunction to the sentence ﴿Say: "My Lord, if You show me that which they are promised"﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 93], in that God commanded him to turn to Him, seeking protection from the polytheists and their harm. In this case, the devils meant are the polytheists, for they are devils of mankind, as He said: (﴿And thus We have made for every prophet an enemy: devils of mankind and jinn﴾ [al-An'am: 112]). This would be in the sense of His saying: ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind﴾ [al-Nas: 1] up to His saying: ﴿who whispers in the breasts of mankind﴾ [al-Nas: 5] ﴿of the jinn and of mankind﴾ [al-Nas: 6]. The meaning would then be: I seek refuge in You from the whisperings of the oppressive people, or from the whisperings of the devils among them.

The literal meaning of al-hamz (the whisper/prodding) is pressing with the hand and jabbing with the finger or the like, and it is used figuratively to mean harming by speech or by gesture. Among its uses is His saying: ﴿a slanderer, going about with malicious gossip﴾ [al-Qalam: 11], and His saying: ﴿Woe to every scorner and mocker﴾ [al-Humazah: 1].

Page 122

In my view, its interpretation here is the figurative meaning, under both views regarding what is meant by the devils. The prodding of the devils of the jinn is evident; as for the prodding of the devils of mankind, it was the harm the polytheists inflicted on the Prophet ﷺ by mocking him, winking at him, and plotting against him.

The meaning of seeking refuge from their prodding is seeking refuge from the effects of that, for among it is that they incite some of their foolish ones against him, as occurred in the story of their inciting a man who brought the entrails of a camel and threw them upon the Prophet ﷺ while he was praying around the Ka'bah. This interpretation of the devils is the most fitting to the final phrase, ﴿until, when death comes to one of them﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 99], as will come.

As for His saying ﴿And I seek refuge in You, my Lord, lest they be present with me﴾, it is a seeking of refuge from their nearness, for when they draw near to him, their harm reaches him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 23, verses 99–100:

﴿Until, when death comes to one of them, he says, "My Lord, send me back,﴾ ﴿that I may do righteousness in what I have left behind." No! It is only a word he is saying; and behind them is a barrier until the Day they are resurrected.﴾

(Ḥattā) is inceptive (ibtidā'iyyah), and you already know its meaning more than once; it was discussed earlier in Surat al-Anbiya'. It does not indicate that what precedes it is limited by it, so there is no need to attach (ḥattā) to (yaṣifūna). The correct view is that (ḥattā) is connected to His saying: ﴿And indeed, We are able to show you what We promise them.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 95]. This is a transition to describing what they will face of punishment in the Hereafter, after their punishment in this world has been mentioned. So His saying here, ﴿until, when death comes to one of them﴾, is a fresh description of their punishment in the Hereafter. It is this that we preferred, namely that the punishment mentioned earlier three times is a punishment in this world and not in the Hereafter. If you take the punishment mentioned earlier to be the punishment of the Hereafter, then that is a general statement, and His saying, ﴿until, when death comes to one of them﴾ through to its end, is a detailed elaboration of it.

Page 123

The pronouns of the third person refer back to what the preceding pronouns referred to, from His saying: (﴿They say, "When we have died and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be resurrected?"﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 82]) up to this point; they do not refer to the devils. The purpose is to weave in a threat with what they will witness of punishment prepared for them, so that they will regret their negligence during their lifetime.

The plural pronoun in (irji'ūnī) is a pronoun of honour for the one addressed. Addressing with the plural form for the purpose of honour is an Arabic usage, and it requires the masculine form; so when a woman is addressed with honour, one says: antum, and one does not say: antunna. Al-'Araji said:

"If you wish, I will forbid women other than you, and if you wish, I will not taste fresh water or cold drink."

He said: "siwākum" (other than you). Ja'far ibn 'Ulbah al-Harithi, one of the poets of al-Hamasah, said:

"So do not think that I have humbled myself after you ∗∗∗ for anything, nor that I am afraid of death."

He said: "ba'dakum" (after you). This I have arrived at by surveying their speech, and I have not seen anyone who has noted it.

The clause of hope (laʿallī...) is in the position of a cause for the content of (irji'ūnī).

The word (tark) here is used in its literal sense, which is the meaning of leaving and parting. The referent of (mā taraktu) is the world. It is also permissible that (tark) be understood in its figurative sense, which is turning away and rejecting, with the relative (mā) referring to belief in God and affirmation of His Messenger. This is what everyone who dies in disbelief has rejected. So the meaning is: "Perhaps I may submit and do righteousness in the state of my submission, which I had rejected." This meaning includes a promise of compliance and an acknowledgment of error regarding what has passed. With this concise construction, the demands of eloquence are fulfilled.

(Kallā) is a deterrent to the listener, so that he knows the futility of the disbeliever's request.

His saying: ﴿It is only a word he is saying﴾ is a construction that functions as a proverb, and it is one of the novel expressions of the Qur'an. The essential meaning is: the statement of the polytheist, "My Lord, send me back" and so on, is nothing more than words uttered by his tongue, with no benefit in them; that is, his request will not be answered by it.

Page 124

The clause (huwa qā'iluhā) is a description of (kalimah), meaning: it is a word, and this is its description. Since it is certain that he is the one who says it, there is no new benefit in describing (kalimah) with it; therefore the predicate must be understood as meaning that its word has no quality other than that it proceeded from the mouth of its speaker.
By this it is known that the emphasis with the particle (inna) serves to establish the meaning for which the description was used.

The word (kalimah) here is used for speech, as in the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The truest word a poet has said is the word of Labid: 'Surely everything other than God is vain.'" And as in their saying: "the word of testimony" and "the word of Islam." His Exalted saying was mentioned earlier in Surat al-Tawbah: ﴿And they did say the word of disbelief﴾ [al-Tawbah: 74].

The word (warā') here is used figuratively for that which will certainly befall a person and overtake him, while he does not suppose it will befall him. It is likened to one who wishes to catch up with a traveller, so he is already overtaking him. This is like His saying: ﴿And God encompasses them from behind﴾ [al-Buruj: 20], and His saying: ﴿Behind them is Hell﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 10], and His saying: ﴿And behind him is a severe punishment﴾ [Ibrahim: 17]. His saying was mentioned earlier: ﴿And there was behind them a king who seized every boat by force﴾ [al-Kahf: 79].

Labid said:

"Is it not behind me that my death has delayed, the holding of a staff on which the fingers bend?"

The barrier (barzakh) is the partition between two places. It was said: what is meant by it in this verse is the grave. It was also said: it is the duration of the life of this world. It was said: it is a realm between this world and the Hereafter in which the spirits settle and are unveiled concerning their future abode. The Sufis inclined to this view. Al-Sayyid said in al-Ta'rifat: "The barzakh is the perceptible realm between the realm of pure meanings and the realm of material bodies, that is, this world and the Hereafter, and it is expressed by it as the realm of the image (ʿālam al-mithāl)," end of quote; that is, according to the ancient philosophers.
The meaning of ﴿until the Day they are resurrected﴾ is that they will not return to life until the Day of Resurrection.

This is a discouragement for them, because they know that the Day of Resurrection that they were promised has no return after it

Page 125

to this world. So the one who said to them (﴿until the Day they are resurrected﴾) is the one who informed them of what resurrection is.

Since it is certain that he is the one who says it, there is no new benefit in describing (kalimah) with it; therefore the predicate must be understood as meaning that its word has no quality other than that it proceeded from the mouth of its speaker.
By this it is known that the emphasis with the particle (inna) serves to establish the meaning for which the description was used.

The word (kalimah) here is used for speech, as in the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The truest word a poet has said is the word of Labid: 'Surely everything other than God is vain.'" And as in their saying: "the word of testimony" and "the word of Islam." His Exalted saying was mentioned earlier in Surat al-Tawbah: ﴿And they did say the word of disbelief﴾ [al-Tawbah: 74].

The word (warā') here is used figuratively for that which will certainly befall a person and overtake him, while he does not suppose it will befall him. It is likened to one who wishes to catch up with a traveller, so he is already overtaking him. This is like His saying: ﴿And God encompasses them from behind﴾ [al-Buruj: 20], and His saying: ﴿Behind them is Hell﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 10], and His saying: ﴿And behind him is a severe punishment﴾ [Ibrahim: 17]. His saying was mentioned earlier: ﴿And there was behind them a king who seized every boat by force﴾ [al-Kahf: 79].

Labid said:

"Is it not behind me that my death has delayed, the holding of a staff on which the fingers bend?"

The barrier (barzakh) is the partition between two places. It was said: what is meant by it in this verse is the grave. It was also said: it is the duration of the life of this world. It was said: it is a realm between this world and the Hereafter in which the spirits settle and are unveiled concerning their future abode. The Sufis inclined to this view. Al-Sayyid said in al-Ta'rifat: "The barzakh is the perceptible realm between the realm of pure meanings and the realm of material bodies, that is, this world and the Hereafter, and it is expressed by it as the realm of the image (ʿālam al-mithāl)," end of quote; that is, according to the ancient philosophers.
The meaning of ﴿until the Day they are resurrected﴾ is that they will not return to life until the Day of Resurrection.

This is a discouragement for them, because they know that the Day of Resurrection that they were promised has no return after it

Page 125

to this world. So the one who said to them (﴿until the Day they are resurrected﴾) is the one who informed them of what resurrection is.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 23, verses 101–104:

﴿So when the Trumpet is blown, there will be no kinship among them that Day, nor will they ask about one another.﴾ ﴿Then whoever's scales are heavy, they are the successful.﴾ ﴿But whoever's scales are light, those are the ones who have lost themselves, abiding in Hell.﴾ ﴿The Fire will scorch their faces, and they therein will be grimacing.﴾

This is a consequence (tafri') of His saying: ﴿until the Day they are resurrected﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 100], for the time of the blowing into the Trumpet is the Day of Resurrection. The implied sense is: "So when the Day they are resurrected comes," but it was turned away from that to ﴿So when the Trumpet is blown﴾ as a depiction of the state of the Day of Resurrection.

The ṣūr (Trumpet) is a horn into which the blower blows for gathering and mobilization. It is something by which one calls to war, and by which the Jews call to prayer, as came in the hadith on the beginning of the adhan in Sahih al-Bukhari. The mention of the Trumpet was already made at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And His is the dominion on the Day the Trumpet is blown﴾ [al-An'am: 73], in Surat al-An'am.

The verb (nufikha, "was blown") is attributed in the passive, because what is of concern is the occurrence of the blowing, not the identity of the one who blows. It is blown either by a command of creation from Allah, Exalted is He, or one of the angels blows into it, and it has been reported that he is the angel Israfil.

The intended consequence is the second consequence, in His saying: ﴿Then whoever's scales are heavy﴾ to the end of it, because it is the basis for explaining the rejection of the words of their speaker: ﴿My Lord, send me back﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 99] ﴿that I may do righteousness in what I have left behind﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 100], which is rejected in summary by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿No! It is but a word he is saying﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 100]. So there was placed before it what serves as a preface to it, namely His saying: ﴿there will be no kinship among them﴾ to the end of it, hastening to despair them of their lineages or their appeals being of any benefit to them.

The more evident view is that the response (jawab) of (idhā) is His later saying: ﴿He will say: "How many years did you remain on the earth?"﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 112], as will come, and everything between them is a parenthetical insertion, some of which arises from some of the rest.

The pronoun in (baynahum, "among them") refers back to what the pronouns of the plural absent third person before it referred to, and those refer to the polytheists.

The meaning of the negation of kinship is the negation of its effects of support, help, and intercession, because those, in their customs, are among the necessities of kinship. Thus His saying: ﴿there will be no kinship among them﴾ is a metonymy for the absence of a helper.

The tasa'ul (asking) is one party asking another. What is meant by it is the asking appropriate to the arrival of the Day of Terror, namely that some of them ask others for aid and help, as in His saying: ﴿and no intimate friend will ask after an intimate friend﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 10].

As for the affirmation of asking on that Day in His saying: ﴿And they will turn to one another, questioning each other﴾ [al-Saffat: 27] ﴿They will say: "Indeed, you used to come to us from the right side."﴾ [al-Saffat: 28] ﴿They will say: "Rather, you were not believers."﴾ [al-Saffat: 29] ﴿And we had no authority over you; rather, you were a transgressing people.﴾ [al-Saffat: 30] ﴿So the word of our Lord has come into effect against us; indeed, we are going to taste [punishment].﴾ [al-Saffat: 31] ﴿So we misled you; indeed, we were misguided.﴾ [al-Saffat: 32] ﴿And indeed, they, that Day, will be sharing in the punishment.﴾ [al-Saffat: 33]

Therefore, their despair of finding a helper or intercessor came after that. In al-Bukhari, a man, who is Nafi' ibn al-Azraq the Kharijite, said to Ibn 'Abbas: "I find in the Qur'an things that contradict me." He said: ﴿So there will be no kinship among them that Day, nor will they ask about one another﴾ and [it] says: ﴿And they will turn to one another, questioning each other﴾ [al-Saffat: 27]. It was already mentioned in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿those who have lost themselves﴾ [al-An'am: 12] in Surat al-An'am, and His saying: ﴿those are the ones who have lost themselves﴾ [al-A'raf: 9] at the beginning of al-A'raf. Here it is an analogy for the state of their disappointment in what they used to hope for from the intercession of their idols, and that they would have salvation in the Hereafter, or from their supposition that they would not return to resurrection. So they denied what Islam brought and reckoned that they had prepared good for themselves, but they found its opposite, and thus their souls were lost, as though they had perished from them. For this reason (anfusahum, "themselves") is put in the accusative as object of (khasiru, "they lost"). The two demonstratives serve to further distinguish the two groups by their attributes.

The clause (﴿the Fire will scorch their faces﴾) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to (﴿those who have lost themselves﴾). The meaning of (﴿the Fire will scorch their faces﴾) is that it burns. Laf'h (la fah) means the intense striking of fire.

Kalih is one who has kulūḥ, which is the contraction of the two lips and the showing of the teeth, from the effect of the facial nerves being tightened at the intensity of pain.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 23, verses 105–107:

﴿Were not My verses recited to you, and did you not deny them?﴾ ﴿They will say: "Our Lord, our wretchedness overcame us, and we were a misguided people.﴾ ﴿Our Lord, bring us out of it; then if we return, we will indeed be wrongdoers."﴾

The clause ﴿Were not My verses recited to you﴾ is the object of an elided verb of speech, meaning: it will be said to them that Day. This is a reference to some of what will take place on that Day. "The verses" (al-ayat) are the verses of the Qur'an, as indicated by the context of His words ﴿recited to you﴾ and His words ﴿and did you not deny them﴾, taking the word in its apparent sense.

Al-tilawa (recitation) means reading. It was discussed earlier at His words, exalted is He: ﴿And they followed what the devils recited over the kingdom of Solomon﴾ [al-Baqara: 102] in Surat al-Baqara, and at His words: ﴿And when His verses are recited to them, it increases them in faith﴾ [al-Anfal: 2] in Surat al-Anfal. The interrogation is a rebuke (inkar).

Al-ghalb (overcoming) in its literal sense is domination and subjugation. Here it is applied to being afflicted with wretchedness rather than to being afflicted with happiness. The object of (ghalabat) is elided, indicated by (shiqwatuna) [our wretchedness], since wretchedness is opposed by happiness; that is, "our wretchedness overcame happiness." The noun governed by (ʿala) after the root of ghalb is the thing being overcome, as in the hadith: the women said, "The men have overcome us (ghalaba ʿalayka al-rijal)." The state of their choosing the causes of wretchedness instead of the causes of happiness is depicted as a state of being submerged within their souls between happiness and misery. The attribution of (shiqwa) to their pronoun is because it is specific to them once it had become dominant over them.

The word (shiqwa), with a kasra on the shin and a sukun on the qaf, is the reading of the majority. It is the pattern of a state (hay'a) derived from misery (shaqa'). Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read (shaqawatuna), with a fatha on the shin and an alif after the qaf, which is a verbal noun of the pattern fa'ala, like (jaza la) and (sadhaja). The addition of the word (qawman) [a people] is to indicate that error is part of their nature and the foundation of their peoplehood, as was discussed earlier at His words: ﴿Indeed, in that are signs for a people who reason﴾ [al-Baqara: 164] in Surat al-Baqara, and at His words: ﴿But signs and warnings do not avail a people who do not believe﴾ [Yunus: 101] at the end of Surat Yunus.

They thought that if they were brought out of the Fire they would return to faith and righteous deeds, so they pledged to God that they would not return to disbelief and denial.

The object of (ʿudna) [we return] is elided, because it is evident from the context, since their being cast into the Fire was on account of association (shirk) and denial, as indicated by their words: ﴿and we were a misguided people.﴾

The wrongdoing in (fa-inna zalimun) is transgression of justice, and what is meant is a further wrongdoing after their first wrongdoing, which is the one at which the request for pardon is cut off.

**[p. 129]**

*(Be silent therein)* is a rebuke and an insult, meaning that they are abased (*khasi'un*), and its sense is that their request is not granted. The verb *khasa'a* belongs to the *mana'a* pattern and means "to be humiliated." They were forbidden to address God, and the purpose is to make them despair of being saved from what they are in.

The clause *﴿Indeed, there was a group of My servants﴾* up to its end is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*, a new sentence that begins a fresh statement), intended to enrage them by contrasting their state on the Day of Punishment with the state of those upon whom God bestowed His favour, and to make them regret how they treated the Muslims.

The statement in *﴿Indeed, there was a group of My servants﴾* up to *(sukhriyyan)* is used to indicate that the speaker knows the content of the report, as evidenced by the fact that the addressees know their own states. The emphasis of the report with *(inna)* (indeed) and the dummy pronoun (*damir al-sha'n*) serves to hasten their terror.

The clause *(Indeed, I have rewarded them)* is the predicate of the first *(inna)*, for added emphasis. A parallel to it occurred in His words: *﴿Indeed, those who believed and did righteous deeds, indeed We do not waste the reward of one who does good work﴾* [al-Kahf: 30] in Surat al-Kahf.

The word *al-sukhriyy* is read with a *ḍamma* on the *sin* by Nafi', al-Kisa'i, Abu Ja'far and Khalaf, and with a *kasra* on the *sin* by the rest of the readers. These are two forms, and their meaning is one according to the careful scholars of the lexicographers, with no difference between them, unlike Abu 'Ubayda, al-Kisa'i and al-Farra', who held that the *kasra* form is derived from *sakhira* meaning "to mock," and the *ḍamma* form is derived from *al-sukhra* (with a *ḍamma* on the *sin*), which means "employment without wages." When the purpose is to intensify the occurrence of the verbal noun, the relative *ya'* (*ya' al-nisba*) is added, as one says *al-khususiyya* from *al-khusus* (particularity).

The verb of taking (*al-ittikhadh*) is applied to the verbal noun for emphasis, just as a noun may be described by a verbal noun. The meaning is: "you took them as those who are mocked," so *(sukhriyyan)* is parsed as a second object of *(ittakhadhtumuhum)*. The word *(hatta)* here is inceptive (*ibtida'iyya*), and the sense of inceptive *hatta* is the sense of the causal *fa'* (*fa' al-sababiyya*), so it is a subsidiary metaphor (*isti'ara tab'iyya*). A strong causation has been likened to an end-point, so *(hatta)* is used for it. The meaning is: you were diverted from reflecting on what the Qur'an brought of remembrance, because they mocked them on account of their being Muslims. Thus they mocked the religion whose following was the cause of their being mocked; how then can one hope that these people will be reminded by that remembrance, when it is one of the things that provoke mockery of its adherents?

The discussion of the verb *(sakhira)* was already given at His words: *﴿So there befell those who mocked them what they used to mock﴾* [al-An'am: 10] in Surat al-An'am, and His words: *﴿So they mock them﴾* [al-Tawba: 79] in Surat Bara'a.

The attribution of causing forgetting (*al-insa'*) to the group is a rational metaphor (*majaz 'aqli*), because they were its cause. Or it is a metaphor by omission, with the estimate: "until the mocking of them made My remembrance forgotten by you." The indicator for the first is semantic, and for the second is verbal.

His words *﴿that they, they are the triumphant﴾* were read by the majority with a *fatḥa* on the hamza of *(anna)*, in the sense of the verbal-noun particle (*masdariyya*) and emphasis, meaning: "I rewarded them because they..." Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with a *kasra* on the hamza of *(inna)*, for emphasis only, in which case it is an explanatory resumptive sentence (*isti'naf bayani*) for the reward.

The pronoun of separation (*damir al-fasl*) indicates exclusivity, i.e., "they are the triumphant, not you."

His words *﴿for what they patiently endured﴾* are an inserted phrase (*idmaj*) to praise patience and to draw attention to the fact that their being mocked by them was a cause of their patience, which earned them the reward. In that there is an added increase in distress for the addressees, in that they were themselves the cause of harm to their own selves, and of benefit to those whom they used to count as their enemies.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with a *kasra* on the hamza of *(inna)*, for emphasis only, in which case it is an explanatory resumptive sentence (*isti'naf bayani*) for the reward.

The pronoun of separation (*damir al-fasl*) indicates exclusivity, i.e., "they are the triumphant, not you."

His words *﴿for what they patiently endured﴾* are an inserted phrase (*idmaj*) to praise patience and to draw attention to the fact that their being mocked by them was a cause of their patience, which earned them the reward. In that there is an added increase in distress for the addressees, in that they were themselves the cause of harm to their own selves, and of benefit to those whom they used to count as their enemies.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 23, verse 112–114:

﴿He said: "How many years did you remain on the earth?"﴾ ﴿They said: "We remained a day or part of a day; so ask those who count."﴾ ﴿He said: "You remained only a little, if you had but known."﴾

The majority of readers read (﴿قالَ كَمْ لَبِثْتُمْ﴾) in the past tense (qāla), so it is determined that this speech occurs at the blowing of the Trumpet and the bringing of the dead back to life from the earth. The most apparent view is that it is the answer to (idhā) in His saying earlier: ﴿Then when the Trumpet is blown﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 101]. The estimation is: God said to them, when the Trumpet is blown: ﴿How many years did you remain on the earth?﴾, and what lies between them consists of parenthetical digressions that arose through the continuation, the conjunction, the circumstantial clauses, and the incidental exchanges within that, as you have known from what preceded in the explanation of those verses. It is not appropriate that this speech take place after the disbelievers have entered the Fire; the exegetes who understood it that way burdened themselves with what does not fit the coherence of the meanings.

Ibn Kathir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (qul) in the imperative form. The address is to the angel charged with reviving the dead.

The clause (﴿فاسْألِ العادِّينَ﴾, "so ask those who count") is a consequence of the clause (﴿لَبِثْنا يَوْمًا أوْ بَعْضَ يَوْمٍ﴾, "We remained a day or part of a day"), because of what it contains of their hesitation in estimating the duration of their stay on the earth. I hold, in explaining this, that they spoke in the manner customary to them in their worldly life, of not precisely keeping account of years, since the knowledge of aligning lunar years with solar years was held by the Banu Kinanah, who had the intercalation (al-nasi') in their hands and were nicknamed "al-Nasa'ah." The Kinani poet said:

"We are the intercalators over Ma'add; we make the sacred months lawful, and we make them forbidden."

The exegetes took the meaning of "those who count" to be the angels, or people who remember the reckoning of the period of stay. But al-Qurtubi said: That is, ask the reckoners who know that, for we have forgotten it.

His saying: ﴿He said: "You remained only a little"﴾ was read by the majority as they read the preceding one, so it is a narration of the exchange; for this reason the verb ﴿قالَ إنْ لَبِثْتُمْ إلّا قَلِيلًا﴾ is not conjoined, and this is the manner of narrating exchanges, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said: "Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30] in Surat al-Baqarah. Ibn Kathir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it in the imperative form, like the one before it.

The question about the number of years of stay on the earth is used for alerting them, so that their error becomes clear to them, since they used to claim that when they were buried in the earth they would not come out of it.

(ʿAdada sinin) is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz) of the interrogative (kam), and the specification is only (sinin). The attachment of the word (ʿadada) to it is an emphasis of the content of (kam), because (kam) is an interrogative noun about number, so mentioning the word (ʿadada) with it is an emphasis of part of its meaning.

Their answer implies that they were on the earth and that they did not recall the length of their stay, with variation in it. The apparent meaning of their saying ﴿a day or part of a day﴾ is that they estimated their stay in the depths of the earth as about one of the days known to them in the world, as His saying, exalted is He, in Surat al-Rum indicates: ﴿And on the Day the Hour is established, the criminals will swear that they had not remained but an hour﴾ [al-Rum: 55].

The exegetes did not turn to clarifying the purpose of their question and their answer to it and its following by what establishes it in the apparent sense. What appears to me in this is that the exposure of their past false belief was brought in the form of a question about the duration of their stay on the earth, as a metaphor for the establishment of their coming out of the earth alive, which is what they used to deny, and as a metaphor for the error of their reasoning in refuting resurrection by the impossibility of life returning to bones and dust. This is a state which does not require the duration of a single century, so how much more so when life has been returned to them after they had remained for many centuries; this is more evident and clearer as to the vastness of divine power, and more effective in refuting their doubt, since its falsity has become clear in what exceeds what they estimated as the cause of the impossibility of life returning to them.

This is indicated by His saying at the end of the verse: ﴿Did you then think that We created you in vain and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 115]. God compelled them to make manifest their belief in the shortness of the period they had spent, in addition to disfiguring their error; for when they perceived themselves to be alive as in their first life, and their former thinking returned to them, the thinking with which they had died, and they used to imagine that when their bodies perished life would not return to them, the completeness of their bodies made them imagine that they had remained in the earth only a short time, in which the bodily frame does not change, so they built upon the root of their mistaken doubt another error.

As for their saying ﴿so ask those who count﴾, it is an acknowledgment that they had not kept track of the duration of their stay; so they referred the questioner to someone who keeps that count, from among those whom they presumed had not ceased to be alive, because they supposed that they had been raised while the world still endured, and they supposed the question was on its apparent footing; thus they disclaimed responsibility for failing to keep an accurate answer.

As for God's response to them with His saying ﴿You remained only a little﴾, it indicates an omitted statement by way of implication (dalalat al-iqtida'), because they had remained much more than a day or part of a day, by a great deal; so how is it made "a little"? Therefore it is determined that the implied sense is: "He said: rather you remained centuries," as in His saying concerning the one who passed by a village: ﴿So God caused him to die for a hundred years, then raised him. He said: "How long did you remain?" He said: "I remained a day or part of a day." He said: "Rather you remained a hundred years"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 259]. For this reason it is determined that the estimate is: "He said: rather you remained centuries, and you remained only a little in what is with God, ﴿and indeed a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count﴾" [al-Hajj: 47].

The indication of this is what (law, "if") conveys of impossibility in His saying: ﴿If you had but known﴾, meaning: if you had known, you would have known that you remained only a little. The impossibility implies that they did not know that they had remained a little, although the plain sense of their answer implies that they knew they had remained a short time. So the reconciliation between the apparent implication of their answer and the implication of the rebuttal against them lies only in the difference of the relation regarding the shortness of the period of stay, when it is related to what is considered in it. When it is related to their doubt about the impossibility of resurrection, it was long, and resurrection occurred after it, so this is an error on their part; and when it is related to what awaits them of the duration of punishment, it was a short period, and this is a warning to them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 23, verse 115:

﴿Did you then suppose that We created you without purpose, and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾

This is part of the statement reported in it, ﴿He said, "How long did you remain on the earth?"﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 112], and it is consequent upon what precedes it. The interrogation concerning their supposition that creation was for the sake of purposelessness is framed to demonstrate the falsity of what they claimed, namely their denial of resurrection (ba'th). The interrogation is one of affirmation and reproach, because the necessary consequence of their denial of resurrection is that the creation of people would involve purposelessness (ʿabath). They are therefore treated as those who held that supposition, and they are affirmed and reproached, taking them to account for the necessary implication of their belief. The particle of restriction (adat al-hasr) is introduced after (hasiba, "he supposed"), which makes the verb govern only one object, namely the verbal noun extracted from (anna ma khalaqnakum, "that We created you").

صفحة ١٣٤
The implied meaning is: "Did you suppose that Our creating you was for the sake of purposelessness?" This is because verbs of supposition and knowledge (af'al al-zann wa al-'ilm) generally govern two objects, since the underlying structure of their two objects is a subject and predicate, that is, a noun of entity and a noun of attribute. Their need for a second object is therefore like the subject's need for a predicate, lest the benefit be lost in a subject left without its predicate. On this basis they differ from the rest of the transitive verbs, which require two objects, because their meaning does not attach to entities. Thus your saying "I supposed Zayd standing" really means, in fact, "I supposed the standing of Zayd," so its object is the verbal noun, and it ought to be a predicate attached to a pronoun referring to its subject. As al-Radi said: that is, the Arabs used them with two objects out of dislike of making the verbal noun an object of the verb directly, as though they avoided confusion between the direct object and the absolute object (al-maf'ul al-mutlaq). This is like how they used verbs of being (af'al al-kawn) with an entity as subject, then after the entity they placed the name of its attribute, and did not at first bring the name of the attribute immediately. Accordingly, when they placed after them the particle of the verbal noun, they were satisfied with it in place of the two objects. It is not heard from them that they governed a clear verbal noun with them. When the object of verbs of supposition is a noun of meaning, namely a clear verbal noun or one formed by the particle, and it omits the benefit, it suffices with the verbal noun, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, I supposed that I would encounter my reckoning﴾ [al-Haqqah: 20].

Since (annama) is composed of (anna), with its hamza open, and the restrictive (ma), its placement after the verb of reckoning is equivalent to the placement of a verbal noun. Were it not for (anna), the sentence would be: "Did you suppose us creating you purposelessly?"

(ʿAbathan) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun of the Majesty, interpreted as an active participle. Ab-ʿabath (purposelessness) is an action that has no benefit in it. Whenever the benefit diminishes, it takes the ruling of nonexistence. So if the creation of humankind in this life were not followed by the requital of doers for their deeds, then its Creator would have brought about in His act something devoid of benefit, and there would be in it a share of purposelessness.

The explanation of its being purposeless is this: if creation were brought into being, the one who does good were to do good and the one who does evil were to do evil, and each were not to receive his recompense, that would be a waste of the rights of the one who does good and a disregard of the corruption that the evildoer had brought about, and that would be an imposition of purposelessness. The meaning of a circumstantial state does not require that its governing element be inseparable from its signified meaning; it suffices that its meaning occurs in some of the states of its governing element.

صفحة ١٣٥
As for His saying, ﴿and that you would not be returned to Us﴾, they supposed that truly, without any reinterpretation, and this is part of the completion of the denial.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read (turjaʿun) with a dammah on the ta' and a fathah on the jim, meaning that God returns them by compulsion. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with a fathah on the ta' and a kasrah on the jim, meaning they return willingly or unwillingly.

﴿So exalted is Allah, the True King; there is no deity except Him, Lord of the Noble Throne.﴾ Following what was previously explained of the proofs of divine unity (al-wahdaniyya), power, and wisdom, it becomes evident that Allah is the King in whose attribution of kingship there is no admixture of the meaning of kingship (as it is found in creatures). His kingship is the complete kingship in its reality, comprehensive in its effectiveness.

The definite article in "al-Malik" is for the genus.

Al-Haqq is that which is opposed to falsehood (al-batil). The implication of this attribute is that the kingship of others is false, meaning that there is in it an admixture of falsehood. This is not from the standpoint of oppression and injustice, since there may exist a kingship without oppression or injustice, such as the kingship of the prophets, the rightly-guided caliphs, and the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) among the caliphs and commanders. Rather, it is from the standpoint that it is a kingship that does not fully realize the reality of ownership. Every person to whom kingship is ascribed, other than Allah Most High, is an owner from one aspect and owned from another, because of the deficiency and need within him. He is owned by what he requires in order to rectify his deficiency to the extent of his need, and by seeking help from others to remedy his need. That is a false kingship, because it is a claim to an incomplete kingship.

The phrase "Ta'ala" may be a statement whose purpose is to remind and to draw an inference from the preceding proofs that clarify the meaning of His exaltedness. It may also be an expression of praise for Him through loftiness.

Al-ta'ali is an intensive form of loftiness (al-'uluww). It is followed by what serves as evidence for it, namely His being singular in divinity, which is an essential attribute, and that He is the owner of the greatest of created things, namely the Throne. This is a proof of the greatness of His power.

[p. 136]

Al-Karim, in the genitive case, is an adjective of the Throne. The nobility of a genus (karam al-jins) is that it fully possesses the virtues of its kind, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, there has been delivered to me a noble letter﴾ (Qur'an 27:29), in Surat al-Naml.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 23, verse 117:

﴿And whoever calls upon another god along with Allah, for which he has no proof, then his account is only with his Lord. Indeed, the disbelievers will not succeed.﴾

When the greatest thing Allah called to was His Oneness (tawhid), and the root of the misguidance of the polytheists was their associating partners with Him, the description of Allah with supreme exaltedness and vast power was followed by an explanation that the reckoning which occurs after the Resurrection will befall those who called upon other deities along with Allah, a claim for which they have no excuse, because it is devoid of proof (burhan), that is, evidence. This is because they did not affirm for Allah complete sovereignty when they associated other deities with Him, and they did not affirm what necessitates for Him the great disposal of affairs when they associated with Him the disposal of deities. So His saying, ﴿for which he has no proof﴾, is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to ﴿whoever calls upon another god along with Allah﴾, and it is a necessary circumstance (hal lazimah), because calling upon a deity along with Allah can never be devoid of proof. A parallel to this circumstance is His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And who is more astray than one who follows his desire without guidance from Allah?﴾ [al-Qasas: 50].

The restriction (qasr) in His saying ﴿then his account is only with his Lord﴾ is a true restriction (qasr haqiqi). In it is the affirmation of the reckoning, and that it belongs to Allah alone, in rebuking them and threatening them.

It is also possible that the restriction is relative (qasr idafi), reassuring the Prophet ﷺ that Allah will not hold him to account for their persistence in disbelief, as in His saying: ﴿Your duty is only to convey the message﴾ [al-Shura: 48], and His saying: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief that they will not be believers﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 3]. This is more fitting with His saying: ﴿And say: My Lord, forgive and have mercy﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 118].

This is indicated by its concluding with the clause ﴿Indeed, the disbelievers will not succeed.﴾ In it is a kind of returning the end to the beginning (radd al-'ajuz 'ala al-sadr), since the surah opened with ﴿Certainly the believers have succeeded﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1] and closed with (﴿Indeed, the disbelievers will not succeed﴾), which is the negation of success for the disbelievers, the opposite of the believers.

[Page 137]

This is conjoined to the sentence "And whoever calls upon another god along with Allah..." (al-Mu'minun 23:117) and so on, in view of His saying: ﴿Indeed, his reckoning is with his Lord﴾ (al-Mu'minun 23:117). The purpose of the sentence is to address the Prophet (ﷺ) and command him to call upon his Lord for forgiveness and mercy. The omission of the object of "forgive" and "have mercy" entrusts to Allah the determination of who is forgiven and who is shown mercy, and the intended meaning is: whoever among the believers they may be. It is also permissible that the meaning be: "Forgive me and have mercy on me," as indicated by the context. His command to supplicate with this implies a promise that the supplication will be answered.

This statement signals the end of the surah, and so it is among the excellences of the conclusion (bara'at al-maqta').

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

Surat al-Nur

This surah has been called "Surat al-Nur" (the Chapter of Light) since the time of the Prophet (ﷺ). It is narrated from Mujahid that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Teach your women Surat al-Nur." I have not found its chain of transmission (isnad). And from Harithah ibn Mudarrib: "Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) wrote to us: 'Learn Surat al-Nisa', Surat al-Ahzab and Surat al-Nur.'" This is its name in the codices (mushafs), in the books of tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis) and in the Sunnah (the prophetic tradition), and no other name for it is known. The reason for the name is that it contains the verse ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth﴾ (al-Nur 24:35).

It is Medinan by the consensus of the scholars, and no dissent on this is known. In some copies of al-Qurtubi's tafsir, at his commentary on the saying of the Exalted: ﴿O you who believe, let those whom your right hands possess ask your permission﴾ (al-Nur 24:58) and so on, in the fourth issue, the phrase appears "and it is Meccan" (referring to the verse). Al-Khafaji, in his glosses on al-Baydawi's tafsir, attributed to al-Qurtubi that this verse is Meccan, and al-Alusi followed him. Yet the reason for its revelation which al-Qurtubi mentions is explicit that it was revealed in Medina. How could that be, when al-Qurtubi said at the beginning of this surah: "It is Medinan by consensus"? Perhaps an alteration crept into the copies of al-Qurtubi's tafsir, and the correct wording is "and it is muhkam" (i.e., not abrogated in its ruling). This phrase occurs in the tafsir of Ibn 'Atiyyah, who said: "And it is muhkam; Ibn 'Abbas said: 'People have abandoned it.'" (Muhkam: a ruling not abrogated; naskh, abrogation, is its opposite.)

It will come that the reason for the revelation of the saying of the Exalted: ﴿The fornicator marries none but a fornicatress or an idolatress﴾ (al-Nur 24:3) and so on, is the case of Marthad ibn Abi Marthad with 'Anaq. Marthad ibn Abi Marthad was martyred in Safar of the third year after the Hijrah, in the expedition of al-Raji'. Therefore the opening verses of this surah were revealed before the third year. The more likely view is that they were revealed at the end of the first year or the beginning of the second year, during the days when the Muslims were migrating one after another, and the polytheists had made them like captives.

[Page 140]

Among its verses are the verses of the story of the slander (al-ifk), which were revealed right after the expedition of Banu al-Mustaliq of Khuza'ah. The more correct view is that the expedition of Banu al-Mustaliq took place in the fourth year, for it was before the Battle of the Trench.

Among its verses is ﴿And those who accuse their wives, and have no witnesses except themselves﴾ (al-Nur 24:6) and so on. It was revealed in Sha'ban of the ninth year, after the Battle of Tabuk. Thus these verses are among what was revealed after the revelation of the opening verses of this surah. This indicates that this surah was revealed in parts, scattered over a long period, and some of its verses were joined to others.

This surah is counted as the hundredth in the order of the revelation of the surahs of the Qur'an according to Jabir ibn Zayd, from Ibn 'Abbas. He said: it was revealed after the surah "When the help of Allah comes" (al-Nasr) and before Surat al-Hajj, that is, according to those who hold that Surat al-Hajj is Medinan.

Its verses number sixty-two according to the count of Medina and Mecca, and sixty-four according to the count of the rest.

The Purposes of This Surah

It contains many of the rulings concerning the association of men with women, and the etiquette of mixing and visiting.

The first matter for which it was revealed was the case of marrying a woman known for fornication, and this is introduced by a statement of the hadd punishment for fornication.

It also includes the punishment of those who accuse chaste women (of fornication), and the ruling on li'an (mutual oath-cursing between spouses).

It addresses the innocence of 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) from what the hypocrites spread against her, the punishment of them, and of those who joined them in talking about it.

It warns against loving the spreading of indecency among the believing men and women.

It commands forgiving harm, with an allusion to the case of Mistah ibn Uthathah.

It contains rulings on seeking permission to enter people's inhabited houses and entering uninhabited houses.

[Page 141]

It contains the etiquette of the Muslim men and women in their dealings,

and the spreading of greeting (salam).

It encourages the marriage of slaves and female slaves.

It encourages their emancipation by contract (mukatabah), that is, freeing them in exchange for a payment they make to their owners.

It forbids prostitution (bigha'), which was widespread in the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic era).

It commands chastity.

It condemns the conditions of the hypocrites and alludes to the evil of their inner intentions toward the Prophet (ﷺ).

It warns against falling into the snares of Satan.

It sets forth the parable of the guidance of faith and the misguidance of disbelief.

It honors the houses of worship and those who devote themselves to them.

Interwoven with all this is a description of the greatness of Allah, the wonders of His creation, and the blessings He bestows upon people.

This is followed by a description of what Allah has prepared for the believers, and that Allah knows what every person conceals, and that the return is to Him and the recompense is in His hand.
